plaquettes in the plane $\{t_1,t_2\}$, starting from $0$ at $t_2=0$, and
then from the plaquettes in the planes $\{t_1,t_3\}$. The plaquettes in the
planes $\{t_1,t_2\}$ with $t_3>0$ then satisfy $d\alpha^0=\theta$ by
closedness, by induction on $t_3$. Each value is a signed sum of at most
$l$, respectively $2l$, angles, so $|\alpha^0|\le2l\rho_s$.

For $k=1$ put $\alpha=\alpha^0$, so $M_1=\max|\alpha|\le2l\rho_s$. For
$k\ge2$, $\alpha$ is already defined on the links of $\Gamma_k$, with
$|\alpha|\le M_{k-1}$, and $\omega=\alpha-\alpha^0$ is closed there.
Hence $\omega=d\lambda$ for a function $\lambda$ on the vertices of
$\Gamma_k$, and $|\lambda(x)-\lambda(y)|\le\lVert\omega\rVert_\infty
d_\Gamma(x,y)$, where $d_\Gamma$ is the path metric of $\Gamma_k$.

We claim $d_\Gamma\le3d_1$, where $d_1$ is the $\ell^1$ metric of the
facet. If $x$ and $y$ lie in one face of $\Gamma_k$, that face contains an
$\ell^1$ geodesic between them. If they lie in adjacent faces $\{t_i=s\}$
and $\{t_j=s'\}$, the path through the point with $t_i=s$, $t_j=s'$ and
third coordinate that of $x$ has length $d_1(x,y)$. If they lie in opposite
faces $\{t_i=0\}$ and $\{t_i=l\}$, then $d_1(x,y)\ge l$. In that case
$\Gamma_k$ contains a face adjacent to both, and the path from $x$ to that
face, across it and on to $y$ has length at most $d_1(x,y)+2l\le3d_1(x,y)$.

So $\lambda$ is $3\lVert\omega\rVert_\infty$-Lipschitz for $d_1$ on
$\Gamma_k$. The function
\[
\tilde\lambda(x)=\min_y\bigl(\lambda(y)+3\lVert\omega\rVert_\infty d_1(x,y)
\bigr)
\]
extends it to the vertices of the facet with the same constant~\cite{McS34}.
Put $\alpha=\alpha^0+d\tilde\lambda$ on the links of the facet. It agrees
with the earlier values on $\Gamma_k$, satisfies $d\alpha=\theta$ on the
facet, and has
\[
|\alpha|\le2l\rho_s+3(M_{k-1}+2l\rho_s).
\]
So $M_k\le3M_{k-1}+8l\rho_s$, which gives $M_8\le13118\,l\rho_s$.

\emph{Extension.} Let $c$ be the centre of $R$, $R_0=l/2$, $r(x)=|x-c|_\infty$
and $\varphi(x)=c+R_0(x-c)/r(x)$, the radial projection of $R\setminus\{c\}$
onto $\partial R$. Let $\hat\alpha$ and $\hat\theta=d\hat\alpha$ be the
lowest-order Whitney forms of $\alpha$ and $\theta$ on the unit cubes of
$\partial R$~\cite{Whi57}. On a unit cube with coordinates $t_1,t_2,t_3$,
$\hat\alpha=\sum_ia_i\,dt_i$, where $a_i$ is the multilinear interpolation of
the values of $\alpha$ on the four links in direction $t_i$; similarly
$\hat\theta=\sum_{i<j}\theta_{ij}\,dt_i\wedge dt_j$. These forms have
continuous tangential components across the faces of the unit cubes, satisfy
$\int_e\hat\alpha=\alpha_e$ for every boundary link, and for tangent
vectors
\[
|\hat\alpha(u)|\le\sqrt3\,M_8|u|,\qquad|\hat\theta(u,w)|\le\sqrt3\,\rho_s
|u||w| .
\]
Put $\tilde B=(r/R_0)^2\varphi^*\hat\alpha$ on $R\setminus\{c\}$. Since
$|\nabla r|=1$ almost everywhere and $|x-c|\le2r$, we have $|d\varphi(v)|\le
3R_0|v|/r$. Then
\[
d\tilde B=d\bigl(r^2/R_0^2\bigr)\wedge\varphi^*\hat\alpha+(r/R_0)^2
\varphi^*\hat\theta
\]
gives
\[
|d\tilde B(v,w)|\le\bigl(12\sqrt3\,M_8/R_0+9\sqrt3\,\rho_s\bigr)|v||w|\le
C\rho_s|v||w| ,
\]
and $|\tilde B|\le3\sqrt3\,M_8r/R_0$ is bounded.

The set $R\setminus\{c\}$ is the union of the cones from $c$ over the unit
cubes of $\partial R$. These cones are convex polytopes cut out by
hyperplanes through $c$. On each of them $\tilde B$ is smooth, and its
tangential components are continuous across them since $\varphi$ is
continuous. Put $B_e=\int_e\tilde B$ for every link $e$ of $R$. Apply
Stokes' theorem on each piece of a plaquette: the boundary terms on the
interior cuts cancel, and the point $c$ contributes nothing since $\tilde B$
is bounded. This gives $(dB)_p=\int_pd\tilde B$, so $|(dB)_p|\le C\rho_s$.
On $\partial R$, $r=R_0$ and $\varphi$ is the identity on tangent vectors,
so $B=\alpha$ on the boundary links.

\emph{Gauge.} The cochain $a-\alpha$ on the boundary links has
$(d(a-\alpha))_p\equiv\theta_p-\theta_p=0$ modulo $2\pi$ on every boundary
plaquette. So it is a flat $\U(1)$-field on the $2$-skeleton of $\partial
R$, which is simply connected, and $a-\alpha\equiv d\mu$ modulo $2\pi$ for a
function $\mu$ on the boundary vertices. Extend $\mu$ by $0$ to the inner
vertices and put $U_e=\exp((B_e+(d\mu)_e)J)$ on the inner links. On the
boundary links $B+d\mu\equiv a$, and every plaquette of $R$ has angle at
most $|(dB)_p|\le C\rho_s$.
\end{proof}

For a general $\SU(2)$-valued boundary field the curvature is not a closed
cochain, and the lift in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:boxextension} is not
available. A lift by gluing local gauges still works when $l^2\rho_s$ is
small. Identify $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ with the imaginary quaternions and write
$|X|$ for the operator norm, which is the Euclidean norm, so that
$|[X,Y]|\le2|X||Y|$, $\lVert e^X-I\rVert\le|X|$ and $\angle e^X=|X|$ for
$|X|\le\pi$. With $d(g,h)=\angle(g^{-1}h)$, the map $X\mapsto e^X$ is
$1$-Lipschitz, since its differential has singular values $1$ and
$\sin|X|/|X|$, and the principal logarithm is $2$-Lipschitz on $\{\angle
h\le\frac12\}$, a geodesically convex ball on which the inverse
differential has singular values at most $\frac12/\sin\frac12<2$. Put
\[
C_1=2,\qquad C_k=11\,C_{k-1}+24\quad(2\le k\le8),
\]
so that $C_8=85\,743\,550$, and
\[
K=42\,C_8+20,\qquad \varepsilon_0=\frac1{100\,C_8^2}.
\]

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:nonabelianfilling}
Let the boundary links $\eta$ of $R$ take values in $\SU(2)$, with
$\angle\eta_p\le\rho_s$ for every boundary plaquette and $l^2\rho_s\le
\varepsilon_0$. Then the inner links can be chosen so that $\angle U_p\le
K\rho_s$ for every plaquette of $R$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For a vertex gauge $g$ write $\eta^g_{xy}=g_x\eta_{xy}g_y^{-1}$. A product
of conjugates of $m$ elements of angle at most $\rho_s$ has angle at most
$m\rho_s$, since $d$ is bi-invariant.

\emph{One facet.} On a facet with coordinates $t_1,t_2,t_3$ let $P_x$ be
the path from the corner to $x$ that moves first in direction $t_1$, then
$t_2$, then $t_3$, and put $g^0_x=\eta(P_x)$, the ordered product of the links along
$P_x$. Then $\eta^{g^0}_{xy}$ is the holonomy of the loop $P_x\,(xy)\,
P_y^{-1}$. For a link in
direction $t_3$ this loop retraces itself. For a link in direction $t_2$ at
height $t_3=c$ it bounds $c$ plaquettes of the planes $\{t_2,t_3\}$, and
for a link in direction $t_1$ at $(t_2,t_3)=(b,c)$ it bounds $b$
plaquettes of a plane $\{t_1,t_2\}$ and $c$ of a plane $\{t_1,t_3\}$. So
the holonomy is a product of conjugates of at most $2l$ plaquette
holonomies, and every link of the facet has $\angle\eta^{g^0}_e\le
2l\rho_s$.

\emph{Gluing.} Take the facets in the order of the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:boxextension}, with the same sets $\Gamma_k$; there
$d_\Gamma\le3d_1$. Two vertices of $\Gamma_k$ joined by a link of the
facet lie in a common face of $\Gamma_k$, since $l\ge2$, so that link
lies in $\Gamma_k$. We construct a gauge $g$ on the boundary vertices with
$\angle\eta^g_e\le M_k=C_kl\rho_s$ on the links of the first $k$ facets.
For $k=1$ take $g=g^0$. For $k\ge2$, let $g^0$ be the gauge of the $k$-th
facet and $t_x=g_x(g^0_x)^{-1}$ for $x\in\Gamma_k$. For a link $xy$ of
$\Gamma_k$, $\eta^g_{xy}=t_x\eta^{g^0}_{xy}t_y^{-1}$, so
\[
d(t_x,t_y)=\angle\bigl(t_x^{-1}t_y\bigr)\le\angle\eta^g_{xy}+\angle
\eta^{g^0}_{xy}\le M_{k-1}+2l\rho_s ,
\]
and $t$ is $3(M_{k-1}+2l\rho_s)$-Lipschitz for $d_1$ on $\Gamma_k$. Fix
$x_0\in\Gamma_k$ and put $h_x=t_{x_0}^{-1}t_x$. The facet has $d_1$-diameter
$3l$, so
\[
\angle h_x\le9l(M_{k-1}+2l\rho_s)=9(C_{k-1}+2)\,l^2\rho_s\le9(C_8+2)
\varepsilon_0<\tfrac12 ,
\]
and $a_x=\log h_x$ is $L$-Lipschitz for $d_1$, with
$L=6(M_{k-1}+2l\rho_s)$. Extend each of the three real coordinates of $a$
to the vertices of the facet by the formula of McShane~\cite{McS34}, as in
the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:boxextension}; the extension $\tilde a$ is
$\sqrt3L$-Lipschitz. Put $g_x=t_{x_0}e^{\tilde a_x}g^0_x$ on the facet; on
$\Gamma_k$ this is the old value. For a link $xy$ of the facet,
$\eta^g_{xy}=\tilde t_x\eta^{g^0}_{xy}\tilde t_y^{-1}$ with $\tilde t_x=
t_{x_0}e^{\tilde a_x}$, so
\[
\begin{split}
\angle\eta^g_{xy}&\le d(\tilde t_x,\tilde t_y)+2l\rho_s\le\sqrt3L+2l\rho_s\\
&=6\sqrt3\,M_{k-1}+(12\sqrt3+2)\,l\rho_s\le M_k .
\end{split}
\]
After the eighth facet, $\angle\eta^g_e\le M=C_8l\rho_s$ on every boundary
link.

\emph{Potential.} Since $M\le C_8\varepsilon_0/l<\frac12$, the logarithms
$A_e=\log\eta^g_e$ are defined, with $|A_e|\le M$ and $A_{-e}=-A_e$. Let
$(dA)_p$ be the signed sum of $A$ over the four links of a boundary
plaquette. For $X_1,\dots,X_q\in\mathfrak{su}(2)$,
\[
\Bigl\lVert e^{X_1}\cdots e^{X_q}-I-\sum_iX_i\Bigr\rVert\le\tfrac12\Bigl(
\sum_i|X_i|\Bigr)^2 ,
\]
by induction on $q$ from $e^Xe^Y-I-X-Y=(e^X-I-X)+(e^Y-I-Y)+(e^X-I)(e^Y-I)$
and $\lVert e^X-I-X\rVert\le|X|^2/2$. Applied to the four links of $p$, and
since $\lVert\eta^g_p-I\rVert=2\sin(\angle\eta_p/2)\le\rho_s$, this gives
\[
|(dA)_p|\le\sigma=\rho_s+8M^2 .
\]
Let $\hat A$ be the lowest-order Whitney form of $A$ on the unit cubes of
$\partial R$, as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:boxextension}, now with
values in $\mathfrak{su}(2)$. Its coefficients are interpolations of values
of $A$, and those of $d\hat A$ are interpolations of values of $dA$, so
\[
|\hat A(u)|\le\sqrt3\,M|u|,\qquad|d\hat A(u,w)|\le\sqrt3\,\sigma|u||w| .
\]
With $r$, $R_0$ and $\varphi$ as there, put $\tilde B=(r/R_0)^2\varphi^*
\hat A$ on $R\setminus\{c\}$ and $\tilde B(c)=0$. The same computation
gives
\[
|\tilde B(v)|\le3\sqrt3\,M\frac r{R_0}|v|,\qquad|d\tilde B(v,w)|\le\kappa_1
|v||w|,
\]
where $\kappa_1=12\sqrt3\,M/R_0+9\sqrt3\,\sigma$.
On each cone from $c$ over a unit cube of $\partial R$, $\tilde B$ is
smooth away from $c$, and its tangential components are continuous across
the cones.

\emph{Transport.} For a link $e$ of $R$, parametrised by $s\in[0,1]$, let
$V_e=T(1)$, where $T'=T\,\tilde B(\dot e)$ and $T(0)=I$; the coefficient is
bounded and piecewise smooth, and $V$ composes along paths in the order of
the links. For a closed path $\gamma$ of length $\ell$,
\[
T(1)-I-\int_\gamma\tilde B=\int_0^1(T-I)\,\tilde B(\dot\gamma)\,ds,
\]
and $\lVert T(s)-I\rVert\le\int_0^s|\tilde B(\dot\gamma)|$,
so the holonomy $V_\gamma$ satisfies $\lVert V_\gamma-I\rVert\le|\int_\gamma
\tilde B|+\frac12(\int_\gamma|\tilde B|)^2$. Let $p$ be a plaquette of $R$
and divide it into $N^2$ squares $q$ of side $h=1/N$. Its holonomy is a
product of conjugates of the holonomies of the boundaries of the squares,
since every inner edge of the subdivision is traversed once in each
direction. For each square, Stokes' theorem on the finitely many convex
polygons in which the cones cut $q$ gives $\int_{\partial q}\tilde B=
\int_qd\tilde B$: the integrals over the interior cuts cancel because the
tangential components agree, and if $c\in q$ a disc of radius $\delta$
around $c$ contributes $O(\delta^2)$, since $|\tilde B|\le3\sqrt3\,Mr/R_0$.
Hence
\[
\lVert V_{\partial q}-I\rVert\le\kappa_1h^2+\tfrac12\bigl(4h\cdot3\sqrt3\,M
\bigr)^2=\kappa h^2,
\]
with $\kappa=\kappa_1+216M^2$.
Since $2\arcsin(x/2)\le x(1+x^2)$ for $0\le x\le1$, summing over the
squares gives $\angle V_p\le\kappa(1+\kappa^2N^{-4})$, and letting
$N\to\infty$, $\angle V_p\le\kappa$. Now $M/R_0=2C_8\rho_s$ and
$M^2=C_8^2l^2\rho_s^2\le\rho_s/100$, so
\[
\begin{split}
\kappa&\le\bigl(24\sqrt3\,C_8+9\sqrt3\bigr)\rho_s+\bigl(72\sqrt3+216\bigr)M^2\\
&<(42\,C_8+20)\,\rho_s=K\rho_s .
\end{split}
\]

\emph{Boundary values.} On $\partial R$, $r=R_0$ and $\varphi$ is the
identity on tangent vectors, and along a boundary link $e$ the tangential
coefficient of $\hat A$ is the constant $A_e$. So $V_e=e^{A_e}=\eta^g_e$.
Extend $g$ by $I$ to the inner vertices and put $U_{xy}=g_x^{-1}V_{xy}g_y$.
Then $U=\eta$ on the boundary links, and $U_p$ is conjugate to $V_p$, so
$\angle U_p\le K\rho_s$ for every plaquette of $R$.
\end{proof}

The boundary fields of Lemma~\ref{lem:nonabelianfilling} with strict
inequalities form an open set of positive Haar measure that contains the
identity field; unlike those of Lemma~\ref{lem:boxextension}, they are not
a null set. The constants are far from optimal.

For $0<\varepsilon\le1$ let $E_\varepsilon$ be the event that at least
$\varepsilon l^4$ of the $l^4$ unit cubes $x+[0,1]^4$, $x\in\{0,\dots,
l-1\}^4$, of $R$ contain a bad plaquette.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:conddensity}
Let $\beta_W\ge1$ and $0<\rho\le1$. Suppose that no boundary plaquette of
$R$ is bad under $\eta$, and that the inner links can be chosen so that
every inner plaquette has angle at most $\kappa$. Then
\[
\begin{split}
-\log\nu_\eta(E_\varepsilon)\ge{}&\frac{\beta_W\rho^2\varepsilon}{16}\,l^4\\
&-6(l+1)^4\bigl(\log\beta_W+C_0+\tfrac12+\beta_W\kappa^2\bigr),
\end{split}
\]
with $C_0$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem:wilsonZ}. In particular, if the boundary
links lie in $T$ with angle at most $\rho_s<\pi/3$ on every boundary
plaquette and $\rho\ge\sqrt2\,\rho_s$, the bound holds with $\kappa=C\rho_s$
and the constant $C$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:boxextension}. If the boundary
links lie in $\SU(2)$ with angle at most $\rho_s$ on every boundary
plaquette, $l^2\rho_s\le\varepsilon_0$ and $\rho\ge\sqrt2\,\rho_s$, it
holds with $\kappa=K\rho_s$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
On $E_\varepsilon$ the bad plaquettes are inner, and each lies in at most
four of the unit cubes. So there are at least $\varepsilon l^4/4$ of them,
each with $s_p>\rho^2/4$, and $\sum_{P^\circ}s_p\ge\rho^2\varepsilon l^4
/16$. Hence the unnormalised weight of $E_\varepsilon$ is at most $\exp(
-\beta_W\rho^2\varepsilon l^4/16)$.

For the normalisation let $\bar U$ be the inner links of the hypothesis,
$t=(4\sqrt{\beta_W})^{-1}$, and consider the inner links $U_e=\bar U_eh_e$
with $\angle h_e\le t$. The angle of $g^{-1}h$ is a bi-invariant distance,
so every inner plaquette has $\angle U_p\le\kappa+4t$ and
\[
s_p\le\tfrac12(\kappa+4t)^2\le\kappa^2+16t^2=\kappa^2+\beta_W^{-1} .
\]
Each $h_e$ has probability at least $8t^3/(3\pi^3)=(24\pi^3\beta_W^{3/2}
)^{-1}$, as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:wilsonZ}. There are $n_P\le6l^2
(l+1)^2$ inner plaquettes and $n_L\le4l(l+1)^3$ inner links, so
\[
Z_\eta\ge\exp\bigl(-n_P(\beta_W\kappa^2+1)\bigr)\bigl(24\pi^3\beta_W^{3/2}
\bigr)^{-n_L}.
\]
Since $C_0=\frac12+\frac23\log(24\pi^3)$, $n_P+n_L\log(24\pi^3\beta_W^{3/2}
)\le6(l+1)^4(\log\beta_W+C_0+\frac12)$, which gives the bound. For the last
assertion, a boundary plaquette has $\delta(U_p,I)\le\sqrt2\,\angle U_p\le
\sqrt2\,\rho_s\le\rho$, so it is not bad, and Lemma~\ref{lem:boxextension}
or Lemma~\ref{lem:nonabelianfilling} gives the inner links.
\end{proof}

So in a box whose boundary is calm at a level $\rho_s$ small compared with
$\rho\sqrt\varepsilon/C$ and $T$-valued, or small compared with
$\rho\sqrt\varepsilon/K$ and $\SU(2)$-valued with $l^2\rho_s\le
\varepsilon_0$, the fraction of bad cubes
exceeds $\varepsilon$ only with probability exponentially small in the
volume once $\beta_W\rho^2\varepsilon$ is large compared with $\log
\beta_W$, uniformly over such exteriors and over $l$. The estimate is
conditional, unlike Theorem~\ref{thm:defects}.

\begin{remark}\label{rem:boxnonabelian}
The exteriors with boundary links in $T$ form a null set for $\mu_L$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:nonabelianfilling} removes the torus at the price of the
smallness $l^2\rho_s\le\varepsilon_0$. In the continuum the corresponding
condition is that of Uhlenbeck's theorem~\cite{Uhl82}, which gives a
Coulomb gauge on a ball when the curvature is small in $L^{n/2}$; on
$3$-dimensional pieces of $\partial R$ of side comparable to $l$ and for
curvature of size $\rho_s$ this norm is of order $l^2\rho_s$. The lemma
replaces the Coulomb gauge by the gluing of the facet gauges. With
$\rho_s$ of the order of the level $\rho(\beta_W)$ of
Corollary~\ref{cor:defectscales}, $\rho_s=c_0(\log\beta_W/\beta_W)^{1/2}$,
it applies for
\[
l\le(\varepsilon_0/c_0)^{1/2}\,(\beta_W/\log\beta_W)^{1/4},
\]
the scale $a_{k_*}$ of Corollary~\ref{cor:defectscales} up to a constant
factor. Along the tuning $\beta_W\sim b\log(1/a)$ the physical side $al$
then tends to $0$, so the lemma does not reach cubes of a fixed physical
size; this is a limitation of the argument, not a proof that such fillings
fail. Moreover Proposition~\ref{prop:conddensity} bounds the fraction of
bad cubes under one exterior and does not compare the laws under two
exteriors, so it gives no contraction coefficient.
\end{remark}

The calm boundary is needed only for the small-curvature filling. If the
boundary layer is paid for instead of filled, every condition on the
exterior disappears, at the price of a surface term that is small against
the volume on large boxes.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:anyexterior}
Let $\beta_W\ge1$, $0<\rho\le1$ and $0<\varepsilon\le1$ with $\varepsilon
l\ge16$. For every boundary field $\eta$,
\[
-\log\nu_\eta(E_\varepsilon)\ge l^4\Bigl(\frac{\beta_W\rho^2\varepsilon}{32}
-6\log\beta_W-C_1-\frac{48\beta_W}{l}\Bigr),
\]
with $C_1=3+4\log(24\pi^3)<31$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
A unit cube $x+[0,1]^4$ with $x\in\{1,\dots,l-2\}^4$ does not meet
$\partial R$, so all its plaquettes are inner; the other $l^4-(l-2)^4\le8l^3
\le\varepsilon l^4/2$ unit cubes meet it. On $E_\varepsilon$ at least
$\varepsilon l^4/2$ cubes of the first kind contain a bad plaquette, which is
inner, and a plaquette lies in at most four unit cubes. So at least
$\varepsilon l^4/8$ inner plaquettes are bad, $\sum_{P^\circ}s_p\ge\rho^2
\varepsilon l^4/32$, and the unnormalised weight of $E_\varepsilon$ is at
most $\exp(-\beta_W\rho^2\varepsilon l^4/32)$.

For the normalisation take inner links $U_e=h_e$ with $\angle h_e\le t=(4
\sqrt{\beta_W})^{-1}$. An inner plaquette whose four links are inner has
$\angle U_p\le4t$ and $s_p\le(2\beta_W)^{-1}$. An inner plaquette spans two
directions and has its other two coordinates in $\{1,\dots,l-1\}$; it
contains a boundary link exactly when its cell in the plane of the two
spanned directions meets the boundary of $[0,l]^2$, which happens for
$4(l-1)$ of the $l^2$ cells. So $24(l-1)^3\le24l^3$ inner plaquettes contain
a boundary link, and on them $s_p\le2$. There are $n_P=6l^2(l-1)^2\le6l^4$
inner plaquettes and $n_L=4l(l-1)^3\le4l^4$ inner links, so, as in the proof
of Proposition~\ref{prop:conddensity},
\[
Z_\eta\ge\exp\bigl(-48\beta_Wl^3-3l^4\bigr)\bigl(24\pi^3\beta_W^{3/2}
\bigr)^{-4l^4}.
\]
Dividing gives the bound, and $24\pi^3<e^7$ gives $C_1<31$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:anyexterior}
Let $\beta_W\ge e^{44}$, $l\ge6144\beta_W^{3/4}$ and $\rho=\varepsilon=
\beta_W^{-1/4}$. Then $\nu_\eta(E_\varepsilon)\le\exp(-\beta_W^{1/4}l^4/64)$
for every boundary field $\eta$. In particular, along $\beta_W\sim b\log
(1/a)$ with $l=\lceil r/a\rceil$ and fixed $r,b>0$, on cubes of fixed
physical side $r$ the fraction of unit cubes that contain a plaquette with
$\delta(U_p,I)>\beta_W^{-1/4}$ is at most $\beta_W^{-1/4}$ with conditional
probability tending to one, uniformly over all exteriors.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Here $\varepsilon l\ge6144\beta_W^{1/2}\ge16$ and $\rho\le1$. The first term
of Proposition~\ref{prop:anyexterior} is $\beta_W^{1/4}/32$, and $48\beta_W
/l\le\beta_W^{1/4}/128$. For $x=\log\beta_W\ge44$ we have $6x+31\le e^{x/4}
/128$: at $x=44$ the left side is $295$ and the right side exceeds $467$, and
$x/4-\log(6x+31)$ increases for $x\ge44$. So $6\log\beta_W+C_1\le\beta_W
^{1/4}/128$ and the bracket is at least $\beta_W^{1/4}(\frac1{32}-\frac1{128}
-\frac1{128})=\beta_W^{1/4}/64$. Along the tuning, $\beta_W\to\infty$ and
$l/\beta_W^{3/4}\to\infty$, so the hypotheses hold for small $a$.
\end{proof}

Like Proposition~\ref{prop:conddensity}, Corollary~\ref{cor:anyexterior}
bounds the bad cubes under one exterior and does not compare the laws under
two, so it gives no contraction coefficient. The bad cubes are rare on cubes
of fixed physical size for every exterior, and the conditional estimate in
(D) remains open.

The same count locates the windows on which the fibre estimates of
Sec.~\ref{ssec:smallfibres} apply. Let the side of the torus be even, let
$B(y)=2y+\{0,1\}^4$ be the blocks of Definition~\ref{def:blockgauge}, and let
$l$ be even, so that $R$ is a union of blocks.

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:localcalm}
Let $G=\SU(2)$, $\beta_W\ge1$, let $W_0$ be a set of $m$ blocks, $0<K\le
10^{-8}$, $\rho=K/(3072m)$, and $0<\varepsilon\le1$ with $\varepsilon l\ge16$.
For every boundary field $\eta$ of $R$, with $\nu_\eta$-probability at least
\[
1-\exp\Bigl(-l^4\Bigl(\frac{\beta_W\rho^2\varepsilon}{32}-6\log\beta_W
-31-\frac{48\beta_W}l\Bigr)\Bigr),
\]
all but fewer than $256m\varepsilon l^4$ of the translates $W=y_0+W_0$ whose
blocks of $W^+$ lie in $[1,l-1]^4$ have the following property: in the tree
gauge the exterior of $W$ has a completion that satisfies the hypothesis of
Corollary~\ref{cor:calmexterior}, namely the field itself.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Outside $E_\varepsilon$, which has the stated probability by
Proposition~\ref{prop:anyexterior}, fewer than $\varepsilon l^4$ unit cubes of
$R$ contain a bad plaquette. A plaquette with a vertex in a block of $W^+$
has all its vertices in $R$ and lies in a unit cube $x+[0,1]^4$ of $R$; if it
is bad, that cube contains a bad plaquette. The vertex lies in a block
$B(y')$ with $y'_i\in\{\lfloor x_i/2\rfloor,\lfloor(x_i+1)/2\rfloor\}$, and
$y'\in\{y\}^+$ for some $y\in W$, so $y_i$ takes at most four values and $y$
lies in a set of at most $256$ blocks determined by $x$; then $y_0\in y-W_0$
takes at most $256m$ values. Hence fewer than $256m\varepsilon l^4$
translates have a bad plaquette with a vertex in a block of $W^+$. At every
other translate these plaquettes have $\delta(U_p,I)\le\rho$. The number
$n_P$ of plaquettes that contain a link of $A_W$ is at most $384m$, so $\rho
\le K/(8n_P)=\kappa/(2\sqrt{n_P})$ with $\kappa=K/(4\sqrt{n_P})$. A gauge
transformation conjugates every plaquette holonomy and leaves $\delta(U_p,
I)$ unchanged, so the field in the tree gauge is a completion of its own
exterior with this property.
\end{proof}

So under every exterior of a box, the windows of a fixed number of blocks
on which Corollary~\ref{cor:calmexterior} applies fill all but at most
$256m\varepsilon l^4$ of the positions, a fraction of about $4096m\varepsilon$. The bound is useful only when
$\beta_W\rho^2\varepsilon$ is large, that is for windows of bounded size,
and the next proposition shows that this restriction cannot be removed.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:calmrare}
Let $G=\SU(2)$, $\beta_W\ge1$ and $0<\rho'\le1$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item Conditionally on all links but one link of a plaquette $p_0$, the
event $\delta(U_{p_0},I)\le\rho'$ has probability at most $14(\beta_W
\rho'^2)^{3/2}$ under the Wilson measure.
\item Let $W$ be a set of blocks with $W^+\ne W$, $0<K\le10^{-8}$ and
$\kappa=K/(4\sqrt{n_P})$. Under the Wilson measure in the tree gauge, the
exterior of $W$ has a completion as in Corollary~\ref{cor:calmexterior} with
probability at most $7\cdot10^{-32}\beta_W^{3/2}|W|^{-3}$, and
$\varepsilon''_W(\kappa^2/2,\beta_W/4)<1$ only if $\beta_W>10^{24}|W|^2$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
(i) As in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:manydefects}, the holonomy of
$p_0$ has a conditional density proportional to $e^{\kappa'h\cdot u}$ with
$0\le\kappa'\le6\beta_W$ and $|h|=1$, and the probability of a cap about $I$
is largest at $h=I$, $\kappa'=6\beta_W$. Since $\delta(u,I)=2\sqrt2\sin(
\angle u/2)$ and $\sin x\ge2x/\pi$ on $[0,\frac\pi2]$, the event forces
$\angle U_{p_0}\le\theta=\pi\rho'/(2\sqrt2)$. With $\cos t-1\ge-t^2/2$ and
$\sin t\ge2t/\pi$ on $[0,\frac\pi2]$,
\begin{multline*}
\int_0^\pi e^{6\beta_W(\cos t-1)}\sin^2t\,dt\\
\ge\frac4{\pi^2}\int_0^{\pi/2}e^{-3\beta_Wt^2}t^2\,dt\ge\frac{4\cdot0.44}
{\pi^2(3\beta_W)^{3/2}},
\end{multline*}
because the integral of $e^{-s^2}s^2$ over $[0,\pi\sqrt3/2]$ exceeds $0.44$.
The integral of $e^{6\beta_W(\cos t-1)}\sin^2t$ over $[0,\theta]$ is at
most $\theta^3/3$, so the ratio is at most
$9.72(\beta_W\theta^2)^{3/2}$, and $(\pi/(2\sqrt2))^3<1.371$.

(ii) Take $y'\in W^+\setminus W$ and a plaquette $p_0$ inside $B(y')$. Its
links have their base in $B(y')$, so none lies in $A_W$, and every
completion of the exterior agrees with the field on $p_0$. A completion as in
Corollary~\ref{cor:calmexterior} therefore needs $\delta(U_{p_0},I)\le
\kappa/(2\sqrt{n_P})=K/(8n_P)$. This event is gauge invariant, so its
probability is the same without gauge fixing, and by (i) it is at most
$14(\beta_WK^2/(64n_P^2))^{3/2}$. Each link of $A_W$ lies in six plaquettes
and a plaquette contains at most four of them, so $n_P\ge73.5|W|$, and
$14\cdot10^{-24}/(512\cdot73.5^3)<7\cdot10^{-32}$. Finally,
$\varepsilon''_W(\kappa^2/2,\lambda)<1$ means $\frac38\lambda\kappa^2>49|W|
\ln(3.45\cdot10^{11}n_P^6/K^6)$, and with $\lambda=\beta_W/4$, $\kappa^2=
K^2/(16n_P)$, $n_P\ge73.5|W|$ and $K\le10^{-8}$ the logarithm exceeds $162.8$,
so $\beta_W>512\cdot49\cdot73.5\cdot162.8\cdot10^{16}|W|^2/3>10^{24}|W|^2$.
\end{proof}

Along the tuning $\beta_W\sim b\log(1/a)$, a cube of fixed physical side $r$
has $|W|=(r/2a)^4$ blocks, so both bounds of (ii) fail for small $a$: on such
a cube the exterior has no calm completion with probability tending to one,
and the fibre estimates of Sec.~\ref{ssec:smallfibres} are vacuous there.
Their entropy factors are powers of $|W|$, so they are estimates for windows
of bounded size, which Corollary~\ref{cor:localcalm} places at almost every
position under every exterior. The exteriors with no calm completion and the
rare fibres of Corollary~\ref{cor:calmexterior} are thus the typical case at
the physical scale and not an exceptional one. The cube condition (D) needs
estimates on the whole cube that are uniform in $|W|$, with the windows that
are not calm split off as in Ba{\l}aban's analysis~\cite{Bal89b}, and that
remains open.

\subsection{Conditioning on a fixed large-field set}\label{ssec:fixedset}

The estimates of Sec.~\ref{ssec:largefields} are statements about the
Wilson measure on the torus. The cube condition (D) takes a supremum over
exteriors, and three facts about conditional laws hold under every
exterior; the setting is that of a Gibbs field whose potential is itself
random, the uniqueness theory of which goes back to Bassalygo and
Dobrushin~\cite{BD86}. The first bounds the excess of the action over its minimum in a
box, with no reflection positivity and no torus. The second says that
restricting a single-link law to a fixed set, however irregular, leaves its
Kantorovich response to the neighbouring links bounded by a constant times
$\beta_W$. The third turns the one-point rarity of a bad set into closeness
of any two Gibbs measures, at order of that rarity, and shows at the same
time why one-point rarity gives closeness and not decay.

\begin{lemma}[excess action]\label{lem:excess}
Let $G=\SU(2)$, let $\Lambda$ be a set of $N$ links of $\Z^4$ and fix the
links outside $\Lambda$. Let $P_\Lambda$ be the plaquettes that contain a
link of $\Lambda$, $S_\Lambda=\sum_{p\in P_\Lambda}s_p$, and $S_{\min}$ the
minimum of $S_\Lambda$ over the links of $\Lambda$. For every $E>0$, under
the Wilson measure conditioned on the links outside $\Lambda$,
\[
\Pr\bigl(S_\Lambda\ge S_{\min}+E\bigr)\le\Bigl(\frac{3\pi^3}{8r^3}\Bigr)^N
e^{-\beta_WE/2},
\]
where $r=\min\{E/(6\pi N),\pi/2\}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The plaquettes that contain no link of $\Lambda$ do not depend on the
links of $\Lambda$, so the conditional law has density $Z^{-1}e^{-\beta_W
S_\Lambda}$ with respect to the product of Haar measures on $\Lambda$. The
unnormalised mass of the event is at most $e^{-\beta_W(S_{\min}+E)}$. For
the lower bound on $Z$, let $U^*$ be a minimiser, which exists by
compactness. If a link of a plaquette $p$ moves by geodesic distance $t$,
the angle $\delta(U_p,I)\in[0,\pi]$ moves by at most $t$, by bi-invariance,
so $s_p=\frac14\delta(U_p,I)^2$ moves by at most $\frac14\,t\cdot2\pi=
\frac\pi2t$. Each link lies in six plaquettes. If every link of $\Lambda$
lies within distance $r$ of its value in $U^*$, then $S_\Lambda\le S_{\min}
+6\cdot\frac\pi2rN\le S_{\min}+E/2$. The Haar measure of a geodesic ball of
radius $r\le\pi/2$ is $\frac2\pi\int_0^r\sin^2t\,dt\ge8r^3/(3\pi^3)$, by
$\sin t\ge2t/\pi$. Hence $Z\ge(8r^3/3\pi^3)^Ne^{-\beta_W(S_{\min}+E/2)}$,
and the quotient of the two bounds is the claim.
\end{proof}

The constant depends on $N$ and $E$ alone, so excess action is rare under
every exterior, at a cost that is exponential in $N$. The minimum itself is
a function of the exterior, and the lemma says nothing about the size of
its plaquettes: it controls the fluctuation of the field about the
configuration the exterior forces, not that configuration.

\begin{lemma}[restriction to a fixed set]\label{lem:fixedset}
Let $G=\SU(2)$, let $e$ be a link and let $h\ge0$ be an integrable function
on $G$ with $\int h\,dU>0$ that does not depend on the other links. For a
configuration $\sigma$ of the other links let $\gamma^h_e(\cdot\mid\sigma)$
be the law on $G$ with density proportional to $e^{-\beta_WS}h$. If
$\sigma$ and $\sigma'$ differ only at a link $e'\ne e$, then
\[
W_1\bigl(\gamma^h_e(\cdot\mid\sigma),\gamma^h_e(\cdot\mid\sigma')\bigr)\le
\frac{\pi^2}8\,\beta_W\,\delta(\sigma_{e'},\sigma'_{e'}),
\]
and the two laws coincide unless $e$ and $e'$ lie in a common plaquette.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Only the plaquettes containing $e$ enter the law, and two distinct links of
$\Z^4$ lie in at most one common plaquette $p_0$; if there is none the
laws are equal. Otherwise move $\sigma_{e'}$ along a unit-speed geodesic
$U(t)$, $0\le t\le T=\delta(\sigma_{e'},\sigma'_{e'})$, and let $\gamma_t$
be the corresponding law. The function $t\mapsto s_{p_0}$ has $|\frac d{dt}
s_{p_0}|\le\frac\pi2$ as in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:excess}, and the
derivative $\dot s_{p_0}$ is a function of $U_e$ with oscillation at most
$\pi$. For a $1$-Lipschitz $f$ on $G$, which has oscillation at most the
diameter $\pi$, $\frac d{dt}\gamma_t(f)=-\beta_W\Cov_{\gamma_t}(f,\dot
s_{p_0})$ because $h$ does not depend on $t$, and $|\Cov(f,\dot s_{p_0})|
\le\sqrt{\Var f\,\Var\dot s_{p_0}}\le\frac\pi2\cdot\frac\pi4$. Integrating
over $t$ and taking the supremum over $f$ gives the bound.
\end{proof}

When $h$ is the indicator of a set $C$ the lemma says that conditioning a
link to lie in $C$ costs nothing in its response, however small or
irregular $C$ is, as long as $C$ is fixed. The responses that are not
bounded are those to a set that moves with the neighbours, such as the
intersection of balls centred at them; this is the difference between
conditioning on a fixed set of bad links and conditioning on a plaquette
being large.

\begin{proposition}[one-point rarity]\label{prop:onepoint}
Let $\mathcal A$ be a set of links, $D$ the diameter of $G$, and
$\gamma_e$, $e\in\mathcal A$, single-link kernels with
\[
W_1\bigl(\gamma_e(\cdot\mid\sigma),\gamma_e(\cdot\mid\sigma')\bigr)\le
\sum_{e'}c_{ee'}(\sigma,\sigma')\,\delta(\sigma_{e'},\sigma'_{e'})
\]
for all $\sigma,\sigma'$. Let $\sigma\mapsto B(\sigma)\subset\mathcal A$ be
measurable, and suppose there are constants $a_{ee'},A_{ee'}\ge0$ with
$c_{ee'}(\sigma,\sigma')\le a_{ee'}$ whenever $e\notin B(\sigma)\cup
B(\sigma')$, $c_{ee'}\le A_{ee'}$ always, $\sup_e\sum_{e'}a_{ee'}\le\theta<1$
and $\sup_e\sum_{e'}A_{ee'}\le\bar A$. If $\mu_1,\mu_2$ are invariant
under every $\gamma_e$ and $\mu_i(e\in B)\le q$ for every $e$ and
$i=1,2$, there is a coupling of $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ with
\[
\sup_{e\in\mathcal A}\E\,\delta(\sigma_e,\sigma'_e)\le\frac{2\bar ADq}
{1-\theta}.
\]
In particular $|\mu_1(F)-\mu_2(F)|\le L_F|S_F|\,2\bar ADq/(1-\theta)$ for
every $F$ with support $S_F$ that is $L_F$-Lipschitz in each link.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Fix $b_0\in\mathcal A$, $\lambda>0$, and let $w_b=e^{-\lambda|b-b_0|}$,
which is summable. As in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:comparison} the
functional $\Psi(\pi)=\sum_bw_b\E_\pi\delta(\sigma_b,\sigma'_b)$ has a
minimiser $\pi^*$ among the couplings, and replacing the pair at one link
$e$ by a sample of an optimal coupling of $\gamma_e(\cdot\mid\sigma)$ and
$\gamma_e(\cdot\mid\sigma')$ gives a coupling again. Only the term at $e$
changes, so minimality gives, with $\varrho(e)=\E_{\pi^*}\delta(\sigma_e,
\sigma'_e)$,
\[
\varrho(e)\le\E_{\pi^*}\sum_{e'}c_{ee'}(\sigma,\sigma')\,\delta(\sigma_{e'},
\sigma'_{e'})
\]
for every $e$, with no weight left. On the event that $e$ is good in both
configurations the coefficients are at most $a_{ee'}$; on its complement,
whose probability is at most $\mu_1(e\in B)+\mu_2(e\in B)\le2q$, they are
at most $A_{ee'}$ and every distance is at most $D$. Hence $\varrho(e)\le
\theta\sup\varrho+2\bar ADq$, and $\sup\varrho\le D$ is finite, which gives
the bound. The last statement follows by writing $F(\sigma)-F(\sigma')$ as
a telescopic sum over the links of $S_F$.
\end{proof}

The proposition is approximate uniqueness: all Gibbs measures of the
specification lie within $2\bar ADq/(1-\theta)$ of each other, link by
link. It is not decay. Its proof sees the bad set only through the
one-point probabilities $q$, and the term $2\bar ADq$ does not shrink with
the distance from the region where $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ are allowed to
differ. The bound $D$ on the distance at a bad link is not what causes
this: replacing it by H\"older's inequality gives $\varrho\le\theta\varrho
+\bar A(qD)^{1/p}\varrho^{1/p'}$, a recursion with the positive fixed point
$\varrho^*$ of order $\bar A^pqD/(1-\theta)^p$. To obtain decay the bad set
has to be held fixed while the comparison runs, as in the disagreement
percolation of van den Berg and Maes~\cite{vdBM94}, where the two
configurations are coupled link by link and the disagreement has to
percolate through the bad set; the price is that the laws conditioned on
that set, not the Wilson measure, then have to satisfy the fibre estimates
of Sec.~\ref{ssec:smallfibres}.

\subsection{Rarity of coarse defects}\label{ssec:coarse}

Theorem~\ref{thm:defects} makes a large plaquette rare at the lattice
scale. The cube condition (D) concerns a cube of fixed physical side, which
along the tuning spans $m\sim\beta_W/b$ scales, and it needs the analogue
of that rarity for the curvature of the block averages at every one of
them. This subsection isolates the two sides of that question. On the
energy side, the coarse curvature of a field is bounded by its action
uniformly in the scale, for linear fields and for group-valued fields in a
torus. On the entropy side, the chessboard estimate applies to coarse
events, and it is the normalisation of Lemma~\ref{lem:wilsonZ}, not the
energy, that makes it useless beyond $O(\log\beta_W)$ scales. A right
translation of the Haar measures gives rarity at every scale and under
every exterior, with a rate governed by the second variation of the action
along a fixed direction; for the abelian theory that second variation is
the energy of the direction, while for $\SU(2)$ it grows like $4^k$ at
scale $k$, and the growth is produced by the gauge orbit of the vacuum.

Throughout, $\Lambda_L$ is the torus of side $L=2^m$, the scale $k$
satisfies $2^{k+2}\le L$, and the lattice of spacing $2^k$ is the torus
$\Lambda_{L'}$ with $L'=L/2^k\ge4$. For a real field $\varphi$ on the links,
$d\varphi$ is its curvature, $d^{\mathsf T}$ the adjoint of $d$, and
$\Delta=d^{\mathsf T}d+dd^{\mathsf T}$, which acts on each component of a
field as the lattice Laplacian $(\Delta f)(x)=8f(x)-\sum_{\pm\nu}f(x\pm
e_\nu)$. The Green function $G_{L'}$ of $\Lambda_{L'}$ is the function of
mean zero with $\Delta G_{L'}=\delta_0-L'^{-4}$; it is invariant under the
permutations and sign changes of the coordinates, and applied to each
component it inverts $\Delta$ on fields whose components have mean zero.
It commutes with $d$, $d^{\mathsf T}$ and the translations.

\begin{lemma}[energy of a coarse defect]\label{lem:coarseenergy}
Let $P$ be a plaquette of the lattice of spacing $2^k$ and $J_{k,P}$ the
field with $(d_kV^{(k)}(\varphi))_P=\ip{\varphi}{J_{k,P}}$ for every field
$\varphi$ on $\Lambda_L$, given by Lemma~\ref{lem:straightpaths}(i). Then
$d^{\mathsf T}J_{k,P}=0$, every field $\varphi$ satisfies
\[
(d_kV^{(k)}(\varphi))_P^2\le\gamma_k\,Q(\varphi),
\]
where
\[
\gamma_k=\ip{J_{k,P}}{G_LJ_{k,P}}=\sup_\varphi\frac{(d_kV^{(k)}(
\varphi))_P^2}{Q(\varphi)},
\]
and $\frac1{432}\le\gamma_k\le\frac12$ for every $k$. In particular
$Q(\varphi)\ge2r^2$ whenever $|(d_kV^{(k)}(\varphi))_P|\ge r$, at every
scale.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{lem:straightpaths}(ii) shows that $V^{(k)}(dh)$ is the
gradient of $\bar h$ on the coarse lattice for every function $h$ on
sites, so $\ip{dh}{J}=0$, the curvature of a gradient vanishing, and
$d^{\mathsf T}J=0$; $J$ is supported on the links of directions $\mu$,
$\nu$ of the plane of $P$, and its component in each direction has mean
zero, the two sides of $P$ entering with opposite signs. Put $u=G_LJ$.
Then $\Delta u=J$, $d^{\mathsf T}u=G_Ld^{\mathsf T}J=0$, and for every
field $\varphi$
\begin{multline*}
\ip{\varphi}{J}=\ip{\varphi}{\Delta u}=\ip{d\varphi}{du}+\ip{d^{\mathsf T}
\varphi}{d^{\mathsf T}u}\\
=\ip{d\varphi}{du}\le\sqrt{Q(\varphi)Q(u)},
\end{multline*}
with $Q(u)=\ip{u}{d^{\mathsf T}du}=\ip{u}{\Delta u}=\ip{u}{J}=\gamma_k$,
and equality at $\varphi=u$. This proves the inequality and the
characterisation of $\gamma_k$ as a supremum.

For the upper bound, by Proposition~\ref{prop:effective}(i), whose proof
is a local identity, $Q_k(V^{(k)}(\varphi))\le Q(\varphi)$ for every field,
so $\gamma_k$ is at most the supremum of $(d_kw)_P^2/Q_k(w)$
over the fields $w$ of $\Lambda_{L'}$. The argument of the first paragraph
on $\Lambda_{L'}$, with $j=d_k^{\mathsf T}e_P$ the field equal to $\pm1$ on
the four sides of $P$, identifies that supremum with $\ip{j}{G_{L'}j}$. The
two sides of $P$ in the direction $\mu$ are the links $(y,\mu)$ and
$(y+e_\nu,\mu)$ with opposite signs, so
\begin{multline*}
\ip{j}{G_{L'}j}=4G_{L'}(0)-2G_{L'}(e_\nu)-2G_{L'}(e_\mu)\\
=4\bigl(G_{L'}(0)-G_{L'}(e_1)\bigr)=\tfrac12\bigl(1-L'^{-4}\bigr),
\end{multline*}
by $(\Delta G_{L'})(0)=8G_{L'}(0)-8G_{L'}(e_1)=1-L'^{-4}$ and the symmetry
of $G_{L'}$.

For the lower bound take $P$ at $y=0$ in the plane $\{1,2\}$, write
$L_k=2^k$, and let $f$ be the function on $\Z/L\Z$ with $f(s)=s/L_k$ for
$0\le s\le L_k$, $f(s)=1$ for $L_k\le s\le2L_k$, $f(s)=1-(s-2L_k)/L_k$ for
$2L_k\le s\le3L_k$ and $f=0$ elsewhere; let $g$ be the indicator of
$[0,2L_k)$; and let $h(s)=(1-\dist(s,[0,L_k))/L_k)_+$. Put $\varphi_{(x,2)}
=L_k^{-1}f(x_1)g(x_2)h(x_3)h(x_4)$ and $\varphi=0$ on the other links;
all supports fit in the torus since $4L_k\le L$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:straightpaths}(i), $V^{(k)}_{y,2}(\varphi)=L_k^{-4}\sum_{x
\in B_k(y)}\sum_{t<L_k}\varphi_{(x+te_2,2)}$, and for $y=0$ and $y=e_1$ the
factors $g$ and $h$ equal $1$ on the ranges that occur, so $V^{(k)}_{0,2}(
\varphi)=\bar f(0)$ and $V^{(k)}_{e_1,2}(\varphi)=\bar f(1)$, the means of
$f$ over $[0,L_k)$ and $[L_k,2L_k)$, which are $(L_k-1)/(2L_k)$ and $1$.
Hence $(d_kV^{(k)}(\varphi))_P=\bar f(1)-\bar f(0)=(L_k+1)/(2L_k)\ge
\frac12$. The curvature of $\varphi$ lives on the plaquettes of the planes
$\{1,2\}$, $\{2,3\}$, $\{2,4\}$, and $g$ is never differenced, so
\begin{multline*}
Q(\varphi)=L_k^{-2}\bigl(\|\nabla f\|^2\|g\|^2\|h\|^4+2\|f\|^2\|g\|^2\|
\nabla h\|^2\|h\|^2\bigr)\\
\le L_k^{-2}\Bigl(\frac2{L_k}2L_k(3L_k)^2+2\cdot3L_k\cdot2L_k\frac2{L_k}
3L_k\Bigr),
\end{multline*}
where $\nabla$ is the forward difference: $f$ and $h$ change by $1/L_k$ on
$2L_k$ steps and by nothing elsewhere, and $f^2$, $g^2$, $h^2$ have sums at
most $3L_k$, $2L_k$, $3L_k$. So $Q(\varphi)\le108$, and $\gamma_k\ge\frac14/108$.
\end{proof}

The fields $J_{k,P}$ are smeared current loops: by
Lemma~\ref{lem:straightpaths}(i) each side of $P$ contributes $\pm L_k^{-4}
c(s)$ on the $L_k^3(2L_k-1)$ links of its direction whose transverse
coordinates lie in the block and whose longitudinal coordinate $s$ ranges
over $[0,2L_k-2]$, with the tent $c(s)=\min\{s+1,L_k,2L_k-1-s\}$. A bare
holonomy around a loop of $n$ links forces action only of order $r^2/n$,
since the loop can be thickened to a tube of any radius; the block average
smears the loop over a four-dimensional region, and this is why its energy
does not decrease with the scale. The lemma is the quadratic part of
Theorem~\ref{thm:effectiveupper}, seen from one coarse plaquette. The
same scale invariance holds for group-valued fields in a torus.

\foreach \s/\c in {0/1,1/2,2/3,3/4,4/3,5/2,6/1} \fill[blue!60!black] (\s,\c) circle (3pt);
\draw[dotted] (3,0) -- (3,4) node[pos=0,below] {\footnotesize $L_k-1$};
\draw[dotted] (6,0) -- (6,1) node[pos=0,below] {\footnotesize $2L_k-2$};
\draw[dotted] (0,4) -- (3,4) node[pos=0,left] {\footnotesize $L_k$};
\end{tikzpicture}
\caption{The smeared current loop $J_{k,P}$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:coarseenergy}
in the plane of $P$, drawn for $L_k=4$. Left: each side of the coarse
plaquette $P$ (thick square) contributes a current of its own direction on
the links of a slab of transverse size $L_k^3$ and length $2L_k-1$ (blue for
the direction $1$, red for the direction $2$), with the signs of the four
sides; the slabs of opposite sides are disjoint and the two directions are
carried by different links. Right: the longitudinal profile $L_k^4J=\pm c(s)$
on a slab, the tent $c(s)=\min\{s+1,L_k,2L_k-1-s\}$, which counts the
straight paths of Lemma~\ref{lem:straightpaths}(i) through the link at
position $s$. The current is divergence free and its energy
$\gamma_k=\ip{J_{k,P}}{G_LJ_{k,P}}$ lies in $[\frac1{432},\frac12]$ at every
scale.}

\begin{proposition}[energy of a coarse defect, torus-valued fields]
\label{prop:torusenergy}
Let $U$ be an $S$-valued field in the tree gauge on $\Lambda_L$, as in
Theorem~\ref{thm:torusscales}, and let $P$ be a plaquette of the lattice
of spacing $2^k$ with $\delta(V^{\sharp,k}(U)_P,I)\ge r$. Then
\[
Q(U)\ge\min\Bigl\{\frac{r^2}{1.001},\frac1{144.2}\Bigr\}\ge\frac{r^2}
{1154}.
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
If some plaquette has $\delta(U_p,I)>1=\rho_G$ then $Q(U)>1\ge r^2/8$,
since $r\le\operatorname{diam}\SU(2)=2\sqrt2$. Otherwise every $\Theta_p$
is defined, and for $\Theta_p=\theta_pJ_p$ with $J_p^2=-I$ one has
$\lVert\Theta_p\rVert^2=2\theta_p^2$ and $\delta(U_p,I)^2=8\sin^2(\theta_p
/2)$, so $\lVert\Theta_p\rVert^2\le1.001\,\delta(U_p,I)^2$ when $\theta_p
\le1/(12\sqrt2)$, that is when $\lVert\Theta_p\rVert\le\eta_G=\frac1{12}$.
Let $j_*$ be the least $j\le k$ with $\max_P\lVert\Theta^{(j)}_P\rVert>
\eta_G$, if there is one. If there is none, \eqref{eq:torushyp} holds for
every $j<k$, and Theorem~\ref{thm:torusscales} gives $r^2\le\delta(V^{
\sharp,k}(U)_P,I)^2\le Q_k(V^{\sharp,k}(U))\le1.001\,Q(U)$. If $j_*=0$,
some plaquette has $\theta_p>1/(12\sqrt2)$ and $Q(U)\ge8\sin^2(\theta_p/2)
\ge1/144.1$. If $1\le j_*\le k$, \eqref{eq:torushyp} holds for $j<j_*$, so
Theorem~\ref{thm:torusscales} at the scale $j_*$ shows that $\Theta^{(j_*)}$
is defined and $\sum_P\lVert\Theta^{(j_*)}_P\rVert^2\le\sum_p\lVert\Theta_p
\rVert^2\le1.001\,Q(U)$, every fine plaquette having $\lVert\Theta_p\rVert
\le\eta_G$; one term of the left side exceeds $1/144$, so $Q(U)\ge1/144.2$.
\end{proof}

The $S$-valued fields form a null set for the Wilson measure, and for
general $\SU(2)$ fields Theorem~\ref{thm:smallscales} controls the
cut-off average only while $\sum_j\eta_j$ stays small; whether a bound of
the form $Q(U)\ge c\,r^2$, uniform in $k$, holds for every $\SU(2)$ field is
not known. The next proposition shows that, whatever the energy of a
coarse defect, the chessboard estimate cannot use it beyond a bounded
number of scales.

\begin{proposition}[chessboard for coarse events]\label{prop:coarsechess}
Let $\beta_W\ge1$, let $b=2^j$ with $2b\mid L$, and let $E$ be an event
determined by the links of the closed cube $[0,b]^4$ on which the action
of the plaquettes of that cube is at least $A$. For $z\in(b\Z/L\Z)^4$ let
$E_z$ be the event obtained from $E$ by the reflections that carry $[0,b]^4$
to $z+[0,b]^4$. Then for every set $Z$ of such $z$,
\[
\mu_L\Bigl(\,\bigcap_{z\in Z}E_z\Bigr)\le\exp\Bigl(|Z|\Bigl(6b^4(\log\beta_W
+C_0)-\frac{\beta_WA}4\Bigr)\Bigr).
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
As in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:defects}, $\mu_L$ is reflection
positive in the hyperplanes through sites, and the chessboard estimate for
functions of the links of the closed blocks $z+[0,b]^4$, $z\in(b\Z/L\Z)^4$,
bounds the probability of $\bigcap_{z\in Z}E_z$ by that of $\bigcap_{z}E_z$
over all $(L/b)^4$ blocks, raised to the power $|Z|(b/L)^4$. Reflection
preserves the Haar measures and $\Tr U_p$, so on every $E_z$ the plaquettes
of the block $z+[0,b]^4$ carry action at least $A$. A plaquette lies in at
most four closed blocks, one for each choice of the two transverse
coordinates of the corner, so on the intersection $S\ge(L/b)^4A/4$, and the
event has unnormalised weight at most $e^{-\beta_W(L/b)^4A/4}$. Dividing by
$Z_L\ge e^{-6L^4(\log\beta_W+C_0)}$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:wilsonZ} and raising
to the power $|Z|(b/L)^4$ gives the bound.
\end{proof}

A plaquette of the lattice of spacing $2^k$ depends, by
Lemma~\ref{lem:localstep} applied at each step, on the fine links of a cube
of side $2^{k+2}-4$, so the event that it carries a large cut-off average is of
the kind in the proposition with $b=2^{k+2}$. Whatever action $A$ that
event forces, the bound is below one only when $6\cdot16^{k+2}(\log\beta_W+
C_0)<\beta_WA/4$, that is $16^k\lesssim\beta_WA/\log\beta_W$. For the
events of Lemma~\ref{lem:coarseenergy} and
Proposition~\ref{prop:torusenergy}, $A$ is of the order of $r^2$ at every
scale, and the loss is entirely in the normalisation: the lower bound of
Lemma~\ref{lem:wilsonZ} charges the full fluctuation volume of the block,
$6b^4(\log\beta_W+C_0)$, against a defect whose energy does not grow with
the block. In the Gaussian theory the two fluctuation volumes, around the
defect and around the vacuum, are the same, and the following translation
argument transfers that cancellation to the group, under every exterior.

\begin{theorem}[Haar tilt]\label{thm:haartilt}
Let $G$ be $\SU(2)$ or $\U(1)$, let $\Lambda$ be a finite set of links,
either all links of $\Lambda_L$ or the inner links of a box $R\subset\Z^4$
whose other links are fixed, and let $\mu$ be the law with density
$Z^{-1}e^{-\beta_WS}$ with respect to the product of the Haar measures on
$\Lambda$, where $S=\sum_ps_p$ runs over the plaquettes meeting $\Lambda$
and $s_p=1-\frac1N\ReTr U_p$. For $r=(r_e)_{e\in\Lambda}$ with $r_e\in\g$
and $\rho_e=\|r_e\|_{\rm op}$ put $U^t_e=U_ee^{tr_e}$,
\[
D_rS(U)=\partial_tS(U^t)\big|_{t=0},\qquad K_r=\sup_U\partial_t^2S(U^t)
\big|_{t=0}.
\]
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item $K_r\le\sum_p\bigl(\sum_{e\subset p,\,e\in\Lambda}\rho_e\bigr)^2\le
24\sum_{e\in\Lambda}\rho_e^2$. For $G=\U(1)$ and $r_e=ia_e$ with $a_e\in\R$,
$K_r\le Q(a)=\sum_p(da)_p^2$.
\item $\E_\mu e^{\beta_WtD_rS}\le e^{\beta_Wt^2K_r/2}$ for every $t\in\R$.
\item For every $x>0$, uniformly in the fixed links,
\[
\mu(D_rS\ge x)\le e^{-\beta_Wx^2/(2K_r)},\qquad\mu(D_rS\le-x)\le
e^{-\beta_Wx^2/(2K_r)}.
\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(i) Order the links of a plaquette $p$ as traversed, so that $U_p=g_1^{
\epsilon_1}\cdots g_4^{\epsilon_4}$ with $\epsilon_i=\pm1$. Since $ge^{tr}
=e^{t\operatorname{Ad}(g)r}g$ and $(ge^{tr})^{-1}=e^{-tr}g^{-1}$, moving
the exponentials to the left gives $U_p(t)=e^{t\tilde a_1}\cdots e^{t\tilde
a_4}U_p$ with $\tilde a_i=\pm\operatorname{Ad}(h_i)r_{e_i}$ for unitary
$h_i$, so $\|\tilde a_i\|_{\rm op}=\rho_{e_i}$, and $\tilde a_i=0$ if
$e_i\notin\Lambda$. Then
\[
\partial_t^2\Tr U_p(t)\big|_{t=0}=\Tr\Bigl[\Bigl(\sum_i\tilde a_i^2+2\sum_{
i<j}\tilde a_i\tilde a_j\Bigr)U_p\Bigr],
\]
and $|\Tr(XU)|\le N\|X\|_{\rm op}$ for unitary $U$, so $|\partial_t^2s_p|
\le(\sum_i\rho_{e_i})^2\le4\sum_{e\subset p}\rho_e^2$; each link lies in
six plaquettes. The second derivative at any other $t$ is the one at $0$
for the field $U^t$, so the bound holds for $K_r$. For $\U(1)$ all factors
commute, $U_p(t)=e^{it(da)_p}U_p$ and $\partial_t^2s_p=(da)_p^2\ReTr U_p
\le(da)_p^2$.

(ii) Right multiplication by the fixed element $e^{-tr_e}$ preserves the
Haar measure of each link of $\Lambda$, so
\[
\int e^{-\beta_WS(Ue^{-tr})}\prod_{e\in\Lambda}dU_e=Z,
\]
that is, $\E_\mu e^{-\beta_W[S(Ue^{-tr})-S(U)]}=1$.
Taylor's formula along $s\mapsto Ue^{-sr}$ with the Lagrange remainder
gives
\begin{multline*}
S(Ue^{-tr})-S(U)=-tD_rS(U)+\tfrac{t^2}2\partial_s^2S(Ue^{-sr})\big|_{s=s_*}\\
\le-tD_rS(U)+\tfrac{t^2}2K_r,
\end{multline*}
the second derivative being even in $r$. Hence
\[
\E_\mu e^{\beta_WtD_rS-\beta_Wt^2K_r/2}\le1.
\]

(iii) By Chebyshev's inequality and (ii), $\mu(D_rS\ge x)\le e^{-\beta_Wtx
+\beta_Wt^2K_r/2}$ for $t>0$; take $t=x/K_r$. The lower tail is the upper
tail for $-r$. Nothing depends on the fixed links.
\end{proof}

The map $U\mapsto Ue^{-tr}$ is the group version of a translation of the
Gaussian field; its Jacobian is one, and no smallness of the field enters.
The observable $D_rS$ is the component of the force along $r$: at a
plaquette, $\partial_ts_p=-\frac1N\ReTr\bigl((\sum_i\tilde a_i)U_p\bigr)$,
the covariant derivative of $r$ in the background $U$ paired with the
sine part of $U_p$. For the abelian theory the second variation is the
energy of the direction, and the theorem gives the rarity of coarse
defects at every scale.

\begin{corollary}[abelian theory]\label{cor:abeliancoarse}
Let $G=\U(1)$, let $\mu_L$ be its Wilson measure on $\Lambda_L$,
$U_e=e^{i\theta_e}$, $\theta_p=(d\theta)_p$ the angle of
$U_p$ in $(-\pi,\pi]$, and let $a=G_LJ_{k,P}$ be the minimiser of
Lemma~\ref{lem:coarseenergy}. For every $k$, every plaquette $P$ of the
lattice of spacing $2^k$ and every $x>0$,
\[
\mu_L\Bigl(\sum_p\sin\theta_p\,(da)_p\ge x\Bigr)\le e^{-\beta_Wx^2}.
\]
Here $\sum_p\theta_p(da)_p=(d_kV^{(k)}(\theta))_P$ for every choice of
link angles $\theta_e$ with $(d\theta)_p\equiv\theta_p$ modulo $2\pi$, up
to $2\pi\sum_pn_p(da)_p$ with the integers $n_p=((d\theta)_p-\theta_p)/2\pi$.
Under a fixed exterior of a box, the same bound holds with $a$ replaced by
its restriction $\tilde a$ to the inner links and $x^2$ replaced by
$x^2/(2Q(\tilde a))$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:haartilt}(i) with $r_e=ia_e$, $K_r\le Q(a)=\gamma_k\le
\frac12$, and $D_rS=\sum_p\sin\theta_p(da)_p$ since $s_p(t)=1-\cos(\theta_p
+t(da)_p)$. Part (iii) gives the bound. For the identity,
$\sum_p(d\theta)_p(da)_p=\ip{\theta}{d^{\mathsf T}da}=\ip{\theta}{\Delta a}
=\ip{\theta}{J_{k,P}}$ because $d^{\mathsf T}a=0$. In a box the tilt acts
on the inner links only, and $K_r\le Q(\tilde a)$.
\end{proof}

For the abelian theory this is the statement that a smeared coarse flux of
size $x$ costs $\beta_Wx^2$ at every scale, uniformly in the exterior; the
four-dimensional abelian theory has no running coupling, and the bound is
consistent with its known behaviour at weak coupling~\cite{Gut80,FS82}. For
$\SU(2)$ the same tilt is available, but its second variation grows with
the scale.

\begin{proposition}[the gauge orbit of the vacuum]\label{prop:tiltgrowth}
Let $G=\SU(2)$ on $\Lambda_L$, $T\in\g$ with $\|T\|_{\rm op}=1$, $a=G_LJ_{
k,P}$ for a plaquette $P$ of the lattice of spacing $2^k$, and $r_e=a_eT$.
Then
\[
\Bigl(\sqrt{2\|a\|^2-\gamma_k}-\sqrt{\gamma_k}\Bigr)_+^2\le K_r\le24\|a\|^2
\]
and
\[
\|a\|^2\ge\frac{\gamma_k^2}{\|J_{k,P}\|^2}\ge\frac{4^k}{1492992},
\]
with $\gamma_k=\ip{J_{k,P}}{G_LJ_{k,P}}$ as in Lemma~\ref{lem:coarseenergy};
in particular $K_r\ge4^k/(3\cdot10^6)$ for $k\ge11$. The lower bound is attained,
up to the stated loss, at a pure gauge field, where $Q(U)=0$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The upper bound is Theorem~\ref{thm:haartilt}(i). For the lower bound let
$U$ be the pure gauge field $U_e=h_xh_{x+e}^{-1}$ of a function $h$ on
sites with values in $\SU(2)$. The action is invariant under gauge
transformations and $U_ee^{tr_e}=h_x\exp(t\operatorname{Ad}(h_{x+e}^{-1})
r_e)h_{x+e}^{-1}$, so $S(Ue^{tr})=S(e^{tr'})$ with $r'_e=\operatorname{Ad}
(h_{x+e}^{-1})r_e$. At the identity field, $U_p(t)=\exp(tX_p+O(t^2))$ with
$X_p=(dr')_p$ the signed sum of the $r'_e$ around $p$, and $s_p=1-\cos\|
X_p(t)\|_{\rm op}$, so $\partial_t^2s_p|_{t=0}=\|(dr')_p\|_{\rm op}^2$ and
$K_r\ge\sum_p\|(dr')_p\|_{\rm op}^2$. Take $h_x=R^{x_2}$ with $R=i\sigma_1$
and $T=i\sigma_3$, which is well defined on the torus since $R^4=I$ and
$4\mid L$, and satisfies $\operatorname{Ad}(R)T=-T$. Then $r'_e=\epsilon_e
a_eT$ with $\epsilon_{(x,\mu)}=(-1)^{x_2}$ for $\mu\ne2$ and $\epsilon_{(x,
2)}=(-1)^{x_2+1}$, and $K_r\ge Q(\epsilon a)$. Since $J_{k,P}$ has
components only in the directions $1$, $2$ of the plane of $P$ and $G_L$
acts on each component, $a_3=a_4=0$; the reflection exchanging the
coordinates $1$ and $2$ carries the component $a_1$ to $-a_2$, so $\|a_1\|^2
=\|a_2\|^2=\frac12\|a\|^2$. On the plaquette at $x$ in the plane $\{1,2\}$
the signs give
\begin{multline*}
(d(\epsilon a))_p=(-1)^{x_2}\bigl[(a_{(x,1)}+a_{(x+e_2,1)})-(a_{(x+e_1,2)}
-a_{(x,2)})\bigr]\\
=(-1)^{x_2}\bigl[\sigma_x-v_x\bigr],
\end{multline*}
so that $Q(\epsilon a)\ge\|\sigma-v\|^2\ge(\|\sigma\|-\|v\|)_+^2$, with
$\|\sigma\|^2=4\|a_1\|^2-\|\nabla_2a_1\|^2$ and $\|v\|^2=\|\nabla_1a_2\|^2$,
where $\nabla_\nu$ is the forward difference in the direction $\nu$. All
directional differences together give $\sum_{\mu,\nu}\|\nabla_\nu a_\mu\|^2
=\ip{a}{\Delta a}=\ip{G_LJ}{J}=\gamma_k$, so $\|\sigma\|^2\ge2\|a\|^2-
\gamma_k$ and $\|v\|^2\le\gamma_k$, which is the lower bound. Finally
$\gamma_k=\ip{J}{a}\le\|J\|\|a\|$, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:straightpaths}(i)
each of the four sides of $P$ contributes $L_k^3$ rows of $2L_k-1$ links
with coefficients $L_k^{-4}c(s)$, $c\le L_k$, so $\|J\|^2\le4L_k^{-8}L_k^3
(2L_k-1)L_k^2\le8\cdot4^{-k}$; with $\gamma_k\ge\frac1{432}$ this gives
$\|a\|^2\ge4^k/(8\cdot432^2)$. For $k\ge11$ that is at least $2$, so
$2\|a\|^2-\gamma_k\ge7\gamma_k$ and $K_r\ge(1-7^{-1/2})^2\cdot\frac78\cdot
2\|a\|^2\ge0.67\|a\|^2\ge4^k/(3\cdot10^6)$.
\end{proof}

So for $\SU(2)$ the tilt of Theorem~\ref{thm:haartilt} proves the rarity
of the force component $D_rS$ at the rate $\beta_Wx^2/(2K_r)$, which is of
order $\beta_Wx^2/4^k$ at scale $k$, and not more: the supremum in $K_r$ is
reached on the gauge orbit of the vacuum, where the field has no action
and no curvature, because a fixed direction $r$ is not gauge covariant and
its covariant derivative in a pure gauge background is as large as $r$
itself. The natural repair is to transport the direction with the field,
$r_e\mapsto\operatorname{Ad}(h(U))r_e$. When the transport runs along a
forest, the translation still preserves the Haar measures; but the
residual gauge freedom of the forest then realises the field of the proof
on the links between the trees, and the constant is reached at zero action
in that gauge as well.

\begin{proposition}[covariant tilt on a forest]\label{prop:foresttilt}
Let $G=\SU(2)$, let $F$ be a set of links of $\Lambda_L$ without cycles,
with one root chosen in every component, and for a site $y$ let $h_y(U)$
be the ordered product of the link variables along the path in $F$ from
the root of its component to $y$, with $h_y=I$ at the roots. For $r=(r_e)$
with $r_e\in\g$ and $r_e=0$ on $F$ put
\[
\Phi_t(U)_e=U_e\exp\bigl(t\operatorname{Ad}(h_y(U)^{-1})r_e\bigr),\quad
y\ \text{the end point of }e,
\]
and $\Phi_t(U)_f=U_f$ for $f\in F$; let $D^F_rS(U)=\partial_tS(\Phi_tU)
|_{t=0}$ and
\[
K^F_r=\sup\bigl\{\partial_t^2S(\tilde Ue^{tr})\big|_{t=0}:\ \tilde U_f=I
\text{ for all }f\in F\bigr\}.
\]
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item $\Phi_t$ preserves the product of the Haar measures for every $t$.
\item $\E_\mu e^{\beta_WtD^F_rS}\le e^{\beta_Wt^2K^F_r/2}$ for every
$t\in\R$, and $\mu(\pm D^F_rS\ge x)\le e^{-\beta_Wx^2/(2K^F_r)}$ for every
$x>0$. $D^F_rS$ is invariant under the gauge transformations that are trivial at
the roots.
\item Let $F$ be one of the sixteen translates $F_o$ of the forest of
Definition~\ref{def:blockgauge}, with blocks $2y+o+\{0,1\}^4$, let
$a=G_LJ_{k,P}$ and $T$ be as in Proposition~\ref{prop:tiltgrowth}, and
let $r_e=a_eT$ on the links outside $F$. Then
\[
K^F_r\ge2\sum_{e\notin F}a_e^2,
\]
and the bound is reached on pure gauge fields, where $Q(U)=0$. For at
least one $o$ the right side is at least $\frac{29}{16}\|a\|^2\ge
\frac{29}{16}\cdot\frac{4^k}{1492992}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
(i) Let $\Gamma(U)=(U_F,\tilde U)$ with $\tilde U_e=h_x(U)U_eh_y(U)^{-1}$
for $e=(x,y)\notin F$. Given the variables on $F$, the map $U_e\mapsto
\tilde U_e$ is a left and a right translation by elements that depend only
on $U_F$, so $\Gamma$ is a bijection of the configuration space that preserves the
product of the Haar measures; this is the change of variables of
Lemma~\ref{lem:gaugefix}. Let $R_t$ multiply every coordinate $\tilde U_e$,
$e\notin F$, on the right by $e^{tr_e}$ and leave $U_F$ alone. Then
\[
(\Gamma^{-1}R_t\Gamma U)_e=h_x^{-1}\bigl(h_xU_eh_y^{-1}e^{tr_e}\bigr)h_y
=U_e\exp\bigl(t\operatorname{Ad}(h_y^{-1})r_e\bigr),
\]
so $\Phi_t=\Gamma^{-1}R_t\Gamma$ is a composition of three maps that
preserve the measure.

(ii) Since the action is gauge invariant, $S(\Phi_tU)=S(\tilde Ue^{tr})$,
and $\tilde Ue^{tr}$ again has trivial links on $F$. Taylor's formula
along $s\mapsto\Phi_{-s}U$ with the Lagrange remainder gives $S(\Phi_{-t}
U)-S(U)\le-tD^F_rS(U)+\frac{t^2}2K^F_r$, and $\int e^{-\beta_WS\circ\Phi_
{-t}}\,dU=Z$ by (i); the rest is the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:haartilt}
(ii), (iii). Under a gauge transformation $g$ the transports change to
$g_oh_yg_y^{-1}$, with $o$ the root of the component of $y$, so $\tilde U$
is conjugated by the root values and $D^F_rS$ is unchanged when they are
trivial.

(iii) The tree links of $F_o$ join sites of one block, so a pure gauge
field $U=I^g$, $U_e=g_xg_{x+e}^{-1}$, with $g$ constant on the blocks has
trivial links on $F_o$, lies in the set of the supremum and has $Q(U)=0$.
By the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:tiltgrowth}, $\partial_t^2S(Ue^{tr}
)|_{t=0}=\sum_p\|(dr')_p\|_{\rm op}^2$ with $r'_e=\operatorname{Ad}(g_{x+e}
^{-1})r_e$, the end point of $e$ taken. Since $a_3=a_4=0$, a plaquette $p$
at $x$ in a plane $\{\mu,\nu\}$ with $\mu\in\{1,2\}$ and $\nu\in\{3,4\}$
has at most two tilted sides, $e=(x,\mu)$ with end point $x+e_\mu$ and
$e'=(x+e_\nu,\mu)$ with end point $x+e_\mu+e_\nu$, and
\[
\|(dr')_p\|_{\rm op}^2=a_e^2+a_{e'}^2-2a_ea_{e'}\ip{\operatorname{Ad}(g_{x
+e_\mu}^{-1})T}{\operatorname{Ad}(g_{x+e_\mu+e_\nu}^{-1})T},
\]
with the inner product of $\g$ in which $\|T\|=1$ and $a_e=0$ on $F_o$.
When $(x-o)_\nu$ is odd the two end points lie in different blocks. Take
the block values $g_B$ independent with Haar law. The adjoint
representation of $\SU(2)$ is irreducible of dimension three, so
$\E\operatorname{Ad}(g_B)=0$, and the expectation of the inner product
vanishes. Every link $e=(x,\mu)\notin F_o$ with $\mu\in\{1,2\}$ is, for
each $\nu\in\{3,4\}$, a side of exactly one such plaquette, at $x$ if
$(x-o)_\nu$ is odd and at $x-e_\nu$ otherwise. Dropping the other
plaquettes, whose terms are nonnegative,
\[
\E_g\,\partial_t^2S(I^ge^{tr})\big|_{t=0}\ge\sum_{\nu\in\{3,4\}}\sum_{e
\notin F_o}a_e^2=2\sum_{e\notin F_o}a_e^2,
\]
and the supremum over the section is at least the expectation. A link
$(x,\mu)$ lies in $F_o$ for one of the sixteen offsets $o$ when $\mu=1$
and for two of them when $\mu=2$. Averaging over
$o$ and using $\|a_1\|^2=\|a_2\|^2=\frac12\|a\|^2$ from the proof of
Proposition~\ref{prop:tiltgrowth},
\[
\frac1{16}\sum_o\sum_{e\notin F_o}a_e^2=\frac{15}{16}\|a_1\|^2+\frac{14}{16}
\|a_2\|^2=\frac{29}{32}\|a\|^2,
\]
so one offset reaches $\frac{29}{32}\|a\|^2$; the last bound is the lower
bound for $\|a\|^2$ of that proposition.
\end{proof}

Proposition~\ref{prop:foresttilt} and Figure~\ref{fig:foresttilt} show where the obstruction sits. The
Haar translation survives gauge covariance along a forest, and for the
block forest the constant it produces is at least $\frac{29}{16}\|a\|^2$,
reached by fields with no action and no curvature at all; the chessboard
estimate and the covariant tilt are therefore lost on the same fields, the
gauge orbit of the vacuum, for different reasons. A bound of the form
\[
\partial_t^2S(\tilde Ue^{tr})\le Q(r)+\mathcal R(\tilde U,r),
\]
with $\mathcal R$ supported on the large-field region, is false for every
forest section, since the left side exceeds $Q(r)$ by a fixed multiple of
$\|a\|^2$ at $\tilde U=I^g$, where the large-field region is empty. A
section that is smooth on the orbits, such as the Landau gauge, has no
such pure gauge fields, but its Jacobian is a Faddeev--Popov determinant
and not one, and part (ii) does not apply to it as it stands.\footnote{The
Wilson measure satisfies no curvature-dimension condition at the values
of $\beta_W$ considered here, so the inequality cannot be obtained from a
Bakry--\'Emery argument either: for one link equal to $-I$ with trivial
neighbours the second variation of $S$ along a unit direction on that link
is $-6$, since each of its six plaquettes contributes $\partial_t^2(1+\cos
t)=-1$, while the Ricci curvature of $\SU(2)$ with unit-speed geodesics
$e^{tr}$, $\|r\|_{\rm op}=1$, is $2$; the Hessian of $\beta_WS$ plus the
curvature is negative as soon as $\beta_W>1/3$.}

because the normalisation charges the whole fluctuation volume of a block
against the defect (Proposition~\ref{prop:coarsechess}), and the tilt stops
after $O(\log\beta_W)$ scales because its second variation grows like $4^k$

Along the tuning $\beta_W\sim b\log(1/a)$ a cube of fixed physical side
spans $m\sim\beta_W/b$ scales. Proposition~\ref{prop:coarsechess} covers
$O(\log\beta_W)$ of them, Propositions~\ref{prop:tiltgrowth}
and~\ref{prop:foresttilt} cover $O(\log\beta_W)$ of them without the torus
and uniformly in the exterior,
and Corollary~\ref{cor:abeliancoarse} covers all of them for the abelian
theory. What the cube condition needs for $\SU(2)$ is a translation of the
Haar measures whose second variation is the energy of the direction up to
a constant independent of the scale, together with a non-perturbative
treatment of the last $O(1)$ scales, where the running coupling is of order
one and coarse defects are not rare at all. Proposition~\ref{prop:foresttilt}
shows that no translation transported along a forest does this: its
constant is reached at zero action, with the growth $4^k$ of the energy of
the smeared current under the residual gauge freedom, so the missing
estimate is not a large-field remainder but a different section of the
gauge orbits, with a Jacobian that enters the argument of part (ii). This
is the content of Ba{\l}aban's large-field expansion~\cite{Bal89b}, and it
is not carried out here. The cube condition itself is a mixing condition
of Dobrushin--Shlosman type, which for compact spins with finite range is
equivalent to a logarithmic Sobolev inequality uniform in the
volume~\cite{SZ92}; the rarity of coarse defects is the part of that
inequality that concerns the large fields.

\section{Labels, islands and the environment}\label{sec:islands}

The cube condition (D) is a statement about conditional laws under every
exterior, and Sec.~\ref{ssec:fixedset} showed that one-point rarity of a
bad set gives closeness of Gibbs measures but not decay. The route that
remains is the one of the large-field expansions: label each block of a
window good or bad, prove decay on the good windows, bound the bad islands
by their rarity, and control the covariance that the labels themselves
carry. This section proves what each of these four steps gives for the
cut-off average of Sec.~\ref{ssec:pathblocks}, and proves, by explicit
examples, where the natural choices of labels fail. The statements are
exact and finite; none of them closes (D), and
Sec.~\ref{ssec:remains} lists what they leave.

Throughout, $G=\SU(2)$ with $\rho_G=1$, the lattice is in the tree gauge of
Definition~\ref{def:blockgauge}, $d(g,h)=\lVert\log(g^{-1}h)\rVert$ is the
bi-invariant geodesic distance in the Hilbert--Schmidt norm, so that
$d(g,I)=\lVert X\rVert$ for $g=e^X$ with $\lVert X\rVert\le\pi\sqrt2$,
and $\delta$ is the chordal distance. A \emph{pair} $k=(y,\mu)$ consists of
a block and a direction; its \emph{path link} is $\ell_k=U_{2y+e_\mu,\mu}$,
its \emph{private links} are the eight links leaving $B(y)$ in the direction
$\mu$, which enter no other cut-off average, and the seven private links
other than $\ell_k$ are its \emph{non-path} links. In the sixteen paths of
$V^\sharp_k$ the path link occurs twice, as the two paths of transverse
offset zero, and each non-path private link occurs twice, each time
multiplied by one link inside $B(y)$ or $B(y+e_\mu)$. For a coarse field
$c$ the reconstruction $R(c)$ of Sec.~\ref{ssec:pathblocks} puts $c_k$ on
the private links of $k$ and $I$ on the links inside the blocks.

\subsection{Backgrounds and the path links}\label{ssec:branches}

The first question is which background the chart of
Theorem~\ref{thm:chartdecay} should be centred at when a window is
conditioned on its labels. The natural label of a link is its distance to
the reconstruction of the coarse field, and the natural background is the
reconstruction itself. The first result shows that this is not enough: a
coarse field all of whose plaquettes are large has a reconstruction at
which every relative link label is good and the constrained action has a
negative second variation along the fibre.

\begin{proposition}[a rough background]\label{prop:roughbackground}
On the periodic lattice of side four, with coarse torus $(\Z/2\Z)^4$, let
$c_{y,\mu}=(-I)^{\sum_{\nu<\mu}y_\nu}$. Then every coarse plaquette of $c$
equals $-I$, the field $U=R(c)$ is in the tree gauge and has
$V^\sharp(U)=c$, and $d(U_e,R_e(c))=0$ for every link. There is a curve
$U(t)=U\exp(t\xi)$, $\xi$ supported on four links, such that
$V^\sharp(U(t))=c$ for all small $|t|$, $d(U_e(t),R_e(c))\le|t|$, and the
Wilson action $S=\sum_p(1-\frac12\ReTr U_p)$ satisfies
\[
\frac{d^2}{dt^2}\Bigl(\beta_WS(U(t))\Bigr)\Big|_{t=0}=-\beta_W,\qquad
T(\xi)=\sum_e\lVert\xi_e\rVert^2=4 .
\]
Every first derivative of $S$ at $U$ vanishes, so the intrinsic Hessian
of $\beta_WS$ on the fibre of $c$ at $U$ has an eigenvalue at most
$-\beta_W/4$, in any smooth chart of the fibre.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The coarse plaquette at $y$ in the plane $\{\mu,\nu\}$, $\mu<\nu$, is the
product of $c_{y,\mu}$, $c_{y+e_\mu,\nu}$, $c_{y+e_\nu,\mu}^{-1}$ and
$c_{y,\nu}^{-1}$; these are central, and the exponent of $-I$ is
$\sum_{\rho<\mu}y_\rho+\sum_{\rho<\nu}(y+e_\mu)_\rho-\sum_{\rho<\mu}(y+e_\nu)_\rho
-\sum_{\rho<\nu}y_\rho=1$ modulo two, since $\mu<\nu$ puts $e_\mu$ inside
the second sum and $e_\nu$ outside the third. So every coarse plaquette is
$-I$, also across the periodic seam. In $U=R(c)$ the links inside the
blocks are $I$, in particular the tree links, and all sixteen paths of a
pair $k$ equal $c_k$, so every $v_x=I$, the cut-off is one and $V^\sharp_k
(U)=c_k$; the relative labels vanish by construction.

Let $T\in\mathfrak{su}(2)$ have $\lVert T\rVert=1$, with eigenvalues $\pm
i/\sqrt2$, and let $\xi_e=a_eT$ with $a_e=-1,+1,+1,-1$ on the links
$((0,1,1,1),1)$, $((0,1,1,1),2)$, $((0,1,0,0),1)$, $((0,0,1,0),2)$ and
$a_e=0$ elsewhere. All four links are private links; the last two are path
links. The pair $((0,0,0,0),1)$ has the non-path link $((0,1,1,1),1)$ with
$a=-1$ and the path link $((0,1,0,0),1)$ with $a=+1$, the pair
$((0,0,0,0),2)$ has $((0,1,1,1),2)$ with $a=+1$ and the path link
$((0,0,1,0),2)$ with $a=-1$, and no other pair contains a link of the
support. Since the background is central, $P_x(t)=c_k\exp(ta_xT)$ for the
sixteen paths, with $a_x$ the value on the private link of the path, so
$v_x(t)=\exp(t(a_x-a_0)T)$ lies in the chart for small $|t|$, the cut-off
is one, and
\[
V^\sharp_k(U(t))=c_k\exp\Bigl(\frac t{16}\sum_xa_xT\Bigr)=c_k ,
\]
because each private link occurs in exactly two paths and the two nonzero
values of each pair cancel. The curve stays in the fibre, and
$d(U_e(t),R_e(c))=|ta_e|\le|t|$.

Write $U_p=s_pI$ with $s_p=\pm1$ and let $q_p=(d\,a)_p$ be the signed
curl of the scalar field $a$ around $p$. Since the perturbations commute
with the background, $U_p(t)=s_p\exp(tq_pT)$ and $\ReTr U_p(t)=2s_p
\cos(tq_p/\sqrt2)$, so
\[
S(U(t))=\sum_p\bigl(1-s_p\cos(tq_p/\sqrt2)\bigr),\qquad
S''(0)=\frac12\sum_ps_pq_p^2 .
\]
The plaquettes with $q_p\ne0$ are those containing a link of the support.
A link $(x,\mu)$ lies in six plaquettes, two in each plane $\{\mu,\nu\}$,
at $x$ and at $x-e_\nu$. Listing the six plaquettes of each of the four
links, the plaquette at $(0,1,1,1)$ in the plane $\{1,2\}$ contains two
links of the support, $((0,1,1,1),1)$ and $((0,1,1,1),2)$, with
$q_p=-1-1=-2$; the other $22$ plaquettes contain one link each, with
$q_p=\pm1$. The sign $s_p$ of a plaquette is
$-1$ exactly when it has an odd number of links on which $U$ equals $-I$;
counting through the four links, which is a finite check, gives twelve
plaquettes with $s_p=1$, $q_p^2=1$, ten with $s_p=-1$, $q_p^2=1$, and the
one with $s_p=-1$, $q_p^2=4$. Hence $\sum_ps_pq_p^2=12-10-4=-2$,
$S''(0)=-1$, and $T(\xi)=4$.

Every plaquette of $U$ is central, so every first derivative of $S$ at $U$
vanishes and the second derivative along any curve through $U$ with
velocity $\xi$ depends only on $\xi$: the intrinsic Hessian on the fibre
has the value $-1$ at $\xi$, which has $T(\xi)=4$. The Haar density of the
fibre, in a chart in which the path links are solved for, is the inverse
Jacobian of the path-link equations, which at $U$ is a fixed positive
number independent of $\beta_W$; its logarithmic second derivatives are
bounded in any fixed chart, so no choice of chart turns the Hessian of
$\beta_WS$ plus the log-density positive for all large $\beta_W$.
\end{proof}

The proposition does not contradict Theorem~\ref{thm:chartdecay}, which
assumes small plaquettes; it shows that the hypothesis of that theorem on
the coarse field cannot be dropped in favour of relative link labels. A
coarse-curvature label is therefore part of any labelling, and the next
lemma shows that it has a witness at the fine scale, so that it is as rare
as a fine defect.

\begin{lemma}[a fine witness for coarse curvature]\label{lem:coarsewitness}
Let $P$ be the coarse plaquette at $y$ in the plane $\{\mu,\nu\}$ and
suppose that $\delta(U_p,I)\le\kappa\le10^{-8}$ for every fine plaquette
$p$ with a vertex in one of the blocks at $\ell^\infty$ distance at most
one from $B(y)$, $B(y+e_\mu)$, $B(y+e_\nu)$ or $B(y+e_\mu+e_\nu)$. Then
$c=V^\sharp(U)$ satisfies
\[
\delta(c_P,I)\le(4+28\pi)\kappa<92\kappa .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For a pair $k$ among the four sides of $P$, Lemma~\ref{lem:smallframes}(i)
gives $\delta(U_e,I)\le3\kappa$ for the link of each path inside a block
and $\delta(U_e,\ell_k)\le21\kappa$ for its private link, so $\delta(P_x,
\ell_k)\le24\kappa$ for every path, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:logbound}
$\lVert\log(\ell_k^{-1}P_x)\rVert\le8\pi\kappa$. The two paths of offset
zero contribute nothing, so $c_k=\ell_kM_k$ with $\lVert\log M_k\rVert\le
\frac{14}{16}\,8\pi\kappa=7\pi\kappa$ and $\delta(c_k,\ell_k)\le7\pi\kappa$.
The four path links around $P$ are the holonomy of the square of side two
at $2y$: the other four links of its sides are the first links of the
straight paths, which are tree links and equal $I$. That square is tiled
by four fine plaquettes, and inserting them with their parallel transports
gives $\delta(\ell_P,I)\le4\kappa$, where $\ell_P$ is that holonomy. Replacing
the four $\ell_k$ by $c_k$ one at a time, bi-invariance of $\delta$ and the
triangle inequality add $4\cdot7\pi\kappa$.
\end{proof}

With the coarse field calm, the chart has a centre. The next lemma shows
that for a pair whose non-path links are near the reconstruction, the
constraint $V^\sharp_k=c_k$ determines the path link, on every branch of
the cut-off, and the fibre of the window over its non-path links is a
single graph.

\begin{lemma}[the path link is determined]\label{lem:branchbound}
Let $k$ be a pair with cut-off average $c_k$, and suppose that each of its
seven non-path private links and each link inside $B(y)$ and
$B(y+e_\mu)$ is within geodesic distance $r$ of its reconstruction value.
Then every path other than the two copies of $\ell_k$ has $d(P_x,c_k)\le
2r$, and every $\ell_k$ with $V^\sharp_k=c_k$ satisfies
\[
d(\ell_k,c_k)\le14r ,\qquad d(v_x,I)\le16r\ \text{for every path}.
\]
If moreover $r\le10^{-4}$, the cut-off equals one at every such $\ell_k$,
and $\ell_k$ is unique: it is the only fixed point of
\[
X\mapsto F(X)=-\frac1{16}\sum_{x}\log\bigl(e^{-X}c_k^{-1}P_x\bigr),
\qquad \ell_k=c_ke^X ,
\]
in the ball $\lVert X\rVert\le14r$, where the sum runs over the fourteen
paths of nonzero offset, and $F$ is a contraction of that ball with
constant less than $0.9$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
A path of nonzero offset is the product of a link inside a block, within
$r$ of $I$, and a non-path private link, within $r$ of $c_k$, in one of
the two orders; bi-invariance of $d$ and the triangle inequality give
$d(P_x,c_k)\le2r$. If the cut-off is zero, $V^\sharp_k=\ell_k$, so $\ell_k=
c_k$. Otherwise every $v_x=\ell_k^{-1}P_x$ has $\delta(v_x,I)<1$, its
principal logarithm is defined and $\lVert\log v_x\rVert=d(v_x,I)=d(\ell_k,
P_x)$. Put $D=d(\ell_k,c_k)$ and $N=\frac1{16}\sum_x\log v_x$, the two
terms of offset zero being zero. Then $c_k=\ell_k\exp(\chi N)$ and
\[
D=d(e^{\chi N},I)\le\chi\lVert N\rVert\le\frac{14}{16}\max_xd(\ell_k,P_x)
\le\frac78(D+2r),
\]
so $D\le14r$, and $d(v_x,I)\le D+2r\le16r$. For $r\le10^{-4}$ this is less
than $\frac12$, so $\chi=1$, and $V^\sharp_k=c_k$ reads $X=F(X)$ for
$\ell_k=c_ke^X$ with $\lVert X\rVert\le14r$. On that ball each $A_x=c_k^{-1}P_x$ has $d(A_x,I)\le2r$, so
$d(e^{-X}A_x,I)\le16r$ and $\lVert F(X)\rVert\le\frac{14}{16}\cdot16r=14r$:
$F$ maps the ball into itself. Writing $e^{-X}A_x=I+M$ with $\lVert M\rVert
\le16r$, the series of the logarithm gives $\lVert D\log(I+M)\rVert\le
1/(1-16r)$, and the differential of $X\mapsto e^{-X}A_x$ has norm at most
$e^{14r}$; hence $\lVert DF\rVert\le\frac78e^{14r}/(1-16r)<0.9$, and the
fixed point is unique by the contraction principle.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[good windows are graphs]\label{prop:graphlaw}
Let $W$ be a finite set of blocks, let $c$ be a coarse field, let $K_W$
be the set of pairs based in $W$ or entering $W$ from a block outside it,
and let $Z_W$ be the set of non-path active links with base in $\bigcup
W$. Free the links of $A_W$ and the path links of the pairs entering $W$,
fix every other link, and condition on $V^\sharp_k=c_k$ for every $k\in
K_W$ and on the event that every link of $Z_W$ and every non-path link of
a pair entering $W$ is within $r\le10^{-4}$ of its reconstruction value.
Then the fibre of these constraints is the graph of a smooth map $\Gamma$
from the product of the $r$-balls of the links of $Z_W$ to the path links
of the pairs of $K_W$, and the conditional law is the Wilson weight times
the Haar disintegration of this graph, whose density with respect to the
product Haar measure on $Z_W$ is the product over $k\in K_W$ of the
inverse Jacobians of $X\mapsto X-F(X)$ at the fixed point.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The constraint of a pair $k\in K_W$ involves its own private links and
the links inside two blocks, so it involves only its own path link, links
of $Z_W$, and fixed links that are within $r$ of their reconstruction
values; no other constraint involves a freed link, since the other pairs
have their supports off the free set. Lemma~\ref{lem:branchbound} applies
to every $k\in K_W$ with the same $r$ and gives one solution for each
pair, a smooth function of the links of $Z_W$ by the implicit function
theorem since $I-DF$ is invertible. The fibre is therefore the graph of $\Gamma$, and the coarea
formula for the submersion $U\mapsto(V^\sharp_k)_{k}$ restricted to the
product of the balls gives the stated density, since the derivative of the
constraint of $k$ in its own path link is $I-DF$ in the chart at $c_k$ and
the cross derivatives between different pairs vanish.
\end{proof}

The proposition says that, once the coarse field is calm and the labels
are placed on the non-path links, the good windows carry the product
structure that the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:chartdecay} needs, with no
branch of the cut-off to discard; the Hessian estimate of that theorem
then applies on the graph. Two further examples show that the two obvious
alternatives fail: labelling all physical links, including the path links,
produces a nonconvex domain, and a bad pair can have several path links.

\begin{proposition}[the all-link label domain is not convex]\label{prop:nonconvex}
Let $c\equiv I$, freeze every link outside the eight private links of one
pair at $I$, and write the seven non-path links as $e^{z_j}$ and the path
link as $e^{X}$. For every sufficiently small $r>0$ the set of
$(z_1,\dots,z_7)$ for which all eight links lie in the geodesic ball of
radius $r$ at $I$ is not convex.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
With the cut-off equal to one, the constraint is $H(X,z)=X+\frac18\sum_{j
=1}^7\log(e^{-X}e^{z_j})=0$, since each non-path link occurs in two of the
sixteen paths and the two paths of offset zero contribute nothing. Take
$A,B\in\mathfrak{su}(2)$ orthonormal for the Hilbert--Schmidt norm, so
that $[A,[A,B]]=-2B$ and $[B,[B,A]]=-2A$, and put $z_1=-\frac a7A+hB$,
$z_2=-\frac a7A-hB$, $z_3=\dots=z_7=-\frac a7A$ with $a>0$ small. The inner automorphism of $\SU(2)$ that fixes $A$ and negates $B$ and
$[A,B]$ exchanges the logarithms of $e^{-xA}e^{z_1}$ and $e^{-xA}e^{z_2}$,
so their sum lies along $A$ when $X=xA$, and the equation reduces to its
$A$-component; by the implicit function theorem the solution is $X=x(a,h)A$
with $x$ analytic, even in $h$ by the same symmetry, and $x(a,0)=a$ since
$\log(e^{-xA}e^{bA})=(b-x)A$ gives $x+\frac78(b-x)=0$ at $h=0$. Let $L(x,b,h)$ be the $A$-component of $\log(e^{-xA}
e^{bA+hB})$. The Baker--Campbell--Hausdorff series through degree three
has one term of degree two in $h$ along $A$, namely $\frac1{12}[hB,[hB,
-xA]]=\frac{xh^2}6A$, so $\partial_h^2L(x,b,0)=\frac x3+O((|x|+|b|)^2)$.
The $A$-component of $H$ is $x+\frac18\bigl(2L(x,-\frac a7,h)+5(-\frac a7
-x)\bigr)$, and $\partial_xL(x,b,0)=-1$; differentiating $H=0$ twice in
$h$ at $h=0$ gives $\frac18\partial_h^2x+\frac14\partial_h^2L=0$, that is
\[
\partial_h^2x(a,0)=-2\,\partial_h^2L(a,-\tfrac a7,0)=-\frac{2a}3+O(a^2)<0 .
\]
Put $\eta=\frac r2$ and take $a$ with $r<a<r(1+\frac{\eta^2}{4})$. The
points $z^\pm$ with $h=\pm\eta$ and their midpoint $z^0$ with $h=0$ have
all seven non-path links within $\sqrt{a^2/49+\eta^2}<r$ of $I$; the path
link of $z^\pm$ is at distance $x(a,\pm\eta)=a-\frac a3\eta^2+O(r^4)\le
r-\frac{r^3}{48}+O(r^4)<r$ from $I$ for small $r$, while that of $z^0$ is
at distance
$x(a,0)=a>r$. So the endpoints lie in the domain and the midpoint does
not.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[a bad pair with three path links]\label{prop:branches}
Let $c\equiv I$, freeze every link outside the eight private links of one
pair at $I$, and take the private links in the one-parameter subgroup
$\operatorname{diag}(e^{iq},e^{-iq})$: one non-path link at the angle
$-\frac12$, the other six at the angle $\frac{49}{100}$. Then there are at
least three values of the path-link angle $q$ with the same cut-off
average, and the derivative of the cut-off average with respect to $q$
vanishes at some $q\in(0,\frac15)$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
On the subgroup all logarithms are scalar and the cut-off average has the
