angle $f(q)=q+\frac{\chi(q)}8\bigl(-\frac12+6\cdot\frac{49}{100}-7q\bigr)$,
where $\chi(q)=\phi(m(q))$, $m(q)=\max_j2\sqrt2\,|\sin((\theta_j-q)/2)|$
and $\theta_1=-\frac12$, $\theta_2=\dots=\theta_7=\frac{49}{100}$, the
factor $2\sqrt2|\sin(\theta/2)|$ being the chordal distance of
$\operatorname{diag}(e^{i\theta},e^{-i\theta})$ from $I$. At $q=0$ the
maximum is attained at $\theta_1$ alone, with $m(q)=2\sqrt2\sin((q+\frac12)
/2)$ near $0$ and $\frac12<m(0)<1$, so $\chi=2-2m$ is smooth near $0$ with
$\chi'(0)=-2\sqrt2\cos\frac14$, and
\[
\begin{split}
f'(0)&=1-\frac78\chi(0)+\frac{\chi'(0)}8\Bigl(-\frac12+\frac{294}{100}\Bigr)\\
&=-\frac34+\sqrt2\Bigl(\frac72\sin\frac14-\frac{61}{100}\cos\frac14\Bigr)
\end{split}
\]
after inserting $\chi(0)=2-4\sqrt2\sin\frac14$. With $\sin\frac14<\frac14$,
$\cos\frac14>\frac{31}{32}$ and $1<\sqrt2<\frac32$ on the positive and the
negative term separately, $f'(0)<-\frac{91}{3200}<0$. Put $\gamma=f(0)$,
which lies in $(0,1)$. For $|q|=1$ the maximal chordal distance exceeds
one, so $\chi(\pm1)=0$ and $f(\pm1)=\pm1$. Since $f$ decreases through
$\gamma$ at $0$ and $f(-1)<\gamma<f(1)$, the intermediate value theorem
gives one preimage of $\gamma$ in $(-1,0)$, one in $(0,1)$, and $q=0$. On
$[0,\frac15]$ the maximiser stays $\theta_1$ and $\frac9{10}<m<1$ at
$q=\frac15$, so $\chi(\frac15)<\frac15$ and $f'(\frac15)>1-\frac7{40}-
3\cdot\frac{13}{100}>0$; with $f'(0)<0$, continuity gives a zero of $f'$ in
$(0,\frac15)$.
\end{proof}

Hence the Jacobian of the path-link constraint, which enters the density of
Proposition~\ref{prop:graphlaw}, has no positive lower bound on the bad
side, and a bad pair contributes a sum over branches to any estimate of
the conditional law. On the good side none of this happens: the labels
of Proposition~\ref{prop:graphlaw} are placed on the non-path links only.

\subsection{The path-link law on its two sides}\label{ssec:pathlaw}

The conditional law of the path link of a pair $k$, given its seven
non-path private links $z=(\ell_a)_{a\ne0}$, the links $u,w$ inside its
two blocks and the rest of the field $\sigma$, is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pathlaw}
\pi(dg\mid z,u,w,\sigma)=\frac1Z\sum_{g:\,V(g;z,u,w)=c_k}\frac{e^{-\beta_W
S(g;\cdot)}}{\lvert\det D_gV(g;z,u,w)\rvert}\,\delta_g ,
\end{equation}
where $V=V^\sharp_k$ as a function of the path link, the sum runs over all
its preimages of $c_k$, and $\lvert\det D_gV\rvert$ is the Jacobian between
tangent spaces of the bi-invariant metric. This is the Haar disintegration
along the Lipschitz map $V$ on the compact three-manifold $\SU(2)$, by the
coarea formula, times the Wilson weight; on the good side it is the
one-point law of Proposition~\ref{prop:graphlaw}, and on the bad side it
carries the branches of Proposition~\ref{prop:branches}. We determine its
response to each kind of exterior link. Throughout, $W_1^\delta$ and
$W_1^d$ are the Kantorovich distances for the chordal and the geodesic
distance, and the facts $\lVert L_X\rVert\le\theta/\sin\theta$ for an
eigenangle $\theta<\pi$ of $X/\sqrt2$, $\lVert E_Y\rVert\le1$ and $d(e^A,
e^B)\le\lVert A-B\rVert$ of Sec.~\ref{ssec:smallfibres} are used as stated
there.

\begin{lemma}[links that enter only the Wilson weight]\label{lem:wilsononly}
Let $e'$ be a link that is neither a private link of $k$ nor inside $B(y)$
or $B(y+e_\mu)$, and let $\sigma,\sigma'$ differ only at $e'$. Then for
every $(z,u,w)$ and $c_k$ for which~\eqref{eq:pathlaw} is a finite
nonzero measure,
\[
W_1^\delta\bigl(\pi(\cdot\mid z,u,w,\sigma),\pi(\cdot\mid z,u,w,\sigma')
\bigr)\le\beta_W\,d(\sigma_{e'},\sigma'_{e'}),
\]
and the two laws coincide unless $e'$ lies in a plaquette with a private
link of $k$. For the law of all eight private links given $u,w,\sigma$ and
restricted to any fixed measurable set $B$ of the non-path links, with the
cost $\sum_a\delta(\ell_a,\ell'_a)$, the same holds with $8\beta_W$. Both
bounds include every branch and the disintegration density.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Only $S$ depends on $\sigma_{e'}$: $V$ is a function of $g,z,u,w$, and so
is the measure $\nu=\sum_g\delta_g/\lvert\det D_gV\rvert$, respectively
$\mathbf1_BJ_8^{-1}\mathrm{vol}_M$ with $M=\{V=c_k\}$ and $J_8$ the
Jacobian of Lemma~\ref{lem:privatesubmersion}. An exterior link lies in at
most one plaquette with a private link: the private links are the eight
$\mu$-links at the sites $x'_a$, whose $\mu$-coordinates agree, so the two
plaquettes in a plane $\{\mu,\nu\}$ through a $\nu$-link, which sit at
different $\mu$-coordinates, cannot both contain one; and a $\mu$-link
$(x,\mu)$ with $x$ not a site $x'_a$ has $x+\varepsilon e_\nu=x'_a$ for at
most one pair $(\nu,\varepsilon)$, since two such relations would put a
coordinate of $x$ outside $\{0,1\}$ in one direction and inside it in
another. If there is no such plaquette $p_0$ the laws are equal. Otherwise
move $\sigma_{e'}$ along a minimal geodesic $\sigma_{e'}e^{t\xi}$,
$\lVert\xi\rVert=1$, $0\le t\le T=d(\sigma_{e'},\sigma'_{e'})$, with laws
$\pi_t$. For bounded $f$, $\frac d{dt}\pi_t(f)=-\beta_W\Cov_{\pi_t}(f,\dot
s_{p_0})$, by differentiation under the integral against the fixed finite
measure $\nu$. Here $\frac d{dt}U_{p_0}(t)=U_{p_0}(t)\xi'$ with
$\lVert\xi'\rVert=1$, $\xi'$ a conjugate of $\pm\xi$, so $\dot s_{p_0}=
-\frac12\ReTr(U_{p_0}\xi')$; in a basis in which $U_{p_0}=\operatorname{diag}
(e^{i\varphi},e^{-i\varphi})$ only the diagonal entries $\pm i\alpha$ of
$\xi'$ contribute, $2\alpha^2\le1$, and $\dot s_{p_0}=\alpha\sin\varphi$.
Hence $|\dot s_{p_0}|\le\frac1{\sqrt2}$, and a link of a plaquette moving
at geodesic speed $v$ gives $|\dot s_p|\le v/\sqrt2$. A function that is
$1$-Lipschitz for $\delta$ has oscillation at most the chordal diameter
$2\sqrt2$ of $\SU(2)$, and at most $8\cdot2\sqrt2$ for the sum cost on
eight links. Since $|\Cov(f,h)|\le\frac14\operatorname{osc}f
\operatorname{osc}h$, $|\frac d{dt}\pi_t(f)|\le\beta_W$, respectively
$8\beta_W$; integrate over $[0,T]$ and use the Kantorovich duality.
\end{proof}

This is Lemma~\ref{lem:fixedset} for the fibre law: the branches and the
density are harmless for every link that enters only through the action.
The links it leaves out are the seven non-path links, which are in the
conditioning, and the inside links $u_a,w_a$, which enter $V$. On the good
side both are harmless, and the radius of Lemma~\ref{lem:branchbound} and
Proposition~\ref{prop:graphlaw} can be taken as $1/32$ rather than
$10^{-4}$.

\begin{proposition}[the good side to radius $1/32$]\label{prop:goodside}
Let $r\le\frac1{32}$, and suppose $d(\ell_a,c_k)\le r$ for $a\ne0$ and
$d(u_a,I),d(w_a,I)\le r$. Put $\theta_0=\frac1{2\sqrt2}$ and $\kappa_0=
\frac78\,\theta_0/\sin\theta_0<0.8935$. Then every solution $g$ of $V(g;z,u,
w)=c_k$ has cut-off equal to one and $d(g,c_k)\le14r$, and there is exactly
one: writing $g=c_ke^X$, $X$ is the unique fixed point of $F(X)=-\frac1{16}
\sum_x\log(e^{-X}c_k^{-1}P_x)$ in $\{\lVert X\rVert\le14r\}$, and $F$ is a
contraction of that ball with constant $\kappa_0$. At the solution the
singular values of $D_gV$ lie in $[1-\kappa_0,1+\kappa_0]$, so the density
$1/\lvert\det D_gV\rvert$ lies in $[(1+\kappa_0)^{-3},(1-\kappa_0)^{-3}]\subset
[0.147,828]$. The law~\eqref{eq:pathlaw} is the point mass at $g=g(z,u,w)$,
and for two configurations satisfying the hypothesis
\begin{multline*}
d(g,g')\le1.1986\sum_{a\ne0}d(\ell_a,\ell'_a)\\
+0.5993\sum_{a\ne0}\bigl(d(u_a,u'_a)+d(w_a,w'_a)\bigr),
\end{multline*}
with no dependence on $\beta_W$, on $c_k$ or on any other link.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The first part is the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:branchbound}, which holds for
every $r$ up to the contraction: every solution has $D=d(g,c_k)\le14r$ and
$d(v_x,I)\le16r\le\frac12$, so $m\le\frac12$ and $\chi=1$, and $V=c_k$ reads
$X=F(X)$, with $F$ mapping the ball into itself. For the contraction
constant, on the ball each $A_x=c_k^{-1}P_x$ has $d(A_x,I)\le2r$, so $Y_x=
\log(e^{-X}A_x)$ has $\lVert Y_x\rVert\le16r$, an eigenangle at most
$16r/\sqrt2\le\theta_0$. Since $e^{-(X+tZ)}A_x=(I-tE_{-X}Z+O(t^2))e^{Y_x}$
and $\log(e^{tW}e^Y)=Y+tL_YW+O(t^2)$, $\lVert DF\rVert\le\frac{14}{16}\cdot
\lVert E_{-X}\rVert\max_x\lVert L_{Y_x}\rVert\le\kappa_0$, as $\theta/\sin
\theta$ increases on $[0,\pi)$; the fixed point is unique by the
contraction principle. For the Jacobian, vary $g\mapsto ge^{tZ}$: then
$v_x\mapsto e^{-tZ}v_x$, $\log v_x\mapsto\log v_x-tL_{Y_x}Z+O(t^2)$, and
with $N=\frac1{16}\sum_x\log v_x$ and $\bar L=\frac1{14}\sum_xL_{Y_x}$,
\[
V^{-1}\frac{dV}{dt}\Big|_{t=0}=\operatorname{Ad}(e^{-N})\bigl(I-\tfrac78
E_N\bar L\bigr)Z ,
\]
by $\frac d{dt}e^{N+tW}e^{-N}=E_NW$. As $\operatorname{Ad}(e^{-N})$ is an
isometry and $\lVert\frac78E_N\bar L\rVert\le\kappa_0$, the singular values
lie in $[1-\kappa_0,1+\kappa_0]$. Finally, the law has one atom, so $W_1^d=
d(g,g')$. Move one link at a time along a minimal geodesic; the geodesic
ball of radius $r$ is convex, so the hypothesis holds along the way, and
$d(g,g')\le\lVert X-X'\rVert$. For $\ell_a\mapsto\ell_ae^{t\zeta}$,
$\lVert\zeta\rVert=1$, the two paths through $\ell_a$ move, $A_{x_a}\mapsto
A_{x_a}e^{t\zeta}$ and $A_{x'_a}\mapsto A_{x'_a}e^{t\operatorname{Ad}(w_a^{-1}
)\zeta}$, and $\log(e^Ye^{t\zeta'})=Y+tL_{-Y}\zeta'+O(t^2)$, so
$\lVert\partial_tF\rVert\le\frac2{16}\theta_0/\sin\theta_0$ and, by the
implicit function theorem, $\lVert dX/dt\rVert\le\frac2{16}\frac{\theta_0}
{\sin\theta_0}\frac1{1-\kappa_0}<1.1986$. For $u_a\mapsto u_ae^{t\zeta}$
one path moves, $A_{x_a}\mapsto A_{x_a}e^{t\operatorname{Ad}(\ell_a^{-1})
\zeta}$, which gives half of it, and likewise for $w_a$.
\end{proof}

The only change from Lemma~\ref{lem:branchbound} is that the series bound
$\lVert D\log(I+M)\rVert\le(1-16r)^{-1}$ is replaced by the exact norm
$\theta/\sin\theta$ of $L_Y$. So on the good side the response of the
path-link law to every exterior link is bounded, with a constant
independent of $\beta_W$, and the bad side begins at $r=\frac1{32}$. On
the bad side the response to the non-path links is not bounded at all.
The configuration of Proposition~\ref{prop:branches} has a fold: a value
$c$ at which two branches are born, with infinite density, and the law
jumps across it. When the paths of a pair lie on one torus, the component
of the cut-off average transverse to that torus has a closed form.

\begin{lemma}[the transverse part of the cut-off average]\label{lem:foldtransverse}
Write $\SU(2)$ as the unit quaternions, with $T=\{e^{iq}\}$, and its Lie
algebra as the pure quaternions, with the Euclidean norm $|\cdot|$. Let
$\theta_1,\dots,\theta_n$ be real and $\varpi_1,\dots,\varpi_n>0$, and for
$g\in\SU(2)$ put $h_x=g^{-1}e^{i\theta_x}$, $\chi(g)=\phi(\max_x\delta(h_x,
I))$ and
\[
V(g)=g\exp Y(g),\qquad Y(g)=\chi(g)\sum_x\varpi_x\log h_x ,
\]
and $Y(g)=0$ if $\chi(g)=0$. For real numbers $q$ and $s$ put $g(q,s)=\cos
s\,e^{iq}+\sin s\,k$, and define $\psi_x\in[0,\pi]$ by $\cos\psi_x=\cos s
\cos(\theta_x-q)$. Then the $j$-component of $V(g(q,s))$ is $0$ and its $k$-component is
$\sin s\,\Xi(q,s)$, where $\Xi=1$ if $\chi=0$ and otherwise
\[
\Xi=\cos|Y|-\frac{\sin|Y|}{|Y|}\,\chi\sum_x\varpi_x\,\psi_x\cot\psi_x ,
\]
with $\sin|Y|/|Y|=1$ at $Y=0$. If $\chi>0$, then $\psi_x<\frac\pi4$ for
every $x$. The function $\Xi$ is continuous in $q$, $s$ and the
$\theta_x$, and $\Xi\le1$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write a quaternion as $\alpha+\beta j$ with $\alpha,\beta\in\C=\R+\R i$. As
$jz=\bar zj$,
\[
(\alpha_1+\beta_1j)(\alpha_2+\beta_2j)=\alpha_1\alpha_2-\beta_1\bar\beta_2+
(\alpha_1\beta_2+\beta_1\bar\alpha_2)j ,
\]
the inverse of a unit quaternion $\alpha+\beta j$ is $\bar\alpha-\beta j$,
and $\beta j$ has $j$-component $\Re\beta$ and $k$-component $\Im\beta$.
Now $g=g(q,s)=\cos s\,e^{iq}+(i\sin s)j$, and with $\varphi_x=\theta_x-q$,
\[
h_x=\cos s\,e^{i\varphi_x}-(i\sin s\,e^{-i\theta_x})j ,
\]
whose real part is $\cos\psi_x$ and whose pure part $P_x$ has norm $\sin
\psi_x$. If $\chi=0$, then $V=g$, whose $j$-part is $(i\sin s)j$. Let $\chi
>0$. Then $\delta(h_x,I)=2(1-\cos\psi_x)^{1/2}<1$, so $\cos\psi_x>\frac34>
\cos\frac\pi4$, and $\log h_x=w_xP_x$ with $w_x=\psi_x/\sin\psi_x$ ($w_x=1$
if $\psi_x=0$). Hence $Y=iy+\eta j$ with
\[
y=\chi\cos s\sum_x\varpi_xw_x\sin\varphi_x,\qquad\eta=-i\chi\sin s\sum_x
\varpi_xw_xe^{-i\theta_x},
\]
and $\exp Y=(C+i\sigma y)+\sigma\eta j$ with $C=\cos|Y|$ and $\sigma=\sin|Y|
/|Y|$. The $j$-part of $V=g\exp Y$ is $\beta j$ with
\[
\begin{split}
\beta&=\cos s\,e^{iq}\sigma\eta+i\sin s\,(C-i\sigma y)\\
&=i\sin s\Bigl(C-\sigma\chi\cos s\sum_x\varpi_xw_xe^{-i\varphi_x}-i\sigma
y\Bigr).
\end{split}
\]
By the formula for $y$ the imaginary part of the bracket vanishes, and
$w_x\cos s\cos\varphi_x=w_x\cos\psi_x=\psi_x\cot\psi_x$, so the bracket is
$\Xi$ and $\beta=i\sin s\,\Xi$. Since $0<\psi\cot\psi\le1$ on $[0,\frac\pi
4)$ and $\sigma\ge0$, $\Xi\le C\le1$. The cut-off $\chi$ is continuous, and
so is $\Xi$ where $\chi>0$; as $\chi\to0$, $|Y|\le\frac\pi4\chi\sum_x
\varpi_x\to0$ and the subtracted term is at most $\chi\sum_x\varpi_x$, so
$\Xi\to1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[the fold of the path-link law]\label{prop:fold}
In the configuration of Proposition~\ref{prop:branches}, with every link
other than the eight private links equal to $I$, let $c_\lambda=
\operatorname{diag}(e^{i\lambda},e^{-i\lambda})$ and let $\pi_\lambda$ be the
law~\eqref{eq:pathlaw} with $c_k=c_\lambda$. Let $f_0$ be the angle of the
cut-off average on the torus, the function $f$ of Proposition~\ref
{prop:branches}, let $q^*\in(0.0741,0.0742)$ be its minimiser on $[-0.005,
0.2227]$, $\gamma^*=f_0(q^*)\in[0.16978261,0.16978263]$, $g^*=e^{iq^*}$,
and $\Lambda=[\gamma^*-10^{-3},\gamma^*+10^{-3}]$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item For $\lambda\in\Lambda$ every preimage of $c_\lambda$ lies on the
torus. For $\lambda<\gamma^*$ there is one, $g_L(\lambda)=e^{iq_L(\lambda)}$
with $q_L\in[-0.0172,-0.0156]$; for $\lambda>\gamma^*$ there are three,
$g_L(\lambda)$ and $g_\pm(\lambda)=e^{iq_\pm}$ with $q_-<q^*<q_+$ and
$|q_\pm-q^*|\le\sqrt{(\lambda-\gamma^*)/2.3}$; for $\lambda=\gamma^*$ there
are two, $g_L$ and $g^*$. Off $\gamma^*$ the value $c_\lambda$ is regular.
\item The weight $e^{-\beta_WS}/\lvert\det D_gV\rvert$ of $g_L(\lambda)$ is
at most $2.78$, and the weights of $g_\pm(\lambda)$ tend to infinity as
$\lambda\downarrow\gamma^*$, for every $\beta_W\ge0$.
\item $\pi_\lambda\to\delta_{g^*}$ as $\lambda\downarrow\gamma^*$ and
$\pi_\lambda\to\delta_{g_L^*}$ as $\lambda\uparrow\gamma^*$, $g_L^*=g_L
(\gamma^*)$, weakly, with $\delta(g^*,g_L^*)\ge0.1268$. Hence for every
$\beta_W\ge0$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there are $\lambda<\gamma^*<\lambda'$ with
$\lambda'-\lambda<\varepsilon$ and $W_1^\delta(\pi_\lambda,\pi_{\lambda'})\ge
0.126$.
\item Fix $c=c_{\gamma^*}$ and move the seven non-path links together,
$\ell_a\mapsto\ell_ae^{it}$, with laws $\pi^{(t)}$. Then $\pi^{(t)}\to
\delta_{g^*}$ as $t\uparrow0$ and $\pi^{(t)}\to\delta_{g_L^*}$ as $t\downarrow
0$. So for every $\beta_W\ge0$ and $\varepsilon>0$ there are two
configurations of the non-path links at total distance $7\sqrt2\,(t'-t)<
10\varepsilon$ whose path-link laws are at $W_1^\delta$ distance at least
$0.126$: the Kantorovich response of the path-link law to its non-path
links is infinite, for every $\beta_W$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Write $g=g_0+g_1i+g_2j+g_3k$ as a unit quaternion, so that the torus $T$ is
$\{e^{iq}\}$, and $\theta_a$ for the angles of the non-path links, $-\frac12$
once and $\frac{49}{100}$ six times. Then $V(g)=g\exp(\chi(m)\frac18\sum_{a
\ne0}\log(g^{-1}\ell_a))$ with $m=\max_a\delta(g^{-1}\ell_a,I)$, since each
$\ell_a$ lies on two paths and $u=w=I$, and the Wilson weight of the path
link is $e^{-\beta_WS(g)}$ with $S(g)=\frac34[\delta(g,I)^2+\delta(g,e^{0.49i})^2]
\in[0,12]$, the three plaquettes through the path link and its partner and
the three through the path link and $I$.

\emph{Step 1, the torus.} For $q\in[q_{lo},q_{hi}]=[\frac{49}{100}-\alpha,
-\frac12+\alpha]\approx[-0.2327,0.2227]$, where $\alpha=\arccos\frac34$, the
maximiser of $\delta(g^{-1}\ell_a,I)$ at $g=e^{iq}$ is the far link when
$q\ge-0.005$ and the six near links when $q\le-0.005$, $m=2\sqrt2\sin(d(q)/2)
\in(\frac12,1)$ with $d(q)=\max\{q+\frac12,\frac{49}{100}-q\}$, and
\[
f_0(q)=q+\frac{\chi(q)}8\Bigl(\frac{244}{100}-7q\Bigr),\qquad\chi(q)=2-4
\sqrt2\sin\frac{d(q)}2 ;
\]
outside $[q_{lo},q_{hi}]$ some $\delta(g^{-1}\ell_a,I)\ge1$, $\chi=0$ and
$f_0(q)=q$. On $[q_{lo},-0.005]$, $\chi'=2\sqrt2\cos\frac{0.49-q}2>0$ and
$\frac{244}{100}-7q>0$, so, as $\chi(-0.005)=2-4\sqrt2\sin0.2475<0.6146$,
\[
f_0'\ge1-\tfrac78\chi\ge1-\tfrac78\cdot0.6146>0.46 :
\]
$f_0$ increases from $q_{lo}$ to $f_0(-0.005)=0.18501\ldots$. On
$[-0.005,q_{hi}]$,
\[
\chi'=-2\sqrt2\cos\tfrac{q+1/2}2<0,\qquad\chi''=\sqrt2\sin\tfrac{q+1/2}2>0,
\]
so $f_0''=\frac18\chi''(\frac{244}{100}-7q)-\frac74\chi'>0$: $f_0$ is strictly
convex, with $f_0'(-0.005^+)=-0.3858\ldots<0$ and $f_0'(q_{hi})=0.7087\ldots
>0$, a unique minimiser $q^*$, and $f_0'(0.0741)<0<f_0'(0.0742)$ places it,
while convexity gives $f_0(0.0741)+10^{-4}f_0'(0.0741)\le\gamma^*\le\min\{
f_0(0.0741),f_0(0.0742)\}$, the stated interval. For $\lambda\in\Lambda
\subset(0.168,0.171)$ a torus preimage $e^{iq}$ with $q\notin[q_{lo},q_{hi}]$
would need $q\equiv\lambda$ modulo $2\pi$, impossible. So the torus
preimages are: one root $q_L$ in $[q_{lo},-0.005]$, which lies in $[-0.0172,
-0.0156]$ because $f_0$ is increasing there and $f_0(-0.0172)<\gamma^*-10^{-3}$,
$f_0(-0.0156)>\gamma^*+10^{-3}$; and in $[-0.005,q_{hi}]$ none if $\lambda<
\gamma^*$, the point $q^*$ if $\lambda=\gamma^*$, and two if $\lambda>
\gamma^*$, as $f_0(-0.005)$ and $f_0(q_{hi})=q_{hi}$ exceed $\lambda$. These
two lie in $[0.05,0.1]$, where $f_0''>4.6$, since $f_0(0.05),f_0(0.1)>
\gamma^*+10^{-3}$, whence $\lambda-\gamma^*\ge\frac{4.6}2(q_\pm-q^*)^2$.
The values of $f_0$, $f_0'$ and $f_0''$ used in this step, and $\alpha\in
(0.7227,0.7228)$, are evaluations with $\sin$ and $\cos$ replaced by their
Taylor polynomials of degree ten, whose remainders are below $10^{-9}$ for
arguments in $[0,0.73]$, and with $1.41421356<\sqrt2<1.41421357$; on
$[0.05,0.1]$ the factors
$\chi''$, $-\chi'$ and $\frac{244}{100}-7q$ of $f_0''$ are monotone and
positive, and their values at the ends give $f_0''>4.8$.

\emph{Step 2, off the torus.} Conjugation by $h\in T$ fixes every $\ell_a$
and $c_\lambda$, so $V(hgh^{-1})=hV(g)h^{-1}$ and the preimages of $c_\lambda$
are invariant under it; every $g\notin T$ is conjugate to $g(q,s)=\cos s\,
e^{iq}+\sin s\,k$ with $s\in(0,\frac\pi2]$. The map $V$ is that of
Lemma~\ref{lem:foldtransverse} with the seven angles $\theta_a$ and
$\varpi_a=\frac18$, so $V_j=0$ and $V_k(g(q,s))=\sin s\,\Xi(q,s)$. Where
$\chi>0$, $\cos s\cos(\theta_a-q)>\frac34$ for every $a$, so $\cos(\theta_a
-q)>0$ and $\psi_a$ is at least the distance of $\theta_a-q$ to $2\pi\Z$.
These distances for the far link and for a near link add up to at least
$\frac{99}{100}$, so $\max_a\psi_a\ge\frac{99}{200}$, $m\ge2\sqrt2\sin
\frac{99}{400}$ and, by $\sin x\ge x-\frac{x^3}6$ and $4\sqrt2>5.6568$,
$\chi\le2-2m<0.6143$. Then $|Y|\le\frac\chi8\sum_a\psi_a<0.6143\cdot
\frac{7\pi}{32}<0.4223$ and $\cos|Y|\ge1-\frac12|Y|^2>0.9108$, while
$\sin|Y|/|Y|\le1$ and $0<\psi_a\cot\psi_a\le1$ bound the subtracted term
of $\Xi$ by $\frac78\chi<0.5376$. Hence $\Xi>\frac13$ at every point, also
where $\chi=0$ and $\Xi=1$, and $V_k(g(q,s))>0$ for $s\in(0,\frac\pi2]$:
$V(g)\notin T$ for $g\notin T$. So $V^{-1}(T)=T$, which with Step 1 gives
(i) except for regularity.

\emph{Step 3, the Jacobian at a torus point.} $D_gV$ at $g=e^{iq}$
commutes with the differential of conjugation by $e^{i\varphi}$, which
fixes the axial line $g\cdot i\R$ and rotates the transverse plane by
$2\varphi$; a linear map commuting with all these rotations preserves the
line and the plane and is a complex scalar $\lambda_\perp e^{i\omega}$ on the
plane. The axial eigenvalue is $f_0'(q)$, and $\lambda_\perp=\lVert\partial_s
V(g(q,s))|_{s=0}\rVert=|\partial_sV_k(q,0)|$, since $\partial_sg=k$ is a unit
transverse vector and $V_j=0$. So $\lvert\det D_gV\rvert=|f_0'(q)|
\lambda_\perp(q)^2$, and by Step~2, as $\Xi$ is continuous,
$\lambda_\perp(q)=\Xi(q,0)\in(\frac13,1]$. At $s=0$ and $q\in[q_{lo},
q_{hi}]$, $\psi_a=|\theta_a-q|$ and $|Y|=\Delta(q):=\frac\chi8(\frac{244}
{100}-7q)=f_0(q)-q$, so
\[
\lambda_\perp(q)=\cos\Delta-\frac{\sin\Delta}\Delta\,\frac\chi8\sum_a
(\theta_a-q)\cot(\theta_a-q).
\]
For $q\in[-0.0172,-0.0156]$ the near links are the maximiser, with $d=
\frac{49}{100}-q\in[0.5056,0.5072]$ and $\chi=2-4\sqrt2\sin\frac d2$, so
$0.07067<\frac\chi8<0.07315$ by $x-\frac{x^3}6\le\sin x\le x$ and
$5.6568<4\sqrt2<5.65686$. The partial fractions $x\cot x=1-2\sum_{n\ge1}
x^2/(n^2\pi^2-x^2)$, with $\frac1{1-u}\ge1+u$, $\sum_nn^{-2}=\frac{\pi^2}6$
and $\sum_nn^{-4}=\frac{\pi^4}{90}$, give $x\cot x\le1-\frac{x^2}3-
\frac{x^4}{45}$ for $0<|x|<\pi$. The far link has $|\theta_a-q|\ge0.4828$
and the near ones $|\theta_a-q|\ge0.5056$, so $\sum_a(\theta_a-q)^2>1.7668$,
$\sum_a(\theta_a-q)^4>0.4464$, and the subtracted term is at most
$\frac{\sin\Delta}\Delta$ times $0.07315\,(7-0.5889-0.0099)<0.4683$. Further
$\Delta\in[0.1801,0.1873]$, $\cos\Delta\ge1-\frac12\Delta^2>0.9824$ and
$\frac{\sin\Delta}\Delta\le1-\frac16\Delta^2+\frac1{120}\Delta^4<0.99461$,
so $\lambda_\perp>0.9824-0.99461\cdot0.4683>0.5166$ on this interval.
At $q_L$ the near links are the strict
maximiser and at $q_\pm$ the far link is, with $m\in(\frac12,1)$, so $V$ is
real-analytic near these points; $f_0'(q_L)\in[1.36,1.37]$ by the formula,
$f_0'(q_\pm)\ne0$ by strict convexity and $\lambda_\perp>0$, so $c_\lambda$
is regular for $\lambda\ne\gamma^*$, and~\eqref{eq:pathlaw} is the
continuous disintegration there. The weight of $g_L$ is at most $1/(1.36
\cdot0.5166^2)<2.78$, and those of $g_\pm$ are at least $e^{-12\beta_W}/
|f_0'(q_\pm)|$, as $\lambda_\perp\le1$, with $f_0'(q_\pm)\to f_0'(q^*)=0$.
This is (ii).

\emph{Step 4, the limits.} Let $f(g)=\delta(g,g^*)$, $1$-Lipschitz for
$\delta$ and at most $2\sqrt2$. For $\lambda\downarrow\gamma^*$,
$\pi_\lambda(f)\le2.78\cdot2\sqrt2/(w_-+w_+)+\sqrt2\max_\pm|q_\pm-q^*|\to0$,
and as $\pi_\lambda$ lives on three points converging to $\{g^*,g_L^*\}$,
$\pi_\lambda\to\delta_{g^*}$. For $\lambda\uparrow\gamma^*$, $\pi_\lambda=
\delta_{g_L(\lambda)}\to\delta_{g_L^*}$. For $\lambda\in\Lambda$, $q^*-q_L
(\lambda)\in[0.0897,0.0914]$, so $\pi_\lambda(f)=2\sqrt2\sin\frac{q^*-q_L}2
\ge0.1268$, and the Kantorovich duality $W_1^\delta(\pi_\lambda,\pi_{\lambda'})
\ge|\pi_\lambda(f)-\pi_{\lambda'}(f)|$ gives (iii).

\emph{Step 5, the exterior form.} Multiplying every path on the right by
$e^{it}$ gives $V(ge^{it};z_t)=V(g;z_0)e^{it}$, the covariance of $V^\sharp$
with $h_1=I$, $h_2=e^{-it}$. So $g$ solves $V(g;z_t)=c_{\gamma^*}$ iff
$g'=ge^{-it}$ solves $V(g';z_0)=c_{\gamma^*-t}$, with the same Jacobian,
and the action at $g=g'e^{it}$ under $z_t$ differs from $S(g')$ by at most
$6|t|$. Hence $\pi^{(t)}$ is the image of $\pi_{\gamma^*-t}$ under the
translation by $e^{it}$, which moves every point by $\sqrt2|t|$, with
weights multiplied by factors in $[e^{-6\beta_W|t|},e^{6\beta_W|t|}]$, and
the limits of Step~4 persist as $t\to0$; each non-path link moves by
$\sqrt2|t'-t|$. This is (iv).
\end{proof}

The mechanism is the one Proposition~\ref{prop:branches} exhibits: at the
fold the density $1/\lvert\det D_gV\rvert$ is infinite, two branches carry
all the mass on one side and do not exist on the other, and the Wilson
weight cannot repair it, since a vanishing Jacobian wins against any fixed
$e^{-\beta_WS}$. The configuration is bad for every $r\le\frac1{32}$. So item
(i) of Sec.~\ref{ssec:remains} in its original form, a Lipschitz bound for the
law~\eqref{eq:pathlaw} in the non-path links, is false; what can be asked is
the response of the law of all eight private links of a bad pair, in which
the non-path links are integrated over the bad set and
Lemma~\ref{lem:privatesubmersion} removes both the branches and the
density. Lemma~\ref{lem:wilsononly} settles that response for every link
that enters only the action; what remains is its response to the inside
links $u_a,w_a$, which move the fibre $\{V=c_k\}$ while the bad set does
not, and the question is the mass that the law gives to the set where the
fibre is tangent to the boundary of the bad set.

\emph{The site of a bad pair.} The response of the eight private links to
the inside links $u_a,w_a$ is avoided by putting those links into the
variables of the law. Let $k=(y,\mu)$, $k'=(y-e_\mu,\mu)$ and
$k''=(y+e_\mu,\mu)$. The inside links of $k'$ in $B(y)$ are the links
$u_a$ of $k$, and the inside links of $k''$ in $B(y+e_\mu)$ are the links
$w_a$ of $k$: consecutive pairs along $\mu$ share their inside
$\mu$-links. The \emph{site} of $k$ is the set $\mathcal S_k$ of the $24$
links $\ell_a$, $u_a$, $w_a$ ($a\ne0$ for the last two) and the path links
$\ell'_0$, $\ell''_0$ of $k'$ and $k''$, with the cost
$\sum_{e\in\mathcal S_k}\delta(\cdot,\cdot)$. Its links are based in
$B(y-e_\mu)\cup B(y)\cup B(y+e_\mu)$, and the cut-off averages that contain
a link of $\mathcal S_k$ are $V^\sharp_k$, which contains site links only,
$V^\sharp_{k'}$, whose other links are the non-path links $z'$ of $k'$ and
its inside links $u'$ in $B(y-e_\mu)$, and $V^\sharp_{k''}$, with $z''$ and
$w''$ in $B(y+2e_\mu)$. Every other link enters the law of the site only
through the Wilson weight.

\begin{lemma}[the law of a site]\label{lem:sitelaw}
Let $r\le\frac1{32}$, suppose $d(\ell'_a,c_{k'})$, $d(u'_a,I)$,
$d(\ell''_a,c_{k''})$, $d(w''_a,I)\le r$ for $a\ne0$, and let $E$ be a
measurable set of site variables contained in $\{d(u_a,I)\le r,\
d(w_a,I)\le r,\ a\ne0\}$. Then the law of the site given the exterior
$\sigma$, the three constraints $V^\sharp_k=c_k$, $V^\sharp_{k'}=c_{k'}$,
$V^\sharp_{k''}=c_{k''}$ and $E$ is
\[
\frac1Z\,e^{-\beta_WS}\mathbf 1_E\,J_{22}^{-1}\mathrm{vol}_{M_k}(d\ell\,du
\,dw)\,\frac{\delta_{\Gamma'}(d\ell'_0)}{\lvert\det D_{\ell'_0}V^\sharp_{k'}
\rvert}\,\frac{\delta_{\Gamma''}(d\ell''_0)}{\lvert\det D_{\ell''_0}
V^\sharp_{k''}\rvert},
\]
where $M_k=\{V^\sharp_k=c_k\}$ in the $22$ variables $(\ell,u,w)$, $J_{22}=
\det(DV^\sharp_kDV^{\sharp*}_k)^{1/2}\ge\sigma_0^3$ almost everywhere,
$\Gamma'=\Gamma'(z',u',u)$ and $\Gamma''=\Gamma''(z'',w'',w)$ are the
unique solutions of Proposition~\ref{prop:goodside} for $k'$ and $k''$, and
the two determinants lie in $[(1-\kappa_0)^3,(1+\kappa_0)^3]$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Only the three named constraints involve site variables. For $k'$ the
hypothesis of Proposition~\ref{prop:goodside} holds, its inside links in
$B(y)$ being the $u_a$, which $E$ keeps within $r$ of $I$; so
$\ell'_0\mapsto V^\sharp_{k'}$ has the single regular preimage $\Gamma'$,
the Haar disintegration of $\ell'_0$ along it is the atom divided by the
determinant, and the determinant bounds are those of the proposition;
likewise for $k''$. The Haar disintegration of $(\ell,u,w)$ along
$V^\sharp_k$ is $J_{22}^{-1}\mathrm{vol}_{M_k}$ by the coarea formula.
Since $DV^\sharp_kDV^{\sharp*}_k$ is the sum over the variables of the
nonnegative terms $D_eV^\sharp_k(D_eV^\sharp_k)^*$, it dominates the sum
over the eight private links, which is at least $\sigma_0^2$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:privatesubmersion}. The product of the three
disintegrations is the disintegration of the product Haar measure along
the three constraints, and the Wilson weight and $\mathbf 1_E$ multiply it.
\end{proof}

The constraint of the site's own pair is thus a fixed measure on
$M_k\cap E$: the exterior enters only through $S$, through the positions
$\Gamma'$, $\Gamma''$ of two atoms, and through two densities on the good
side, whose variation the next lemma bounds.

\begin{lemma}[the good-side density is log-Lipschitz]\label{lem:goodsidedensity}
Under the hypothesis of Proposition~\ref{prop:goodside}, let one link of
the pair move along a unit-speed geodesic. Then
$\bigl|\frac d{dt}\log\lvert\det D_gV\rvert\bigr|\le64.94$ when the link
is a non-path link and $\le32.47$ when it is an inside link.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:goodside}, $\lvert\det D_gV\rvert=
\lvert\det T\rvert$ with $T=I-\frac78E_N\bar L$, so $\frac d{dt}\log
\lvert\det T\rvert=\operatorname{tr}(T^{-1}\dot T)$, which is at most
$3\lVert T^{-1}\rVert\lVert\dot T\rVert$ on the three-dimensional $\g$, with
$\lVert T^{-1}\rVert\le(1-\kappa_0)^{-1}$ and $\dot T=-\frac78(\dot E_N\bar L
+E_N\dot{\bar L})$, $\lVert\bar L\rVert\le\Lambda_0:=\theta_0/\sin\theta_0
=1.02115$, $\lVert E_N\rVert\le1$.

For a power series $\varphi$ whose radius of convergence exceeds the
spectral radius of a normal operator $A$ with spectral projections $P_i$
and eigenvalues $\lambda_i$, the derivative is
$d\varphi(A)[B]=\sum_{i,j}\varphi[\lambda_i,\lambda_j]P_iBP_j$, with the
divided differences $\varphi[\lambda_i,\lambda_j]$ of
Daleckii--Krein~\cite{DK65}; the blocks $P_iBP_j$ are orthogonal for the
Hilbert--Schmidt product, so $\lVert d\varphi(A)[B]\rVert\le\max_{i,j}
\lvert\varphi[\lambda_i,\lambda_j]\rvert\lVert B\rVert_{HS}$, and by the
Hermite--Genocchi formula $\varphi[\lambda_i,\lambda_j]=\int_0^1\varphi'(
(1-u)\lambda_i+u\lambda_j)\,du$ this maximum is at most the maximum of
$\lvert\varphi'\rvert$ on the convex hull of the spectrum. With
$E_Y=e(\operatorname{ad}Y)$, $L_Y=f(\operatorname{ad}Y)$, $e(x)=(e^x-1)/x$,
$f(x)=x/(e^x-1)$, and $\lVert\operatorname{ad}W\rVert_{HS}=2\lVert W\rVert$,
this gives $\lVert\dot L_{Y}\rVert\le2M_L\lVert\dot Y\rVert$ and
$\lVert\dot E_N\rVert\le2M_E\lVert\dot N\rVert$, where $M_L$ and $M_E$ bound
$\lvert f'\rvert$ and $\lvert e'\rvert$ on the segments $i[-a',a']$,
$a'\le\sqrt2\cdot16r\le\frac{\sqrt2}2$, and $i[-b',b']$,
$b'\le\sqrt2\cdot14r\le0.6188$, which contain the spectra $\{0,\pm ia'\}$
of $\operatorname{ad}Y_x$ and $\{0,\pm ib'\}$ of $\operatorname{ad}N$. Since
$e'(z)=\int_0^1te^{tz}\,dt$, $\lvert e'(iy)\rvert\le\frac12$, so $M_E=\frac12$.
Since $f'(iy)=-\frac12-i\frac{\sin y-y}{4\sin^2(y/2)}$, and $y-\sin y\le
\frac{y^3}6$, $\sin\frac y2\ge\frac y2(1-\frac{y^2}{24})$,
$M_L\le\bigl(\frac14+\frac{a^2}{36}(1-\frac{a^2}{24})^{-4}\bigr)^{1/2}\le
0.5149$ at $a=\frac{\sqrt2}2$.

Along the motion the fixed point $X$ moves with $\lVert\dot X\rVert\le\dot x$,
$\dot x=1.1986$ for a non-path link and $0.5993$ for an inside link, by the
proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:goodside}. For a path that does not contain
the moving link, $\dot Y_x=-L_{Y_x}E_{-X}\dot X$, so $\lVert\dot Y_x\rVert\le
\Lambda_0\dot x$; for a path that contains it, $\log(e^Ye^{t\zeta'})=Y+
tL_{-Y}\zeta'+O(t^2)$ adds $\Lambda_0$. With $n=2$ moving paths for a
non-path link and $n=1$ for an inside link, $\lVert\dot N\rVert\le
\frac{\Lambda_0}{16}(14\dot x+n)$ and $\lVert\dot{\bar L}\rVert\le2M_L
\Lambda_0(\dot x+\frac n{14})$. Hence
\[
\Bigl|\frac d{dt}\log\lvert\det T\rvert\Bigr|\le\frac{21}8\,
\frac{2M_E\Lambda_0\lVert\dot N\rVert+\lVert\dot{\bar L}\rVert}{1-\kappa_0},
\]
which is at most $64.94$ and $32.47$ in the two cases, with
$(1-\kappa_0)^{-1}\le9.390$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[the site of a bad pair responds boundedly]\label{thm:site}
Under the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:sitelaw}, let $\sigma,\sigma'$ differ
only at one link $e'$ outside $\mathcal S_k$, and let $\pi(\cdot\mid\sigma)$
be the law of the site of that lemma. Then
\[
W_1\bigl(\pi(\cdot\mid\sigma),\pi(\cdot\mid\sigma')\bigr)\le C_{e'}\,
d(\sigma_{e'},\sigma'_{e'}),
\]
for the cost $\sum_{e\in\mathcal S_k}\delta$, with $C_{e'}=24\,n_p(e')
\beta_W$ if $e'$ enters only the Wilson weight, $n_p(e')\le6$ the number of
its plaquettes that contain a site link, $C_{e'}=197\beta_W+2206$ if $e'$
is a non-path link of $k'$ or $k''$, and $C_{e'}=87\beta_W+1103$ if $e'$
is an inside link of $k'$ in $B(y-e_\mu)$ or of $k''$ in $B(y+2e_\mu)$. The
constants do not depend on $c_k$, $c_{k'}$, $c_{k''}$, $E$ or the rest of
$\sigma$, and every branch of $V^\sharp_k=c_k$ inside the site is
integrated, not compared.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Move $\sigma_{e'}$ along a unit-speed geodesic, $0\le t\le T=d(\sigma_{e'},
\sigma'_{e'})$; geodesic balls of radius $r\le\frac1{32}$ are convex, so
the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:sitelaw} hold along the way. By that
lemma, $\pi_t=(\Phi_t)_*\mu_t$ with
$\Phi_t(\ell,u,w)=(\ell,u,w,\Gamma'_t,\Gamma''_t)$ and $\mu_t$ the law on
$M_k\cap E$ with density $h_t=e^{-\beta_WS_t}J'^{-1}_tJ''^{-1}_t$ against
the fixed measure $\mathbf 1_EJ_{22}^{-1}\mathrm{vol}_{M_k}$; plaquettes
without a site link are constant on $M_k$ and cancel. For $f$ Lipschitz
with constant one for the site cost, whose oscillation is at most the
diameter $24\cdot2\sqrt2$,
\[
\pi_T(f)-\pi_0(f)=(\mu_T-\mu_0)(f\circ\Phi_T)+\mu_0(f\circ\Phi_T-f\circ
\Phi_0).
\]
The second term is at most $\dot x\,T$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:goodside},
since one atom moves, and it vanishes when $e'$ enters only the Wilson
weight. For the first, $\frac d{dt}\mu_t(\varphi)=\Cov_{\mu_t}(\varphi,
\partial_t\log h_t)$ and $\lvert\Cov(\varphi,\psi)\rvert\le\frac14
\operatorname{osc}\varphi\operatorname{osc}\psi$, so the first term is at
most $24\sqrt2\,T\sup\lvert\partial_t\log h_t\rvert$, and
$\lvert\partial_t\log h_t\rvert\le\beta_W\lvert\partial_tS_t\rvert+
\lvert\partial_t\log J'_t\rvert$. Links of a plaquette moving at total
geodesic speed $v$ give $\lvert\dot s_p\rvert\le v/\sqrt2$, by the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:wilsononly}. If $e'$ enters only the Wilson weight,
$\operatorname{osc}\partial_tS_t\le\sqrt2\,n_p(e')$ and $J'$ does not move,
which gives $24n_p\beta_W$. If $e'=\ell'_a$, it shares at most one
plaquette with a site link, and the atom $\Gamma'$ moves at speed at most
$1.1986$ through its six plaquettes, so $\lvert\partial_tS_t\rvert\le(1+6
\cdot1.1986)/\sqrt2\le5.793$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:goodsidedensity} bounds the
density term by $64.94$; hence $C_{e'}\le24\sqrt2(5.793\beta_W+64.94)+
1.1986<197\beta_W+2206$. If $e'=u'_a$, it shares no plaquette with a site
link, the atom moves at speed at most $0.5993$, $\lvert\partial_tS_t\rvert
\le6\cdot0.5993/\sqrt2\le2.543$, and $C_{e'}\le24\sqrt2(2.543\beta_W+32.47)
+0.5993<87\beta_W+1103$. Kantorovich duality gives the bound on $W_1$.
\end{proof}

\emph{The eight private links alone.} The fold of
Proposition~\ref{prop:fold} is also reached by moving one inside link, and
the law of the eight private links restricted to a fixed set of non-path
links then has no response bound that holds for every such set. The
direction matters: a link $(x,\mu)$ with $o_\mu=0$ is a tree link when
$o_\nu=0$ for every $\nu>\mu$, so a block has $p_\mu=8-2^\mu$ active
inside $\mu$-links, $7$, $6$, $4$ and $0$ for $\mu=0,1,2,3$. For $\mu=3$
every $u_a$ and $w_a$ is a tree link, the law of the eight private links
does not depend on them, and Lemma~\ref{lem:wilsononly} is the whole
answer. For the other three directions the next two results show that
the answer depends on the set over which the non-path links are
integrated.

\begin{proposition}[an inside link at the fold]\label{prop:insidefold}
Take the configuration of Proposition~\ref{prop:fold} for a direction
$\mu\le2$, with $c_k=c_{\gamma^*}$ and the offsets chosen so that the
inside link $u_b$ of one of the six non-path links at the angle
$\frac{49}{100}$ is active. Replace $u_b$ by $u_b(t)=\operatorname{diag}
(e^{it},e^{-it})$, keep every other link, and let $\pi^{(t)}$ be the
law~\eqref{eq:pathlaw}. There is $\tau>0$ such that for $0<|t|<\tau$
every preimage of $c_k$ lies on the torus and is regular; for $t>0$ there
is one, $g_L(t)$, and for $t<0$ there are three, $g_L(t)$ and $g_\pm(t)=
e^{iq_\pm(t)}$ with $q_\pm(t)\to q^*$, where $g_L(t)\to g_L^*$. The weight
of $g_L(t)$ tends to that of $g_L^*$, at most $2.78$, and the weights of
$g_\pm(t)$ tend to infinity as $t\uparrow0$, for every $\beta_W\ge0$.
Hence $\pi^{(t)}\to\delta_{g^*}$ as $t\uparrow0$ and $\pi^{(t)}\to
\delta_{g_L^*}$ as $t\downarrow0$, and for every $\beta_W\ge0$ and
$\varepsilon>0$ there are $t<0<t'$ with $d(u_b(t),u_b(t'))=\sqrt2\,(t'-t)
<\varepsilon$ and $W_1^\delta(\pi^{(t)},\pi^{(t')})\ge0.126$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\emph{The action and the paths.} The inside link $u_b$ has $\mu$-coordinate
$2y_\mu$ and the private links $2y_\mu+1$, and the two $\mu$-links of a
plaquette have the same $\mu$-coordinate, so $u_b$ shares no plaquette
with the path link and $S(g)$ is that of Proposition~\ref{prop:fold}. All
links lie in $T$, so conjugation by $T$ is still a symmetry, and the
fourteen paths of nonzero offset have the angles $-\frac12$ twice,
$\frac{49}{100}$ eleven times, and $\frac{49}{100}+t$ once, on the path from
$x_b$. For $g=g_0+g_1i+g_2j+g_3k$ with $g_0+ig_1=\varrho e^{iq}$,
$\varrho>0$, the real part of $g^{-1}e^{i\theta}$ is $\varrho\cos(\theta-q)$,
and $\delta(h,I)$ decreases in the real part of $h$; so the order of the
distances $\delta(v_x,I)$ is the order of the numbers $|\theta-q|$, for
every such $g$ and not only on $T$.

\emph{Localisation.} $V$ is jointly continuous in $(g,t)$ and $\SU(2)$ is
compact, and by Proposition~\ref{prop:fold}(i) the preimages of $c_k$ at
$t=0$ are $g_L^*$ and $g^*$. So for open neighbourhoods $U_L$ of $g_L^*$
and $U^*$ of $g^*$ there is $\tau>0$ such that every preimage at $|t|<\tau$
lies in $U_L\cup U^*$; take $\tau\le10^{-3}$.

\emph{Near $g^*$.} For $q\in[0.05,0.1]$ and $|t|\le10^{-3}$, $(\frac12+q)-
(\frac{49}{100}+|t|-q)\ge0.109$, so the far link is the strict maximiser,
$m=2\sqrt2\sin\frac{q+1/2}2\in(0.76,0.84)\subset(\frac12,1)$, and $V$ is
real-analytic in $(g,t)$ near $(g^*,0)$. On $T$ its angle is
\begin{gather*}
f(q;t)=f_0(q)+\frac{\chi_0(q)}{16}\,t ,\\
\chi_0(q)=2-4\sqrt2\sin\tfrac{q+1/2}2\in(0.32,0.48),
\end{gather*}
since only the angle sum changes, by $t$. Since $|\chi_0''|=\sqrt2\sin
\frac{q+1/2}2$ is less than $\frac12$, the second derivative of $f$
exceeds $4.6-10^{-4}$ on $[0.05,0.1]$, and by Step~1 of the proof of
Proposition~\ref{prop:fold} both $f(0.05;t)$ and $f(0.1;t)$ exceed
$\gamma^*+10^{-3}-\frac{|t|}{32}>\gamma^*$. Hence for $t>0$, $f(q;t)>f_0(q)\ge\gamma^*$ on
$[0.05,0.1]$ and there is no torus preimage in $U^*$, and for $t<0$,
$f(q^*;t)<\gamma^*$ and strict convexity give exactly two, $q_-(t)<q^*<
q_+(t)$, with $f'(q_\pm(t);t)\ne0$; since $f(\cdot;t)\to f_0$ in $C^2$ and
$q^*$ is the only zero of $f_0-\gamma^*$ on $[0.05,0.1]$, $q_\pm(t)\to q^*$
and $f'(q_\pm(t);t)\to f_0'(q^*)=0$. Off the torus, every $g\in U^*$ is
$T$-conjugate to $g(q,s)=\cos s\,e^{iq}+\sin s\,k$ with $s\ge0$ small and $q$
near $q^*$, and conjugation by $T$ preserves $d(\cdot,g^*)$. The
paths lie in $T$, so $V$ is the map of Lemma~\ref{lem:foldtransverse} with
the fourteen angles above and $\varpi_x=\frac1{16}$: $V_j=0$ and $V_k(q,s;t)=
\sin s\,\Xi_t(q,s)$, with $\Xi_t$ continuous in $(q,s,t)$, and
$\Xi_0(q^*,0)>\frac13$ by Step~2 of the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:fold}.
So $\Xi_t>0$ near $(q^*,0,0)$ and $V_k(q,s;t)>0$ for small $s>0$:
shrinking $U^*$ and $\tau$, there is no preimage off $T$ in $U^*$. As in
Step~3 of that proof, $\lvert\det D_gV\rvert=|f'|\lambda_\perp^2$ at torus
points, with $\lambda_\perp=\Xi_t(q,0)\le1$; so the weights of $g_\pm(t)$
are at least $e^{-12\beta_W}/|f'(q_\pm(t);t)|\to\infty$.

\emph{Near $g_L^*$.} For $q\in[-0.0182,-0.0146]$ and $|t|\le10^{-3}$, the
six near paths are farther from $g$ than the far link by at least
$(\frac{49}{100}-q-10^{-3})-(\frac12+q)\ge0.0182$ in angle, and their
chordal distance $2\sqrt2\sin\frac{\theta}2$, $\theta\in[0.503,0.510]$,
lies in $(0.70,0.72)\subset(\frac12,1)$. Let $\Psi_+$ and $\Psi_-$ be the
cut-off averages computed with the maximum taken, respectively, at the
path from $x_b$, of angle $\frac{49}{100}+t$, and at an unmoved near path,
of angle $\frac{49}{100}$. Both are real-analytic in $(g,t)$ near
$(g_L^*,0)$, and both equal $V(\cdot;0)$ near $g_L^*$ at $t=0$, when the
two paths coincide. The difference of the real parts of the two path
variables is
\[
\varrho\bigl(\cos(\tfrac{49}{100}-q)-\cos(\tfrac{49}{100}+t-q)\bigr)
=2\varrho\sin(\tfrac{49}{100}+\tfrac t2-q)\sin\tfrac t2 ,
\]
and $\sin(\frac{49}{100}+\frac t2-q)>0.48$, so near $g_L^*$ the moved path
is the maximiser for $t>0$ and an unmoved one for $t<0$: $V=\Psi_+$ for
$t\ge0$ and $V=\Psi_-$ for $t\le0$. Since $D_g\Psi_\pm(g_L^*,0)=D_gV(g_L^*;0)$
is invertible, with determinant $f_0'(q_L^*)\lambda_\perp(q_L^*)^2>0$, the
implicit function theorem gives a closed ball $\bar U_L$ about $g_L^*$ and
$\tau>0$ such that each equation $\Psi_\pm(g;t)=c_k$, $|t|<\tau$, has
exactly one solution in $\bar U_L$, at which $D_g\Psi_\pm$ is invertible.
Conjugation by $T$ fixes $g_L^*$ and maps $\bar U_L$ onto itself, so the
solution is fixed by it and lies in $T$. This is the one preimage $g_L(t)$
in $U_L$, for either sign of $t$; it is regular, it tends to $g_L^*$, and
its weight tends to that of $g_L^*$, which is at most $2.78$ by
Proposition~\ref{prop:fold}(ii).

\emph{The limits.} For $t>0$, $\pi^{(t)}=\delta_{g_L(t)}\to\delta_{g_L^*}$.
For $t<0$, with $f=\delta(\cdot,g^*)$ and $w_\pm$ the weights of
$g_\pm(t)$, $\pi^{(t)}(f)\le2.78(1+o(1))\,2\sqrt2/(w_++w_-)+\max_\pm\delta(g_\pm(t),g^*)\to0$, so $\pi^{(t)}\to
\delta_{g^*}$. As $\delta(g^*,g_L^*)\ge0.1268$ by
Proposition~\ref{prop:fold}(iii), Kantorovich duality with $f$ gives the
last statement; $t\mapsto e^{it}$ has geodesic speed $\sqrt2$.
\end{proof}

So the path-link law responds to an inside link as it does to the
non-path links in Proposition~\ref{prop:fold}(iv). The law of all eight
private links is the one that the bad side asks about, and the next
theorem shows that its response to an inside link is not bounded
independently of the set $B$ of non-path links over which it is
restricted, in contrast with Lemma~\ref{lem:wilsononly}.

\begin{theorem}[no bound uniform in the restricting set]\label{thm:eightlinkuniform}
In the configuration of Proposition~\ref{prop:insidefold}, let $z_0$ be its
seven non-path links, let $B_\varepsilon$ be the set of $z$ with
$d(\ell_a,\ell_a(z_0))<\varepsilon$ for $a\ne0$, and let $Q_{t,\varepsilon}$
be the law of the eight private links given $u_b=u_b(t)$, the other links,
$V^\sharp_k=c_k$ and $z\in B_\varepsilon$, that is $\frac1Z\mathbf
1_{B_\varepsilon}J_8^{-1}e^{-\beta_WS}\mathrm{vol}_M$. For every $\beta_W
\ge0$ and $L>0$ there are $t<0<t'$ with $\sqrt2\,(t'-t)<1/L$ and
$\varepsilon>0$ such that
\[
W_1\bigl(Q_{t,\varepsilon},Q_{t',\varepsilon}\bigr)\ge0.12
\]
for the cost $\sum_a\delta(\ell_a,\ell'_a)$. For $\varepsilon<0.4$ the set
$B_\varepsilon$ lies in the bad set $\{\max_{a\ne0}d(\ell_a,c_k)>r\}$ for
every $r\le\frac1{32}$. So there is no constant $C$, for any $\beta_W$,
with $W_1\le C\,d(u_b,u'_b)$ for the law of the eight private links
restricted to every fixed measurable set of non-path links.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Step 1, the fibre over $B_\varepsilon$.} Fix $t$ with $0<|t|<\tau$,
and let $g_1,\dots,g_n$ be the preimages at $z_0$ of
Proposition~\ref{prop:insidefold}, all regular.
By compactness and continuity, for small $\varepsilon$ every solution of
$V(g,z)=c_k$ with $z\in B_\varepsilon$ has $g$ in one of disjoint balls
$U_i$ about the $g_i$. At $g_\pm(t)$ ($t<0$) the far link is the strict
maximiser, and at $g_L(t)$ for $t>0$ the moved path is, by the margins of
that proof; there $V$ is real-analytic in $(g,z)$ near $(g_i,z_0)$, and the
implicit function theorem gives a smooth $G_i$ on $B_\varepsilon$ with
$M\cap(U_i\times B_\varepsilon)=\{(G_i(z),z)\}$. At $g_L(t)$ for $t<0$ the
maximum at $(g_i,z_0)$ is attained by the six functions $m_a=\delta(g^{-1}
\ell_a,I)$ of the near offsets $a$ (for $a=b$ through the path from
$x'_b$) and by no other path, since the moved path is shorter by a margin
proportional to $|t|$ and the far link by $0.0182$. Near $(g_i,z_0)$, $V$
equals at each point one of the six real-analytic functions $\Psi_a=g\exp(
\phi(m_a)N)$, one with the largest $m_a$, and at $z=z_0$ the six coincide
as functions of $g$. In the chart $F(X,z)=\log(c_k^{-1}V(g_ie^X,z))$,
with $F_a$ defined from $\Psi_a$ in the same way, the derivatives
$D_XF_a(0,z_0)$ are therefore one invertible map $A_i$, and the function $s\mapsto F(X+s(X'-X),z)$ is
a continuous selection of finitely many $C^1$ functions; at a point of
differentiability that is not an isolated point of any of the closed sets
where it equals one of them, its derivative equals theirs, and the
exceptional points are countable. Hence, for $\lVert X\rVert,\lVert X'
\rVert\le\varrho$ and $z\in B_\varepsilon$,
\[
\bigl\lVert F(X',z)-F(X,z)-A_i(X'-X)\bigr\rVert\le\eta\,\lVert X'-X\rVert,
\]
with $\eta=\eta(\varrho,\varepsilon)\to0$, as every $D_X F_a$ is within
$\eta$ of $A_i$ there. With $\eta\lVert A_i^{-1}\rVert\le\frac12$ and
$\varepsilon$ small, $X\mapsto X-A_i^{-1}F(X,z)$ is a contraction of the
$\varrho$-ball into itself, and $V(\cdot,z)=c_k$ has exactly one solution
$G_i(z)$ there, Lipschitz in $z$ with constant at most $2\lVert A_i^{-1}
\rVert\operatorname{Lip}_zV$. In all cases $M\cap(\SU(2)\times
B_\varepsilon)$ is the disjoint union of the graphs $\Gamma_i$ of the
$G_i$, and $\lvert\det D_gV\rvert$, wherever $V$ is differentiable on
$\Gamma_i$, lies within a factor $1\pm\eta'$ of $\lvert\det A_i\rvert$,
$\eta'\to0$ with $\varrho,\varepsilon$.

\emph{Step 2, the density on a graph.} At a point of $\Gamma_i$ where $V$ is
differentiable and $G_i$ is differentiable at $z$, write $DV=(A\ B)$ with
$A=D_gV$, $B=D_zV$; then $DG_i=-A^{-1}B$, and by the determinant identity
$\det(I+PQ)=\det(I+QP)$,
\[
J_8=\det(AA^*+BB^*)^{1/2}=\lvert\det A\rvert\det(I+DG_i^*DG_i)^{1/2}.
\]
The second factor is the area element of the Lipschitz graph $\Gamma_i$
over $z$, so $J_8^{-1}\mathrm{vol}_M=\lvert\det D_gV\rvert^{-1}dz$ on
$\Gamma_i$, $dz$ Haar measure on the seven links carried by $G_i$,
provided the two differentiability conditions hold for almost every $z$.
For $G_i$ this is Rademacher's theorem. $V$ is differentiable at
$(G_i(z),z)$ except where two of the six $m_a$ tie, and for $a\ne a'$ the
tie set is null: write $\ell_a=he^{is}$ along the circles $\ell_aT$, along
which Haar measure is uniform, fix the other coordinates, and let
$\psi(s)$ be $m_a-m_{a'}$ at $(G_i(z_s),z_s)$. Its almost-everywhere
derivative is at least $\partial_sm_a-\lVert D_gm_a-D_gm_{a'}\rVert\,
\sqrt2\operatorname{Lip}G_i$; here $\partial_sm_a=\sqrt2\cos\frac\theta2$
on $T$, with $\theta$ the angle of $g^{-1}\ell_a$, which is at least
$1.36$ at $(g_i,z_0)$ and exceeds $1.3$ near it, while $D_gm_a-D_gm_{a'}$ vanishes at $z=z_0$, where
$\ell_a=\ell_{a'}$. So $\psi$ is strictly increasing for small $\varrho,
\varepsilon$, has one zero on each circle, and the tie set is null by
Fubini, the circles meeting $B_\varepsilon$ in arcs.

\emph{Step 3, the limit $\varepsilon\to0$.} By Steps 1 and 2,
\[
Q_{t,\varepsilon}(\varphi)=\frac{\sum_i\int_{B_\varepsilon}\varphi(G_i(z),
z)\,e^{-\beta_WS}\lvert\det D_gV\rvert^{-1}\,dz}{\sum_i\int_{B_\varepsilon}
e^{-\beta_WS}\lvert\det D_gV\rvert^{-1}\,dz},
\]
the integrands evaluated at $(G_i(z),z)$. As $\varepsilon\to0$, $G_i(z)\to
g_i$ uniformly on $B_\varepsilon$ and the weights converge uniformly to
those of $g_i$ in $\pi^{(t)}$, so $Q_{t,\varepsilon}(\varphi)\to\pi^{(t)}
(\varphi(\cdot,z_0))$ for every continuous $\varphi$.

\emph{Step 4, the gap.} Let $\varphi(\ell)=\delta(\ell_0,g^*)$, which is
$1$-Lipschitz for the cost. By Proposition~\ref{prop:insidefold} choose
$t<0<t'$ with $\sqrt2\,(t'-t)<1/L$, $\pi^{(t)}(\varphi)\le0.0017$ and
$\pi^{(t')}(\varphi)\ge0.1268-0.0017$, then $\varepsilon$ by Step~3 with
$|Q_{t,\varepsilon}(\varphi)-\pi^{(t)}(\varphi)|\le0.0017$ and likewise
for $t'$. Kantorovich duality gives $W_1\ge0.1268-4\cdot0.0017=0.12$.
Finally $d(\ell_a(z_0),c_k)\ge\sqrt2\,(\frac{49}{100}-\gamma^*)>0.45$ for the
near links, so $B_\varepsilon$ lies in the bad set for $\varepsilon<0.4$.
\end{proof}

The proof uses that $B_\varepsilon$ is chosen after $t$ and $t'$: the
boundary of $B_\varepsilon$ meets the fibre near a fold of its projection
to the non-path links, which is the tangency named after
Proposition~\ref{prop:fold}. On a bad block the labels of
Sec.~\ref{ssec:factorisation} restrict the non-path links to two sets only, and neither has its boundary
near a fold.

\begin{proposition}[the sets of the labels]\label{prop:eightlabels}
Let $k=(y,\mu)$, $r\le\frac1{32}$, and fix every link other than the eight
private links of $k$. The event that the labels of a set of blocks
containing $y$ take given values, with $y$ bad, restricts $z$ to
$\SU(2)^7$ if $y$ is bad through a coarse plaquette or through a non-path
active link that is not private to $k$, and to
\[
B^{\mathrm{bad}}_r=\Bigl\{z:\max_{a\ne0}d(\ell_a,c_k)>r\Bigr\}
\]
otherwise. In the second case $d(u_a,I),d(w_a,I)\le r$ for $a\ne0$, and
over the shell $\{z:r\le\max_{a\ne0}d(\ell_a,c_k)\le\frac1{32}\}$, which
contains the boundary of $B^{\mathrm{bad}}_r$, the fibre $M$ is the graph
of one smooth map $z\mapsto g(z)$, with $\lvert\det D_gV\rvert^{-1}\in
[0.147,828]$ and $J_8^{-1}\mathrm{vol}_M=\lvert\det D_gV\rvert^{-1}dz$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The private links of $k$ are non-path active links of $k$ only, so they
enter the label of $y$ and of no other block, and the label of $y$ is the
union of the events $G_e^c$ over the non-path active links $e$ of the
four pairs based at $y$ and of the coarse events at the corner $y$. Given
the other links, this union is everything when one of its other members
holds, and is $B^{\mathrm{bad}}_r$ otherwise; in the second case the
fourteen inside $\mu$-links of $k$, which are non-path active links of $k$
or tree links, are within $r$ of $I$. Over the shell the hypothesis of
Proposition~\ref{prop:goodside} holds, so $V=c_k$ has exactly one solution,
regular, with the stated density, and it is smooth in $z$ by the implicit
function theorem, the cut-off being one; Step~2 of the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:eightlinkuniform} gives the last identity.
\end{proof}

\emph{The relative chart.} The folds of
Proposition~\ref{prop:insidefold} and Theorem~\ref{thm:eightlinkuniform}
are folds of the projection of the fibre $M=\{V^\sharp_k=c_k\}$ to the
seven non-path links. In the coordinates $g=\ell_0$ and
$\xi_a=g^{-1}\ell_a$, $a\ne0$, the fibre is a single graph over $\xi$ as
soon as the inside links of $B(y)$ are within $\frac1{32}$ of $I$, and the
response of the law of the eight private links to an inside link reduces
to one condition on a Jacobian. In these coordinates the paths are
\[
v_{x_a}=g^{-1}u_ag\,\xi_a,\qquad v_{x'_a}=\xi_aw_a,\qquad v_{2y}=I,
\]
so $V^\sharp_k=g\,E(g,\xi)$ with $E=\exp(\chi N)$, $\chi=\phi(m)$,
$m=\max_x\delta(v_x,I)$ and $N=\frac1{16}\sum_x\log v_x$, and $E$
depends on $g$ only through the conjugates $\tilde u_a=g^{-1}u_ag$. For
fixed $g$ the map $(\ell_a)_{a\ne0}\mapsto\xi$ preserves Haar measure.
With $\alpha=2\arcsin\frac1{2\sqrt2}$ and $\Lambda=\alpha/\sin\alpha$ as
in Sec.~\ref{ssec:smallfibres}, put
\begin{gather*}
\lambda=\frac1{32}\Bigl(2\sqrt2\cdot\frac78\sqrt2\,\alpha+\frac7{16}
\sqrt2\,\Lambda\Bigr)<0.1002,\\
L=\frac{2\cdot\frac78\sqrt2\,\alpha+\frac1{16}\Lambda}{1-\lambda}<2.064 ,
\end{gather*}
by $0.7227<\alpha<0.7228$, $\Lambda<1.0927$ and $\sqrt2<1.41422$.

\begin{lemma}[the relative chart]\label{lem:relchart}
Fix every link other than the eight private links of $k$, and suppose
$d(u_a,I)\le\frac1{32}$ for $a\ne0$; the links $w_a$ are arbitrary.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item For fixed $\xi$, $d(E(g,\xi),E(g',\xi))\le\lambda\,d(g,g')$, and
$V^\sharp_k=c_k$ has exactly one solution $g=G(\xi)$, the fixed point of
the contraction $g\mapsto c_kE(g,\xi)^{-1}$.
\item If one link $u_b$ or $w_b$ moves from $e$ to $e'$, the $u_a$
staying within $\frac1{32}$ of $I$, then $d(G(\xi),G'(\xi))\le L\,d(e,e')$
for every $\xi$, and the eight private links $G(\xi)$, $G(\xi)\xi_a$ move
by at most $8L\,d(e,e')$ in the cost $\sum_a\delta$.
\item Wherever $g\mapsto F(g)=gE(g,\xi)$ is differentiable, its
differential has singular values in $[1-\lambda,1+\lambda]$, so
$D(\xi)=\lvert\det D_gF(G(\xi))\rvert\in[(1-\lambda)^3,(1+\lambda)^3]
\subset[0.728,1.332]$.
\item For almost every $c_k$ and every measurable set $B$ of non-path
links, the law $\frac1Z\mathbf 1_BJ_8^{-1}e^{-\beta_WS}\mathrm{vol}_M$ of
the eight private links is the image under $\xi\mapsto(G(\xi),G(\xi)\xi)$
of
\begin{gather*}
\hat Q(d\xi)=\frac1Z\,\mathbf 1_B(G(\xi)\xi)\,e^{-\beta_WS}\,D(\xi)^{-1}
\,d\xi ,\\
Z=\int\mathbf 1_B(G(\xi)\xi)\,e^{-\beta_WS}D(\xi)^{-1}d\xi ,
\end{gather*}
$S$ evaluated at $(G(\xi),G(\xi)\xi)$ and $d\xi$ Haar measure on
$\SU(2)^7$.
\end{enumerate}
If every $u_a$ equals $I$, then $E$ does not depend on $g$, $D\equiv1$,
and (ii) holds with $L$ replaced by $1.857$. If every $w_a$ equals $I$,
the same holds with $u$ arbitrary in the coordinates $\xi_a=\ell_ag^{-1}$,
in which $V^\sharp_k=\exp(\chi N')\,g$ with $N'=\frac1{16}\sum_x\log(P_x
g^{-1})$, $P_{x_a}g^{-1}=u_a\xi_a$ and $P_{x'_a}g^{-1}=\xi_a$.

More generally, put $\kappa=\frac74\sqrt2\,\alpha+\frac7{16}\Lambda$, so
that $\kappa<2.2670$, and
\[
\sigma_u=\max_{a\ne0}\lVert\operatorname{Ad}(u_a)-1\rVert,\qquad
\sigma_w=\max_{a\ne0}\lVert\operatorname{Ad}(w_a)-1\rVert .
\]
If $\sigma_u<1/\kappa$, then (i)--(iv) hold for every $w$ with $\lambda$
replaced by $\lambda_u=\kappa\sigma_u$ and $L$ by $L_u=(\frac74\sqrt2\,
\alpha+\frac1{16}\Lambda)/(1-\lambda_u)$, the range of $D$ being
$[(1-\lambda_u)^3,(1+\lambda_u)^3]$, provided in (ii) that $\sigma_u<1/
\kappa$ along the move. If $\sigma_w<1/\kappa$, the same holds for every
$u$ in the coordinates $\xi_a=\ell_ag^{-1}$, with $\sigma_w$ in place of
$\sigma_u$; there $P_{x'_a}g^{-1}=\xi_a\,gw_ag^{-1}$. As $\lVert\operatorname
{Ad}(u)-1\rVert=2\sin\theta$ for $u$ with eigenangles $\pm\theta$,
$\theta\in[0,\pi]$, the first condition holds when $\sin\theta\le0.2205$
for every $u_a$, $a\ne0$, and $d(u_a,I)\le\frac1{32}$ gives $\lambda_u
\le\lambda$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(i) Let $g_t=ge^{t\zeta}$, $\lVert\zeta\rVert=1$. If $d(u,I)=\sqrt2\,
\theta$, then $\operatorname{Ad}(u)-1$ has the eigenvalues $0$ and
$e^{\pm2i\theta}-1$, so its norm is $2\sin\theta\le\sqrt2\,d(u,I)$, and by
bi-invariance and $d(e^A,e^B)\le\lVert A-B\rVert$,
\begin{multline*}
d(\tilde u_a(t),\tilde u_a(t'))=d\bigl(e^{(t'-t)\operatorname{Ad}(\tilde
u_a^{-1})\zeta},e^{(t'-t)\zeta}\bigr)\\
\le\sqrt2\,d(u_a,I)\,|t'-t| .
\end{multline*}
So each $v_{x_a}$ moves at geodesic speed at most $\frac{\sqrt2}{32}$,
and the other paths are fixed. Since $\delta(\cdot,I)$ is $1$-Lipschitz
for $d$, $m$ moves at speed at most $\frac{\sqrt2}{32}$ and $\chi$ at most
$\frac{2\sqrt2}{32}$. On an interval where $\chi>0$, every $\delta(v_x,I)
<1$, so every eigenangle $\theta$ of $v_x$ has $2\sqrt2\sin\frac\theta2<1$,
$\theta<\alpha$, $\lVert\log v_x\rVert=\sqrt2\,\theta<\sqrt2\,\alpha$, and
the differential of $\log$ along the path has norm at most $\Lambda$; the
two paths of offset zero contribute nothing, so $\lVert N\rVert\le
\frac78\sqrt2\,\alpha$ and $N$ moves at speed at most $\frac7{16}\Lambda
\frac{\sqrt2}{32}$. Hence $Y=\chi N$ moves at speed at most $\lambda$
there. The set where $\chi>0$ is open and $Y=0$ off it, so $Y$ is
$\lambda$-Lipschitz along the whole geodesic, and $d(E(g),E(g'))\le
\lVert Y(g)-Y(g')\rVert\le\lambda\,d(g,g')$. Since $V^\sharp_k=gE(g,\xi)$,
the equation $V^\sharp_k=c_k$ reads $g=c_kE(g,\xi)^{-1}$, and
$d(c_kE^{-1},c_kE'^{-1})=d(E,E')$: the map is a contraction of the
complete space $\SU(2)$, with a unique fixed point.

(ii) A unit-speed move of $u_b$ moves $\tilde u_b$ and $v_{x_b}$, and a
move of $w_b$ moves $v_{x'_b}$, at speed one, and no other path; so $m$
moves at speed at most $1$, $\chi$ at most $2$, $N$ at most
$\frac1{16}\Lambda$, and $Y$ at fixed $(g,\xi)$ at most
$2\cdot\frac78\sqrt2\,\alpha+\frac1{16}\Lambda=(1-\lambda)L$. For the two
fixed points, $d(G,G')\le d(E(G),E(G'))+(1-\lambda)L\,d(e,e')$, with
$E,E'$ before and after the move at the same point, so $d(G,G')\le\lambda
d(G,G')+(1-\lambda)L\,d(e,e')$. The geodesic ball of radius $\frac1{32}$
is convex, so the hypothesis holds along the move. The eight private
links are $G$ and $G\xi_a$, each at distance $d(G,G')$ from its new value,
and $\delta\le d$.

(iii) The derivative of $F$ along $ge^{t\zeta}$, translated back to the
identity, is $F^{-1}\dot F=\operatorname{Ad}(E^{-1})\zeta+E^{-1}\dot E$,
and $E^{-1}\dot E=E_{-Y}\dot Y$ has norm at most $\lVert\dot Y\rVert\le
\lambda$ by (i). So $D_gF=\operatorname{Ad}
(E^{-1})(I+K)$ with $\lVert K\rVert\le\lambda$, and $\operatorname{Ad}
(E^{-1})$ is an isometry.

(iv) For fixed $\xi$, $(1-\lambda)d(g,g')\le d(F(g),F(g'))\le(1+\lambda)
d(g,g')$ by (i) and bi-invariance, and $F$ is onto by (i), so $F$ is a
bi-Lipschitz homeomorphism of $\SU(2)$ with inverse $c\mapsto G_c(\xi)$.
The area formula gives $\int h(F(g))\lvert\det D_gF\rvert\,dg=\int h(c)\,dc$,
so for bounded measurable $\psi$ and $f$,
\begin{multline*}
\int\!\!\int\psi(F(g,\xi))f(g,\xi)\,dg\,d\xi\\
=\int\psi(c)\int
\frac{f(G_c(\xi),\xi)}{\lvert\det D_gF(G_c(\xi),\xi)\rvert}\,d\xi\,dc ,
\end{multline*}
the Jacobian being defined at $(G_c(\xi),\xi)$ for almost every $\xi$ for
almost every $c$, by Fubini and the area formula applied to the null set
where $F$ is not differentiable. The inner integral is a disintegration of
Haar measure on the eight links along $V^\sharp_k$; so is
$J_8^{-1}\mathrm{vol}_M$ by the coarea formula, and two disintegrations
agree for almost every $c$. Multiplying by $\mathbf 1_Be^{-\beta_WS}$ gives
(iv). If every $u_a=I$, then $\tilde u_a=I$, $E=E(\xi)$, $\lambda$ may be
taken zero and the speed bound of (ii) is $1.857$. If every $w_a=I$,
multiplying the paths by $g^{-1}$ on the right and conjugating the
logarithms by $g$ gives the stated form, in which $g$ enters only as the
right factor; the same proof applies with $\lambda=0$, and right
translation preserves Haar measure.

For the last part, the hypothesis on $u$ enters the proof only through the
speed of $\tilde u_a$ in (i), which is at most $\lVert\operatorname{Ad}
(\tilde u_a^{-1})-1\rVert=\lVert\operatorname{Ad}(u_a)-1\rVert\le\sigma_u$,
since $\operatorname{Ad}(\tilde u_a^{-1})$ is conjugate to $\operatorname
{Ad}(u_a)^{-1}$ and $\operatorname{Ad}(u_a)$ is orthogonal. With this
bound, $m$ moves at speed at most $\sigma_u$, $\chi$ at most $2\sigma_u$
and $N$ at most $\frac7{16}\Lambda\sigma_u$, so $Y$ is $\kappa\sigma_u
$-Lipschitz in $g$, and (i)--(iv) follow as before. In the coordinates
$\xi_a=\ell_ag^{-1}$, conjugating by $g$ gives $V^\sharp_k=\exp(\chi N')\,g$
with $N'=\frac1{16}\sum_x\log(P_xg^{-1})$, $P_{x_a}g^{-1}=u_a\xi_a$ and
$P_{x'_a}g^{-1}=\xi_a\,gw_ag^{-1}$, and $m=\max_x\delta(P_xg^{-1},I)$; so
$g$ enters $N'$ and $m$ only through $gw_ag^{-1}$, which moves at speed at
most $\sigma_w$, and the fixed-point equation $g=E'(g,\xi)^{-1}c_k$,
$E'=\exp(\chi N')$, is treated in the same way. Finally $\kappa<2.2670$
by $\alpha<0.7228$, $\Lambda<1.0927$ and $\sqrt2<1.41422$, and $2\cdot
0.2205\cdot2.2670<1$.
\end{proof}

The normaliser has a lower bound that does not depend on the chart. Let
$S_{\mathrm{dep}}$ be the sum of $1-\frac12\ReTr U_p$ over the plaquettes
that contain a private link of $k$; the other plaquettes do not depend on
the eight links and cancel from the normalised law, so $S$ may be replaced
by $S_{\mathrm{dep}}$, and $Z$ below is defined with it.

\begin{lemma}[the normaliser]\label{lem:relnorm}
There are $36$ plaquettes that contain a private link of $k$, so $0\le
S_{\mathrm{dep}}\le72$. For every $c_k$, every inside and exterior link and
every $\beta_W\ge0$,
\[
Z_{\SU(2)^7}\ge\tfrac12e^{-72\beta_W},\qquad
Z_{B^{\mathrm{bad}}_r}\ge\bigl(\tfrac12-b_r\bigr)e^{-72\beta_W},
\]
with $b_r=(2\vartheta-\sin2\vartheta)/(2\pi)$ and $\vartheta=r/\sqrt2$,
where $Z_B=\int\mathbf 1_Be^{-\beta_WS_{\mathrm{dep}}}J_8^{-1}\mathrm{vol}_M$,
and $b_r<2.3\cdot10^{-6}$ for $r\le\frac1{32}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
A private link $(x'_a,\mu)$ lies in two plaquettes of each plane $\{\mu,
\nu\}$, at $x'_a$ and at $x'_a-e_\nu$, and the other $\mu$-link of exactly
one of them, $(x'_a\pm e_\nu,\mu)$, is private. So the $48$ incidences
cover $12$ plaquettes twice and $24$ once, $36$ in all, each term lying
in $[0,2]$. Let $A$ be the set of configurations with $\ell_0=c_k$ and
$\Re\Tr(c_k^{-1}u_1\ell_1)<0$. There $v_{x_1}=c_k^{-1}u_1\ell_1$ has
$\delta(v_{x_1},I)^2=4-2\Re\Tr v_{x_1}>4$, so $m>1$ near $A$, the cut-off
vanishes and $V^\sharp_k=\ell_0$ near $A$: the fibre contains $A$, and on it
$D_{\ell}V^\sharp_k$ is the projection to the path link, so $J_8=1$ and
$\mathrm{vol}_M$ is Haar measure in $\ell_1,\dots,\ell_7$. The map $\ell_1
\mapsto c_k^{-1}u_1\ell_1$ preserves Haar measure and $X\mapsto-X$ exchanges
the signs of $\Re\Tr X$, so $A$ has Haar measure $\frac12$ in $(\ell_a)_{a
\ne0}$; with $S_{\mathrm{dep}}\le72$ this is the first bound. A point of
$A$ outside $B^{\mathrm{bad}}_r$ has $d(\ell_1,c_k)\le r$, a geodesic ball
whose Haar measure is $\frac2\pi\int_0^\vartheta\sin^2t\,dt=b_r$, the Haar
density of the eigenangle $t\in[0,\pi]$ being $\frac2\pi\sin^2t$ and
$d=\sqrt2\,t$. Finally $2\vartheta-\sin2\vartheta\le\frac43\vartheta^3$
gives $b_r\le\frac{2\vartheta^3}{3\pi}\le\frac2{3\pi(32\sqrt2)^3}<2.3\cdot
10^{-6}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[the response in the relative chart]\label{thm:relresponse}
Let $k$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lem:relchart}, let $B$ be $\SU(2)^7$ or
$B^{\mathrm{bad}}_r$ with $r<\frac1{32}$, and in the second case suppose
also $d(w_a,I)\le\frac1{32}$ for $a\ne0$. Let one of the links $u_b$,
$w_b$, $b\ne0$, move from $e$ to $e'$, the hypotheses holding along the
geodesic, and write $Q,Q'$ for the two laws of the eight private links,
$\hat Q,\hat Q'$, $D,D'$ for the objects of Lemma~\ref{lem:relchart}(iv).
Suppose that
\[
\textup{(J)}\qquad\int\bigl\lvert\log D-\log D'\bigr\rvert\,d\hat Q\le
K\,d(e,e')
\]
for every such pair along the geodesic. Then, for the cost $\sum_a\delta$,
\begin{multline*}
W_1(Q,Q')\le\bigl(16.52+2898\beta_W+41.37K\\
+238.1\,\iota\,e^{72\beta_W}\bigr)\,d(e,e'),
\end{multline*}
with $\iota=0$ for $B=\SU(2)^7$ and $\iota=1$ for $B=B^{\mathrm{bad}}_r$.
If every $u_a$ equals $I$ and $e$ is a link $w_b$, or every $w_a$ equals
$I$ and $e$ is a link $u_b$, then \textup{(J)} holds with $K=0$, and for
$B=\SU(2)^7$ the bound holds with $u$, respectively $w$, otherwise
arbitrary. For $B=\SU(2)^7$ and $\sigma_u<1/\kappa$ along the move, or
$\sigma_w<1/\kappa$ in the coordinates $\xi_a=\ell_ag^{-1}$, with
$\lambda_u,L_u$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:relchart} (respectively $\lambda_w,L_w$)
and (J) in that chart,
\[
W_1(Q,Q')\le\Bigl(8L_u+16\sqrt2\,R_u\bigl(24\sqrt2\,L_u\beta_W+K\bigr)
\Bigr)\,d(e,e'),
\]
where $R_u=(1+\lambda_u)^3/(1-\lambda_u)^3$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Since $W_1$ is a metric, it suffices to prove the bound with an error
$o(d(e,e'))$ for nearby pairs and to add along a subdivision of the
geodesic. Couple $\hat Q$ and $\hat Q'$ so that $\xi=\xi'$ with
probability $1-\mathrm{TV}(\hat Q,\hat Q')$, and use the maps of
Lemma~\ref{lem:relchart}(iv): by (ii) of that lemma the cost is at most
$8L\,d(e,e')<16.52\,d(e,e')$ where $\xi=\xi'$, and at most the diameter
$8\cdot2\sqrt2$ otherwise. So $W_1\le16.52\,d(e,e')+16\sqrt2\,
\mathrm{TV}(\hat Q,\hat Q')$, and with $f,f'$ the unnormalised densities,
$\mathrm{TV}(\hat Q,\hat Q')\le\frac1Z\int\lvert f-f'\rvert\,d\xi$.

\emph{The action.} The links $u_b,w_b$ share no plaquette with a private
link, the two $\mu$-links of a plaquette having one $\mu$-coordinate, so
$S_{\mathrm{dep}}$ changes only through the eight links, each of which moves
by at most $L\,d(e,e')$. Each of the $48$ incidences of a private link
with a plaquette contributes at most $\frac1{\sqrt2}$ times its speed, by the
proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:wilsononly}, so $\lvert S_{\mathrm{dep}}-
S'_{\mathrm{dep}}\rvert\le\frac{48L}{\sqrt2}d(e,e')<70.06\,d(e,e')$ at every
$\xi$, and
\[
\int_{B\cap B'}\frac{\lvert e^{-\beta_WS}-e^{-\beta_WS'}\rvert}{D'}\,d\xi
\le\bigl(e^{70.06\beta_Wd(e,e')}-1\bigr)\Bigl(\frac{1+\lambda}{1-\lambda}
\Bigr)^3Z ,
\]
with $(\frac{1+\lambda}{1-\lambda})^3<1.828$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:relchart}(iii); here $B,B'$ denote the sets of $\xi$ with
$G(\xi)\xi$, respectively $G'(\xi)\xi$, in $B$.

\emph{The Jacobian.} With $\varDelta=\log D-\log D'$, $\lvert\varDelta\rvert
\le3\log\frac{1+\lambda}{1-\lambda}$ and $\lvert e^{\varDelta}-1\rvert\le
1.828\lvert\varDelta\rvert$, so $\int_{B\cap B'}e^{-\beta_WS}\lvert D^{-1}-
D'^{-1}\rvert\,d\xi\le1.828\,Z\int\lvert\varDelta\rvert\,d\hat Q\le1.828\,
KZ\,d(e,e')$.

\emph{The restricting set.} For $B=\SU(2)^7$ there is nothing to do. For
$B=B^{\mathrm{bad}}_r$ let $\mathcal M(\xi)=\max_ad(G(\xi)\xi_a,c_k)$ and
$\varepsilon=L\,d(e,e')$, with $r+\varepsilon\le\frac1{32}$. Then $\lvert
\mathcal M-\mathcal M'\rvert\le d(G,G')\le\varepsilon$, so $B\setminus B'$
and $B'\setminus B$ consist of $\xi$ whose eight links, before
respectively after the move, satisfy $r<\max_ad(\ell_a,c_k)\le r+
\varepsilon\le\frac1{32}$. On that shell, with every inside link within
$\frac1{32}$ of $I$, Proposition~\ref{prop:goodside} with radius
$\frac1{32}$ and the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:eightlabels} show that
the fibre is a graph over the non-path links with $J_8^{-1}\mathrm{vol}_M
=\lvert\det D_gV\rvert^{-1}dz$, $\lvert\det D_gV\rvert^{-1}\le828$. Since
$e^{-\beta_WS_{\mathrm{dep}}}\le1$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:relchart}(iv)
identifies both disintegrations,
\[
\int_{B\setminus B'}f\,d\xi+\int_{B'\setminus B}f'\,d\xi\le2\cdot828
\cdot7\cdot\frac{\varepsilon(r+\varepsilon)^2}{\sqrt2\,\pi},
\]
since the Haar measure of the shell $\{s<d(\ell,c)\le s+\varepsilon\}$
is
\[
\frac2\pi\int_{s/\sqrt2}^{(s+\varepsilon)/\sqrt2}\sin^2t\,dt\le
\frac{\varepsilon(s+\varepsilon)^2}{\sqrt2\,\pi} .
\]
Divided by $Z\ge(\frac12-2.3\cdot10^{-6})
e^{-72\beta_W}$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:relnorm}) and with $r\le\frac1{32}$, this is
at most $10.52\,e^{72\beta_W}d(e,e')+o(d(e,e'))$.

Adding the three parts,
\begin{multline*}
\mathrm{TV}(\hat Q,\hat Q')\le\bigl(128.07\beta_W+1.828K+10.52\,\iota
e^{72\beta_W}\bigr)\,d(e,e')\\
+o(d(e,e')),
\end{multline*}
with $1.828\cdot70.06<128.07$; multiplied by $16\sqrt2$, with
$16\sqrt2\cdot128.07<2898$, $16\sqrt2\cdot1.828<41.37$ and $16\sqrt2\cdot
10.52<238.1$, this gives the constants. If every $u_a=I$ and $e=w_b$, then $D\equiv D'\equiv1$
by Lemma~\ref{lem:relchart}, and (J) holds with $K=0$; likewise in the
coordinates $\xi_a=\ell_ag^{-1}$ if every $w_a=I$ and $e=u_b$, where
Lemma~\ref{lem:relchart} needs no bound on $u$, and the case $B=\SU(2)^7$
uses no bound on the inside links at all. For the last statement the case
$B=\SU(2)^7$ uses Lemma~\ref{lem:relchart} only, through the displacement
$8L$ of the eight links, the ratio $(\frac{1+\lambda}{1-\lambda})^3$ of the
bounds on $D$, which bounds $e^{\lvert\varDelta\rvert}$ and the ratio of
$D'^{-1}$ to $D^{-1}$, and the change $\frac{48L}{\sqrt2}=24\sqrt2\,L$ of
the action per unit move; with $\lambda_u,L_u$ in place of $\lambda,L$ the
same three steps give the stated bound.
\end{proof}

The Jacobian $D$ of Lemma~\ref{lem:relchart}(iii) jumps
only where the maximal path changes. Write $f_x(\xi)=\delta(v_x,I)$ at
$g=G(\xi)$, so that $m=\max_xf_x$. Call $\xi$ \emph{flat} if $m\notin
(\frac12,1)$ or the maximum is attained only at paths from points $x'_c$,
and of \emph{type} $a$ if $\frac12<m<1$ and the maximum is attained at
$x_a$ only, $a\ne0$. The two paths of index $a$ \emph{tie at the top} at
$\xi$ if $f_{x_a}=f_{x'_a}=m\in(\frac12,1)$ and $f_y<m$ for every other
path $y$.

Near a tie at the top of index $a$ the map $g\mapsto F(g)=gE(g,\xi)$ has
two branches. Put $f^{(1)}(g,\xi)=\delta(\tilde u_a\xi_a,I)$, which depends
on $g$, and $f^{(2)}(\xi)=\delta(\xi_aw_a,I)$, which does not, and
$Y_i=\phi(f^{(i)})N$, $F_i=g\exp Y_i$. Since $\phi$ decreases, $Y=Y_1$
where $f^{(1)}\ge f^{(2)}$ and $Y=Y_2$ where $f^{(2)}\ge f^{(1)}$, as long
as the other paths stay below. At a tie $\xi_0$ with $g_0=G(\xi_0)$ the
two branches agree, and the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:relchart}(iii) applies
to each of them, so $D_gF_i$ is invertible; $\log$ is analytic on
$\{\delta(v,I)<1\}$ and $\phi$ is affine on $(\frac12,1)$, so the
implicit function theorem gives analytic maps $G_i$ near $\xi_0$, also
analytic in the inside links, with $G_i(\xi_0)=g_0$ and $F_i(G_i(\xi),\xi)
=c_k$. Put $D_i=\det D_gF_i(G_i)$ and $h_i(\xi)=f^{(1)}(G_i(\xi),\xi)-
f^{(2)}(\xi)$. Tangent vectors $\eta=(\eta_b)_{b\ne0}$ at $\xi$ are
derivatives of $\xi_be^{s\eta_b}$, with $\lVert\eta\rVert^2=\sum_b\lVert
\eta_b\rVert^2$, and $\nabla h_2$ is the gradient for this metric.

\begin{lemma}[the ties]\label{lem:ties}
Let $\xi_0$ be a tie at the top of index $a$, and suppose $d(u_b,I)\le
\frac1{32}$ for every $b\ne0$, $d(w_a,I)\le\frac1{32}$, and $d(w_c,I)\le
\frac1{32}$ for some $c\ne0,a$. At $(g_0,\xi_0)$ let $\ell=D_gf^{(1)}$,
$A_2=\Phi(\operatorname{ad}Y)\,\phi\,D_gN$ and $\kappa_0=\ell((1+A_2)^{-1}N)$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item Near $\xi_0$, $h_1$ and $h_2$ have the same sign; $G=G_1$ and $D=D_1$
where it is positive, and $G=G_2$ and $D=D_2$ where it is negative.
\item At $\xi_0$, $D_1=D_2\,(1-2\kappa_0)$ and $\lvert\kappa_0\rvert<0.04039$.
\item At $\xi_0$, $\lvert\log D_1-\log D_2\rvert\le1.9811\,\lvert\nabla
h_2\rvert$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(i) For real $\tau$ near $0$ let $\Gamma(\tau)$ be the solution near $g_0$
of
\[
g\exp\bigl((\phi(f^{(2)})-2\tau)N\bigr)=c_k .
\]
As in the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:relchart}(ii),
\[
d(\Gamma(\tau),\Gamma(\tau'))\le\lambda\,d(\Gamma(\tau),\Gamma(\tau'))+
2\lVert N\rVert\,\lvert\tau-\tau'\rvert ,
\]
so $\Gamma$ is Lipschitz with constant $2\cdot0.8945/(1-\lambda)<1.989$.
Since $\phi(t)=2-2t$ on $(\frac12,1)$, $\phi(f^{(2)})-2\tau=\phi(f^{(2)}+
\tau)$, so $\Gamma(0)=G_2$ and $\Gamma(h_1)=G_1$. Let $k(\tau)=f^{(1)}
(\Gamma(\tau),\xi)-f^{(2)}-\tau$. By the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:relchart}(i), $f^{(1)}$ is $\sigma$-Lipschitz in $g$, with
$\sigma=\frac{\sqrt2}{32}$, so $k(\tau')-k(\tau)\le-(1-1.989\,\sigma)
(\tau'-\tau)$ for $\tau'>\tau$, and $1.989\,\sigma<0.088$. As $k(0)=h_2$
and $k(h_1)=0$, $h_1$ and $h_2$ have the same sign. If $h_1>0$, then
$f^{(1)}>f^{(2)}$ at $G_1$, so $F=F_1$ near $G_1$ and $F(G_1)=c_k$; by
uniqueness in Lemma~\ref{lem:relchart}(i), $G=G_1$ and $D=\lvert\det
D_gF_1\rvert=D_1$, the determinant being positive since $\lVert A\rVert
\le\lambda$. The case $h_2<0$ is the same with $F_2$.

(ii) At $\xi_0$, $G_1=G_2=g_0$ and $Y_1=Y_2=Y$, while $D_gY_1=
\phi'(f^{(1)})\,N\otimes\ell+\phi\,D_gN=-2N\otimes\ell+\phi\,D_gN$ and
$D_gY_2=\phi\,D_gN$. Since $[Y,N]=0$, $\Phi(\operatorname{ad}Y)N=N$, so
$1+A_1=(1+A_2)-2N\otimes\ell$, and the determinant of a rank-one
perturbation gives $D_1=D_2(1-2\ell((1+A_2)^{-1}N))$. The operator
$\operatorname{ad}Y$ is normal with eigenvalues $0,\pm i\rho$, and $\lvert
\Phi(i\rho)\rvert=\lvert\sin\frac\rho2\rvert/\frac\rho2\le1$, so $\lVert
\Phi(\operatorname{ad}Y)\rVert\le1$. By the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:relchart}(i), $\lVert D_gN\rVert\le\frac7{16}\Lambda\sigma
<0.02113$, $\lVert\ell\rVert\le\sigma$ and $\lVert N\rVert<0.8945$, so
$\lvert\kappa_0\rvert\le0.044195\cdot0.8945/(1-0.02113)<0.04039$.

(iii) Identify $\SU(2)$ with the unit quaternions, and write $\langle X,
Y\rangle=-\Tr(XY)$ on $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and $\Pi(z)=\frac12(z-z^*)$ for
the projection of $2\times2$ matrices to $\mathfrak{su}(2)$, orthogonal for
$\ReTr(X^*Y)$. For $z\in\SU(2)$, $\delta(z,I)^2=4-2\ReTr z$, so the
derivative of $\delta(ze^{s\eta},I)$ at $s=0$ is $-\ReTr(z\eta)/\delta=
\langle\Pi(z),\eta\rangle/\delta$. At fixed $g$, with $z_1=\tilde u_a
\xi_a$ and $z_2=w_a\xi_a$, and since $\ReTr(\xi_ae^{s\eta}w_a)=\ReTr(w_a
\xi_ae^{s\eta})$, the derivatives of $f^{(1)}$ and $f^{(2)}$ along
$\eta_a$ are $p(\eta_a)=\langle\Pi(z_1),\eta_a\rangle/m$ and $q(\eta_a)=
\langle\Pi(z_2),\eta_a\rangle/m$. If $z=\cos\theta+\sin\theta\,n$ with
$n\in\mathfrak{su}(2)$, $n^2=-1$, then $\Pi(z)=\sin\theta\,n$ and $\lVert
n\rVert=\sqrt2$, so $\lvert p\rvert=\sqrt2\sin\theta/(2\sqrt2\sin
\frac\theta2)=\cos\frac\theta2=:\gamma$, and $\lvert q\rvert=\gamma$ as
$z_2$ has the same $\delta$. As $m<1$, $\theta<\alpha$, so $\gamma^2>
\cos^2\frac\alpha2=\frac12(1+\cos\alpha)=\frac78$, since $\cos\alpha=1-2
\sin^2\frac\alpha2=\frac34$. Also $\lvert p-q\rvert\le\lVert z_1-z_2
\rVert/m=\lVert\tilde u_a-w_a\rVert/m\le(\delta(u_a,I)+\delta(w_a,I))/m<
\frac18$, because $m>\frac12$. Hence $\lvert p+q\rvert^2=4\gamma^2-
\lvert p-q\rvert^2>\frac72-\frac1{64}$. Let $\eta_a$ be the vector dual to
$(p+q)/(\gamma^2+\langle p,q\rangle)$; as $\gamma^2+\langle p,q\rangle=
\frac12\lvert p+q\rvert^2>0$, $p(\eta_a)=q(\eta_a)=1$ and $\lVert\eta_a
\rVert=2/\lvert p+q\rvert<2/(\frac72-\frac1{64})^{1/2}<1.0715$.

Differentiating $F_2(G_2(\xi),\xi)=c_k$, translated to the identity as in
the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:relchart}(iii), gives $(1+A_2)\,dG_2(\eta)=
-\Phi(\operatorname{ad}Y)(-2q(\eta_a)N+\phi\,\partial N(\eta))$, where
$\partial N$ is the derivative of $N$ in $\xi$ at fixed $g$. With $\ell'=
\ell\circ(1+A_2)^{-1}\Phi(\operatorname{ad}Y)$, so that $\ell'(N)=\kappa_0$,
\begin{align*}
dh_2(\eta)&=\ell(dG_2(\eta))+(p-q)(\eta_a)\\
&=(p-q)(\eta_a)+2\kappa_0\,q(\eta_a)-\phi\,\ell'(\partial N(\eta)) .
\end{align*}
In the translated form the differential of $\log$ at $v=e^X$ is
$\psi(\operatorname{ad}X)$ with $\psi(z)=z/(1-e^{-z})$, since $e^{-X}
de^X=\Phi(-\operatorname{ad}X)\,dX$ and $\Phi(-z)\psi(z)=1$; and
$\xi_be^{s\eta}w_b=\xi_bw_be^{s\operatorname{Ad}(w_b^{-1})\eta}$. So
$\partial N(\eta)=\frac1{16}\sum_bT_b\eta_b$ with $T_b=\psi(\operatorname
{ad}X_b)+\psi(\operatorname{ad}X'_b)\operatorname{Ad}(w_b^{-1})$, $X_b=
\log v_{x_b}$, $X'_b=\log v_{x'_b}$. If $X$ has eigenangle $\vartheta<
\alpha$, $\operatorname{ad}X$ is normal with eigenvalues $0,\pm2i\vartheta$,
and $\psi(\pm2i\vartheta)=\vartheta e^{\pm i\vartheta}/\sin\vartheta$; so
$\lVert\psi(\operatorname{ad}X)\rVert\le\Lambda$, and the symmetric part
of $\psi(\operatorname{ad}X)$ has eigenvalues $1$ and $\vartheta\cot
\vartheta\ge\alpha\cot\alpha=3\alpha/\sqrt7>0.8194$. Every path has
$\delta<1$ at a tie at the top, so $\lVert T_a\rVert\le2\Lambda$, and, with
$\lVert\operatorname{Ad}(w_c^{-1})-1\rVert\le\sigma$ as in the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:relchart}(i),
\[
\langle T_c\zeta,\zeta\rangle\ge(2\cdot0.8194-1.0927\,\sigma)\lVert\zeta
\rVert^2>1.5905\,\lVert\zeta\rVert^2 .
\]
Take $\eta_b=0$ for $b\ne a,c$, and $\eta_c=0$ if $\ell'=0$, otherwise
$\eta_c$ the vector dual to $-\ell'(T_a\eta_a)\,T_c^*\ell'/\lvert T_c^*
\ell'\rvert^2$. Then $\ell'(\partial N(\eta))=0$, and $\lvert T_c^*\ell'
\rvert\,\lvert\ell'\rvert\ge\langle T_c\ell'^\sharp,\ell'^\sharp\rangle$
gives $\lvert T_c^*\ell'\rvert\ge1.5905\,\lvert\ell'\rvert$, so $\lVert
\eta_c\rVert\le2\Lambda\lVert\eta_a\rVert/1.5905<1.3741\,\lVert\eta_a
\rVert$ and $\lVert\eta\rVert<1.0715\,(1+1.3741^2)^{1/2}<1.8210$. Hence
$dh_2(\eta)=2\kappa_0$ and $2\lvert\kappa_0\rvert\le1.8210\,\lvert\nabla h_2
\rvert$. Finally $\lvert\log(1-x)\rvert\le\lvert x\rvert/(1-\lvert x
\rvert)$ for $\lvert x\rvert<1$ and $2\lvert\kappa_0\rvert<0.0808$ give
$\lvert\log D_1-\log D_2\rvert\le2.1758\,\lvert\kappa_0\rvert\le2.1758\cdot
0.9105\,\lvert\nabla h_2\rvert<1.9811\,\lvert\nabla h_2\rvert$.
\end{proof}

Near a tie at the top of index $a$ the ties of index $a$ are exactly the
zeros of $h_2$, by (i). Let $Z_a$ be the set of those ties at the top of
index $a$ at which $\nabla h_2\ne0$, a hypersurface of $\SU(2)^7$, and let
$H^{20}$ be its Hausdorff measure for the metric above, under which
$\SU(2)$ has volume $V=4\sqrt2\,\pi^2$. Put
\[
\mathcal A_{\mathrm{tie}}=\sup V^{-7}H^{20}(Z_a),
\]
the supremum over $a\ne0$, over $c_k$ and over inside links within
$\frac1{32}$ of $I$.

\begin{proposition}[the Jacobian across the ties]\label{prop:jreduce}
Let $k$, $B$ and the move $e\to e'$ be as in
Theorem~\textup{\ref{thm:relresponse}}, with $d(u_a,I),d(w_a,I)\le\frac1
{32}$ for $a\ne0$ along the geodesic. Then
\[
\int\bigl\lvert\log D-\log D'\bigr\rvert\,d\xi\le\bigl(53.96+15.134\,
\mathcal A_{\mathrm{tie}}\bigr)\,d(e,e')
\]
for $d(e,e')\le0.08$, with $d\xi$ Haar measure on $\SU(2)^7$, and
\textup{(J)} holds with $K\le(148.2+41.6\,\mathcal A_{\mathrm{tie}})\,e^{72\beta_W}$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
\emph{Where the type is kept.} On flat points $D_gY=\phi(m)\,D_gN$, since
$\phi'(m)D_gm=0$ there: either $\phi'(m)=0$, or the maximum sits at a path
that does not depend on $g$. At points of type $a$, $D_gY=-2N\otimes
D_gf_{x_a}+\phi(m)D_gN$. With $\Phi(z)=(e^z-1)/z$, the translated
differential of $F$ is $\operatorname{Ad}(E^{-1})(1+A)$ with $A=\Phi(
\operatorname{ad}Y)\,D_gY$, so $D=\det(1+A)$ and $\lVert A\rVert\le
\lambda$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:relchart}(iii). Let $\xi$ keep one type, or
stay flat, for the parameters $t$ of an interval of the move, at unit
speed along the geodesic from $e$ to $e'$. Then $\frac d{dt}\log D=
\operatorname{tr}((1+A)^{-1}\dot A)$, of modulus at most $3\lVert\dot A
\rVert/(1-\lambda)$. We bound $\dot A$ with $\sigma=\frac{\sqrt2}{32}<
0.044195$, the norm $\lVert\operatorname{Ad}(u_a)-1\rVert\le\sigma$, and
$\sigma L<0.09122$.
\begin{itemize}
\item By Lemma~\ref{lem:relchart}(ii), $G$ moves at speed at most $L$, so
each $\tilde u_c$ moves at speed at most $\sigma L$, plus $1$ for the
moving link; every $v_x$, every $f_x$ and $m$ therefore move at speed at
most $1+\sigma L<1.0913$, and $Y$ at speed at most $\lambda L+(1-\lambda)
L=L$.
\item $\lVert N\rVert\le\frac78\sqrt2\,\alpha<0.8945$, $\lVert D_gN\rVert
\le\frac7{16}\Lambda\sigma<0.02113$, $\lVert D_gf_{x_a}\rVert\le\sigma$,
and $\lVert\dot N\rVert\le\frac1{16}\Lambda(1+7\sigma L)<0.1120$.
\item On $\mathfrak{su}(2)$, $\lVert\operatorname{ad}X\rVert=\sqrt2\lVert
X\rVert$, so $\lVert\operatorname{ad}Y\rVert\le r=1.2651$. The series of
$\Phi$ gives $\lVert\Phi(\operatorname{ad}Y)\rVert\le1$ and
\begin{align*}
\lVert\Phi(\operatorname{ad}Y)-\Phi(\operatorname{ad}Y')\rVert
&\le\frac{re^r-e^r+1}{r^2}\sqrt2\,\lVert Y-Y'\rVert\\
&\le1.715\,\lVert Y-Y'\rVert .
\end{align*}
\item $D_gf_{x_a}=\nabla\delta(v)\circ\operatorname{Ad}(\xi_a^{-1})
(1-\operatorname{Ad}(\tilde u_a^{-1}))$ in translated form. At a point
of type $a$, $\delta(v,I)=2\sqrt2\sin\frac\theta2\ge\frac12$, so $\sin
\frac\theta2\ge\frac1{4\sqrt2}$. The metric of $\SU(2)$ is that of the
round sphere of radius $\sqrt2$, and the Hessian of the radial function
$\delta$ has norm at most $\max\{\frac1{2\sqrt2}\sin\frac\theta2,\cos\theta
/(2\sqrt2\sin\frac\theta2)\}$, at most $2\cos\theta\le2(1-\frac2{32})=
\frac{15}8$. The translated derivative of the gradient adds $\frac12
\lVert\operatorname{ad}\rVert\le0.7072$. With $\lVert\frac d{dt}
\operatorname{Ad}(\tilde u_a^{-1})\rVert\le\sqrt2(1+\sigma L)$, this gives
$\lVert\frac d{dt}D_gf_{x_a}\rVert\le2.5822\cdot1.0913\,\sigma+
1.41422\cdot1.0913<1.6679$.
\item $D_gN=\frac1{16}\sum_c\mathrm d\!\log_{v_{x_c}}\circ
\operatorname{Ad}(\xi_c^{-1})(1-\operatorname{Ad}(\tilde u_c^{-1}))$. In
translated form $\mathrm d\!\log_v=\psi(\operatorname{ad}X)$, where $X=
\log v$ and $\psi(z)=z/(1-e^{-z})=1+\frac z2+\frac{z^2}{12}-\frac{z^4}
{720}+\dots$. With $\lVert\operatorname{ad}X\rVert\le2\alpha<1.4457$ the
series gives Lipschitz constant $0.76\sqrt2\,\Lambda<1.176$ in $v$. Hence
$\lVert\frac d{dt}D_gN\rVert\le\frac1{16}(1.176\,\sigma+\sqrt2\Lambda)
(1+7\sigma L)<0.1636$.
\end{itemize}
Since $\phi'\in\{0,-2\}$ is constant along the interval and $\phi$ is
$2$-Lipschitz,
\begin{multline*}
\Bigl\lVert\frac d{dt}D_gY\Bigr\rVert\le2\bigl(0.1120\,\sigma+0.8945\cdot
1.6679\bigr)\\
+2\cdot1.0913\cdot0.02113+0.1636<3.204 ,
\end{multline*}
and $\lVert\dot A\rVert\le1.715\,L\lambda+3.204<3.559$. So $\lvert\frac
