by the step. The conditioning on boundary values, which defeats the almost
sure bound in Theorem~\ref{thm:sfshelllin}, is replaced by Royen's Gaussian
correlation inequality, used in the mean over the boundary values. The
$\SU(2)$ step is not treated, and the nonlocality of the Gaussian form is
not decided here; Remark~\ref{rem:sfglsu2} states what the $\SU(2)$ step
needs beyond this paragraph.

Let $\Lambda$ be a torus of even side at least four, with the blocks
$B(y)$ of Definition~\ref{def:blockgauge}, coarse torus $\Lambda'$, tree
links and active links as there, and $\Pi(y)$ the $96$ plaquettes owned by
the block $y$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:lfowned}). Let $\mathcal A(\Lambda)$ be the
space of real fields on the active links, $Q_\Lambda(\varphi)=\sum_p
(d\varphi)_p^2$ over the plaquettes of $\Lambda$, and $V:\mathcal A(\Lambda)
\to\R^{\Lambda'\times\{0,\dots,3\}}$ the block averages. For a real field
$\gamma$ on the coarse links put $\mathcal V_\gamma=\{\varphi\in\mathcal A
(\Lambda):V(\varphi)=\gamma\}$, with Lebesgue measure $m_\gamma$ in the
coordinates given by the values on the links other than the path links, as
in the linear model. Since the path link of a pair enters its average alone,
with coefficient $\frac18$, and enters no other average, $\mathcal V_\gamma$
is not empty and $m_\gamma$ is the image of $m_0$ under $\psi\mapsto\varphi_0
+\psi$ for every $\varphi_0\in\mathcal V_\gamma$. The proofs of
Theorem~\ref{thm:blockgap}, of Lemma~\ref{lem:blocktree} and of
Proposition~\ref{prop:effective}(i),~(ii) use only the plaquettes and links
of one block and of two neighbouring blocks, and their counts are the same
on such a torus; so they hold on $\Lambda$, and on $\Lambda'$ when its side
is even and at least four.

\begin{definition}\label{def:sfglclass}
$\mathcal G(\Lambda)$ is the set of positive semidefinite quadratic forms
$q$ on $\mathcal A(\Lambda)$ with $q\ge Q_\Lambda$. For $q\in\mathcal G
(\Lambda)$ and $\lambda>0$, $\mu_q$ is the probability measure on
$\mathcal V_0$ with density $Z_q^{-1}e^{-\lambda q}$ with respect to $m_0$,
where $Z_q=\int_{\mathcal V_0}e^{-\lambda q}\,dm_0$.
\end{definition}

The restriction of $Q_\Lambda$ to $\mathcal A(\Lambda)$ belongs to
$\mathcal G(\Lambda)$.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:sfglsplit}
Let $q\in\mathcal G(\Lambda)$ and $\lambda>0$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item $Z_q<\infty$. For every $\gamma$ the form $q$ has a unique minimiser
$\varphi^*_q(\gamma)$ on $\mathcal V_\gamma$, which is linear in $\gamma$,
and with $q'(\gamma)=q(\varphi^*_q(\gamma))$,
\[
q\bigl(\varphi^*_q(\gamma)+\psi\bigr)=q'(\gamma)+q(\psi)\qquad
(\psi\in\mathcal V_0).
\]
\item $q'(\gamma)\ge Q_{\Lambda'}(\gamma)$ for every real field $\gamma$ on
the coarse links. If the side of $\Lambda'$ is at least four, the restriction
of $q'$ to $\mathcal A(\Lambda')$ belongs to $\mathcal G(\Lambda')$. If
$q(\varphi+d\tilde h)=q(\varphi)$ for every function $\tilde h$ constant on
the blocks, then $q'(\gamma+d'h)=q'(\gamma)$ for every function $h$ on the
coarse sites, where $(d'h)_{y,\mu}=h_y-h_{y+e_\mu}$.
\item For distinct plaquettes $p_1,\dots,p_n$ of $\Lambda$ the covariance
matrix $\Sigma$ of $((d\psi)_{p_1},\dots,(d\psi)_{p_n})$ under $\mu_q$
satisfies $\Sigma\le(2\lambda)^{-1}I$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(i) By Theorem~\ref{thm:blockgap} with $W$ the set of all blocks, $q(\psi)
\ge Q_\Lambda(\psi)\ge\frac1{52}\sum_e\psi_e^2$ on $\mathcal V_0$, so $q$ is
positive definite there and $Z_q<\infty$. Fix $\varphi_0\in\mathcal
V_\gamma$ depending linearly on $\gamma$, for instance the field of
Proposition~\ref{prop:effective}(ii). The function $\psi\mapsto q(\varphi_0+
\psi)$ on $\mathcal V_0$ is a quadratic polynomial with positive definite
leading part, so it has a unique minimiser, a linear function of
$\varphi_0$. At the minimiser $\varphi^*$ the derivative vanishes:
$q(\varphi^*,\psi)=0$ for the bilinear form of $q$ and every $\psi\in
\mathcal V_0$, which gives the identity.

(ii) By Proposition~\ref{prop:effective}(i), $q'(\gamma)=q(\varphi^*_q
(\gamma))\ge Q_\Lambda(\varphi^*_q(\gamma))\ge Q_{\Lambda'}(V(\varphi^*_q
(\gamma)))=Q_{\Lambda'}(\gamma)$, and $q'$ is positive semidefinite as a
minimum of a positive semidefinite form over an affine family depending
linearly on $\gamma$. For $h$ on the coarse sites let $\tilde h$ equal $h_y$
on $B(y)$. Then $d\tilde h$ vanishes on the links inside the blocks, so
$d\tilde h\in\mathcal A(\Lambda)$, and $V(\varphi+d\tilde h)=V(\varphi)+
d'h$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:blocktree}(ii). So $\varphi\mapsto\varphi+d\tilde h$
maps $\mathcal V_\gamma$ onto $\mathcal V_{\gamma+d'h}$ and preserves $q$.

(iii) Identify $\mathcal V_0$ with $\R^N$ by the coordinates of $m_0$ and
write $q(\psi)=\psi^{\rm T}K\psi$ with $K$ positive definite. Then $\mu_q$ is
the centred Gaussian law with covariance $(2\lambda K)^{-1}$, and for a
linear function $\ell(\psi)=l^{\rm T}\psi$, by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality
for the inner product of $K$,
\[
\Var_{\mu_q}(\ell)=\frac{l^{\rm T}K^{-1}l}{2\lambda}=\frac1{2\lambda}
\sup_{\psi\ne0}\frac{\ell(\psi)^2}{q(\psi)} .
\]
For $a\in\R^n$ and $\ell(\psi)=\sum_ia_i(d\psi)_{p_i}$, $\ell(\psi)^2\le
|a|^2\sum_i(d\psi)_{p_i}^2\le|a|^2Q_\Lambda(\psi)\le|a|^2q(\psi)$, as the
plaquettes are distinct. So $a^{\rm T}\Sigma a\le|a|^2/(2\lambda)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:sfgltail}
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item If $Z$ is a centred real Gaussian variable with $\Var Z\le\sigma^2$,
then $\Pr(|Z|>s)\le e^{-s^2/(2\sigma^2)}$ for every $s\ge0$.
\item If $(Z_1,\dots,Z_n)$ is a centred Gaussian vector with covariance at
most $\sigma^2I$ and $s^2\ge\sigma^2$, then
\[
\Pr\Bigl(\sum_iZ_i^2>ns^2\Bigr)\le\Bigl(\frac{es^2}{\sigma^2}\Bigr)^{n/2}
e^{-ns^2/(2\sigma^2)} .
\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(i) It suffices to take $\Var Z=\sigma^2>0$ and $\sigma=1$, since
$\Pr(|Z|>s)$ increases with the variance. Let $f(u)=e^{-u^2/2}-
\sqrt{2/\pi}\int_u^\infty e^{-v^2/2}dv$. Then $f(0)=0$, $f(u)\to0$ as
$u\to\infty$, and $f'(u)=e^{-u^2/2}(\sqrt{2/\pi}-u)$, so $f$ increases and
then decreases, and $f\ge0$ on $[0,\infty)$. (ii) Write the covariance as
$ODO^{\rm T}$ with $O$ orthogonal and $D$ diagonal with entries $d_i\le
\sigma^2$. Then $\sum_iZ_i^2$ has the law of $\sum_id_ig_i^2$ with
independent standard Gaussian $g_i$, and for $0\le\theta<1/(2\sigma^2)$,
$\E e^{\theta\sum_id_ig_i^2}=\prod_i(1-2\theta d_i)^{-1/2}\le(1-2\theta
\sigma^2)^{-n/2}$. By Markov's inequality the probability is at most
$(1-2\theta\sigma^2)^{-n/2}e^{-\theta ns^2}$, and $\theta=(1-\sigma^2/s^2)/
(2\sigma^2)$ gives the bound.
\end{proof}

Royen's Gaussian correlation inequality, in the form proved
in~\cite{LM17}, states that a centred Gaussian measure $\mu$ on $\R^N$ has
$\mu(K\cap K')\ge\mu(K)\mu(K')$ for any two closed convex sets $K$, $K'$
symmetric about the origin. Taking complements, $\mu(K'\setminus K)\le
\mu(K')\bigl(1-\mu(K)\bigr)$. For a slab $K$ and $K'$ an intersection of
slabs this is the inequality of \v{S}id\'ak.

\emph{Thresholds on the fluctuation.} Let $q\in\mathcal G(\Lambda)$,
$\lambda>0$ and $\kappa_{\rm f}>0$. For $\varphi\in\mathcal V_\gamma$ let
$\psi=\varphi-\varphi^*_q(\gamma)\in\mathcal V_0$ be its fluctuation. A block
$y$ of $\Lambda'$ is \emph{calm relative to the background} if $|(d\psi)_p|
\le\kappa_{\rm f}$ for every $p\in\Pi(y)$, and \emph{rough relative to the
background} otherwise; $R^{\rm f}(\varphi)$ is the set of these rough
blocks, and for $\psi\in\mathcal V_0$, $R^{\rm f}(\psi)$ is taken at
$\gamma=0$. For $X\subset\Lambda'$ put
\[
Z_X(\gamma)=\int_{\mathcal V_\gamma}e^{-\lambda q}\,\mathbf 1\{R^{\rm f}=X\}
\,dm_\gamma,\qquad\pi_X=\mu_q\{R^{\rm f}=X\},
\]
and, with $t=\lambda\kappa_{\rm f}^2$,
\[
\epsilon_1(t)=96\sqrt{2et}\,e^{-t},\qquad\epsilon(t)=\frac{\epsilon_1(t)}
{(1-e^{-t})^{96}} .
\]

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:sfglstep}
Let $q\in\mathcal G(\Lambda)$, $\lambda>0$, $\kappa_{\rm f}>0$ and $t=
\lambda\kappa_{\rm f}^2\ge\frac12$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item For every coarse field $\gamma$ and every $X\subset\Lambda'$,
\[
Z_X(\gamma)=Z_q\,\pi_X\,e^{-\lambda q'(\gamma)},
\]
and $\sum_X\pi_X=1$, so that $\int_{\mathcal V_\gamma}e^{-\lambda q}\,
dm_\gamma=\sum_XZ_X(\gamma)=Z_qe^{-\lambda q'(\gamma)}$.
\item For every set $Y$ of blocks, $\mu_q\{Y\cap R^{\rm f}=\emptyset\}\ge
(1-e^{-t})^{96|Y|}$; in particular $\pi_\emptyset\ge(1-e^{-t})^{96|
\Lambda'|}$.
\item For disjoint sets $X$, $Y$ of blocks,
\[
\mu_q\{X\subset R^{\rm f},\ Y\cap R^{\rm f}=\emptyset\}\le\epsilon_1(t)^{|X|}
\,\mu_q\{Y\cap R^{\rm f}=\emptyset\}.
\]
\item For every $X\subset\Lambda'$, $\pi_X\le\epsilon(t)^{|X|}\pi_\emptyset$.
\item $\epsilon$ decreases on $[\frac12,\infty)$, and $\epsilon(t)<e^{-9.2}$
for $t\ge16$.
\end{enumerate}
The bounds do not depend on $\gamma$, on the side of $\Lambda$ or on $q\in
\mathcal G(\Lambda)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(i) By Lemma~\ref{lem:sfglsplit}(i) and the translation $\varphi=\varphi^*_q
(\gamma)+\psi$, which maps $m_0$ to $m_\gamma$,
\[
Z_X(\gamma)=e^{-\lambda q'(\gamma)}\int_{\mathcal V_0}e^{-\lambda q(\psi)}
\mathbf 1\{R^{\rm f}(\psi)=X\}\,dm_0(\psi),
\]
since $R^{\rm f}$ depends on $\varphi$ only through $\psi$. The events
$\{R^{\rm f}=X\}$ partition $\mathcal V_0$.

(ii) The event is the intersection of the slabs $\{|(d\psi)_p|\le\kappa_{\rm
f}\}$, $p\in\Pi(Y)$, which are closed, convex and symmetric, and $|\Pi(Y)|=
96|Y|$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:lfowned}(i). Removing one slab at a time with the
correlation inequality gives $\mu_q\ge\prod_p\mu_q\{|(d\psi)_p|\le\kappa_{\rm
f}\}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:sfglsplit}(iii), $\Var(d\psi)_p\le(2\lambda)^{-1}$,
so by Lemma~\ref{lem:sfgltail}(i) each factor is at least $1-e^{-\lambda
\kappa_{\rm f}^2}$.

(iii) If $X\subset R^{\rm f}$, every $y\in X$ owns a plaquette $p_y$ with
$|(d\psi)_{p_y}|>\kappa_{\rm f}$; the $p_y$ are distinct, and $\sum_{y\in X}
(d\psi)_{p_y}^2>|X|\kappa_{\rm f}^2$. So $\{X\subset R^{\rm f}\}$ is
contained in the union, over the at most $96^{|X|}$ choices of $(p_y)_{y\in
X}$ with $p_y\in\Pi(y)$, of the events $E=\{\sum_y(d\psi)_{p_y}^2>|X|
\kappa_{\rm f}^2\}$. The complement of $E$ and $C_Y=\{Y\cap R^{\rm f}=
\emptyset\}$ are closed, convex and symmetric, so $\mu_q(E\cap C_Y)\le
\mu_q(E)\mu_q(C_Y)$ by the correlation inequality. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:sfglsplit}(iii) the covariance of $((d\psi)_{p_y})_{y\in X}$
is at most $(2\lambda)^{-1}I$, and Lemma~\ref{lem:sfgltail}(ii) with
$\sigma^2=(2\lambda)^{-1}$, $s=\kappa_{\rm f}$, $s^2/\sigma^2=2t\ge1$ and
$n=|X|$ gives $\mu_q(E)\le(2et)^{|X|/2}e^{-t|X|}$.

(iv) Let $Y=\Lambda'\setminus X$. By (iii), $\pi_X\le\mu_q\{X\subset R^{\rm
f},\ Y\cap R^{\rm f}=\emptyset\}\le\epsilon_1^{|X|}\mu_q(C_Y)$. By the
correlation inequality and (ii), $\pi_\emptyset=\mu_q(C_X\cap C_Y)\ge
\mu_q(C_X)\mu_q(C_Y)\ge(1-e^{-t})^{96|X|}\mu_q(C_Y)$, and $\mu_q(C_Y)>0$.

(v) The derivative of $\log\epsilon(t)$ is $\frac1{2t}-1-\frac{96e^{-t}}
{1-e^{-t}}<0$ for $t>\frac12$. With $\log96=5\log2+\log3$ and the bounds
on $\log2$, $\log3$ of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:lfkp}(ii),
\[
\log\epsilon_1(16)=\tfrac{15}2\log2+\log3-15.5<-9.20278 .
\]
As $e>2.7$, $e^{16}>2.7^{16}>7.9\cdot10^6$, and $-\log(1-x)\le x/(1-x)$
gives $-96\log(1-e^{-16})<10^{-4}$. So $\log\epsilon(16)<-9.2$.
\end{proof}

The large-field remainder of the Gaussian layer is therefore exact: the
weight of a fibre is the Gaussian factor $e^{-\lambda q'(\gamma)}$ times a
constant, the calm part carries the factor $\pi_\emptyset$, and the parts with
a rough region $X$ carry $\pi_X\le\epsilon(t)^{|X|}\pi_\emptyset$, none of
which depends on $\gamma$. The weights $\pi_X$ need not factorise over the
components of $X$, and no polymer representation of them is needed, since
they do not depend on the coarse field. For $t\ge16$ they satisfy the bound
$e^{-9|X|}$ that Theorem~\ref{thm:lfkp} asks of activities, and
$-\log\pi_\emptyset\le96|\Lambda'|e^{-t}/(1-e^{-t})$. Part (iii) is the
analogue of Theorem~\ref{thm:lfsuppression}(ii) without its hypothesis on the
exterior: the exterior is not fixed but integrated, under the condition that
it is calm.

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:sfglscales}
Let $\Lambda_0$ be a torus of side $2^m$, $m\ge2$, let $\Lambda_k$ be its
$k$-th coarse torus, $q_0=Q_{\Lambda_0}$, and for $k\le m-3$ let $q_{k+1}$ be
the restriction of $q_k'$ to $\mathcal A(\Lambda_{k+1})$. Then for $0\le k
\le m-2$, $q_k\in\mathcal G(\Lambda_k)$, $q_k$ is invariant under the
gauge transformations of $\Lambda_k$ that are constant on its blocks, and
Theorem~\ref{thm:sfglstep} holds at the scale $k$ with the same $\lambda$,
the same $\kappa_{\rm f}$ and the same $\epsilon(t)$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
$Q_{\Lambda_0}$ is invariant under all gauge transformations. For $k\le
m-3$ the side of $\Lambda_{k+1}$ is even and at least four, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:sfglsplit}(ii) passes both properties from $q_k$ to
$q_{k+1}$: the gauge transformations of $\Lambda_{k+1}$ constant on its
blocks are of the form $d'h$.
\end{proof}

So the hypotheses of the Gaussian layer reproduce themselves exactly: the
form at the next scale again dominates the plaquette form of its lattice,
the coupling $\lambda$ does not change, and every constant of
Theorem~\ref{thm:sfglstep} is the same at every scale. The restriction to
$\mathcal A(\Lambda_{k+1})$ is the tree gauge of the coarse field. By the
gauge invariance in Lemma~\ref{lem:sfglsplit}(ii), and since every coarse
field is $\gamma_0+d'h$ with $\gamma_0\in\mathcal A(\Lambda_{k+1})$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:blocktree}(i) on $\Lambda_{k+1}$, the weight
$e^{-\lambda q_k'}$ is determined by its values on $\mathcal
A(\Lambda_{k+1})$, as the weight of $\SU(2)$ is by Lemma~\ref{lem:sfgaugeinv}.

\emph{The shell in the mean.} At $\gamma=0$ the background vanishes and
the thresholds relative to the background are the thresholds of the linear
model. For $X\subset T$ with components $X_i$ let $K^{\rm lin}_{X_i}$ and
$S^{\rm lin}_{X_i}$ be the integrals of Theorem~\ref{thm:lfmarkov}(i) and of
the calm weight $S_{X_i}$, formed in the linear model at $\gamma=0$ as
$K^{\rm lin}_X$ and $S^{\rm lin}_X$ are for $X=\{y\}$, and $\rho^{\rm lin}
_{X_i}=K^{\rm lin}_{X_i}/S^{\rm lin}_{X_i}$, defined almost surely under the
calm law $\mu^\circ$ of the linear model.

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:sfglshell}
In the linear model on the torus $\Lambda_L$ with $\gamma=0$, let $\kappa>0$
and $\lambda\kappa^2\ge\frac12$. For every nonempty $X\subset T$ with
components $X_i$,
\[
\E_{\mu^\circ}\Bigl[\prod_i\rho^{\rm lin}_{X_i}\Bigr]\le\epsilon(\lambda
\kappa^2)^{|X|},
\]
and $\mu^\circ\{\prod_i\rho^{\rm lin}_{X_i}>R\}\le\epsilon(\lambda\kappa^2)
^{|X|}/R$ for $R>0$. For $\lambda\kappa^2\ge16$ the mean is at most
$e^{-9.2|X|}$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Lemma~\ref{lem:sfkernel} and the factorisation of
Theorem~\ref{thm:lfmarkov}(i) concern only which links a factor involves, so
they hold in the linear model, and as in the proof of
Proposition~\ref{prop:sfrelative}(i) the law of the outer variables of $X$
under $\mu^\circ$ has density $Z^{-1}_\emptyset\varPhi_X\prod_iS^{\rm lin}
_{X_i}$ with respect to Lebesgue measure on them, where $Z_\emptyset=\int
e^{-\lambda Q}\prod_ys_y\,dm_0$. Hence
\[
\E_{\mu^\circ}\Bigl[\prod_i\rho^{\rm lin}_{X_i}\Bigr]\le Z_\emptyset^{-1}
\int\varPhi_X\prod_iK^{\rm lin}_{X_i},
\]
and
\[
Z_\emptyset^{-1}\int\varPhi_X\prod_iK^{\rm lin}_{X_i}=\frac{\int
e^{-\lambda Q}\,\mathbf 1\{R=X\}\,dm_0}{\int e^{-\lambda Q}\,\mathbf 1\{R=
\emptyset\}\,dm_0}=\frac{\pi_X}{\pi_\emptyset},
\]
the last for $q=Q_{\Lambda_L}$, $\gamma=0$ and $\kappa_{\rm f}=\kappa$, where
the rough set $R$ of the linear model is $R^{\rm f}$. Apply
Theorem~\ref{thm:sfglstep}(iv),~(v) and Markov's inequality.
\end{proof}

So in the linear model the relative activities are not essentially bounded
under the calm law (Theorem~\ref{thm:sfshelllin}) but are bounded in the
mean, with the explicit bound $\epsilon(\lambda\kappa^2)^{|X|}$, uniformly in
the volume and for every $X$; the boundary values of
Theorem~\ref{thm:sfshelllin}, at which the ratio is large, have calm-law
probability at most $\epsilon^{|X|}/R$. This is the mean form asked for in
Remark~\ref{rem:sfconditioning}. In the mean the regress of
Remark~\ref{rem:sfshell} does not arise, because the outer variables are
integrated and not fixed in the shell.

\emph{The sharp threshold away from $\gamma=0$.} For $\gamma\ne0$ the
threshold of the linear model is placed on $\varphi=\varphi^*_q(\gamma)+
\psi$. When the background is calm with a margin, the sharp calm weight
lies within the factor $\pi_\emptyset$ of the Gaussian form.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:sfglbackground}
Let $L\ge32$ and $q=Q_{\Lambda_L}$, and for a coarse field $\gamma$ let
$\kappa_c(\gamma)$ be the largest $|(d'\gamma)_P|$ over the coarse
plaquettes $P$. Then for every plaquette $p$ of $\Lambda_L$,
\[
\bigl|(d\varphi^*_q(\gamma))_p\bigr|\le K_*\,\kappa_c(\gamma),\qquad K_*<
1.64\cdot10^{19}.
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
In the notation of Theorem~\ref{thm:sfprop}, $\varphi^*_q(\gamma)=L_0\gamma-
PH^{-1}B^{\rm T}\gamma$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:effective}(ii) every
plaquette of $L_0\gamma$ is $0$ or a curvature $(d'\gamma)_P$, and since
$\gamma^{\rm T}Bv=\sum_p(dL_0\gamma)_p(dPv)_p$,
\[
(B^{\rm T}\gamma)_i=\sum_p(dL_0\gamma)_p(dPe_i)_p,\qquad|(B^{\rm T}\gamma)_i|
\le12\sqrt2\,\kappa_c(\gamma),
\]
by the bound $\sum_p|(dPe_i)_p|\le6\cdot2\sqrt2$ of the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:sfprop}(i). With $\sum_j|(dPe_j)_p|\le4p_1$ from the same
proof and $S_H=\max_i\sum_j|(H^{-1})_{ij}|$,
\[
\bigl|(d\varphi^*_q(\gamma))_p\bigr|\le\bigl(1+48\sqrt2\,p_1S_H\bigr)\kappa_c
(\gamma)=\bigl(1+\bar SS_H\bigr)\kappa_c(\gamma).
\]
By Theorem~\ref{thm:sfprop}(ii) at $\alpha=\frac1{500}$, $|(H^{-1})_{ij}|\le
66.3\,e^{-\alpha d(i,j)}$. A block carries $17+28=45$ coordinates, and at
most $(2d+1)^4-(2d-1)^4=64d^3+16d$ blocks lie at distance $d\ge1$ from a
given one. With $x=e^{-\alpha}$, $\sum_{d\ge1}dx^d\le(1-x)^{-2}$ and
$\sum_{d\ge1}d^3x^d=x(1+4x+x^2)(1-x)^{-4}\le6(1-x)^{-4}$, and $1-x\ge\alpha-
\alpha^2/2$ gives $(1-x)^{-1}<500.51=:r$, so $r^2<250511$ and $r^4<6.2756
\cdot10^{10}$. Hence
\begin{align*}
S_H&\le66.3\cdot45\bigl(1+384r^4+16r^2\bigr)\\
&<66.3\cdot45\cdot2.4100\cdot10^{13}<7.20\cdot10^{16},
\end{align*}
and $K_*=1+\bar SS_H<1+227.40\cdot7.20\cdot10^{16}<1.64\cdot10^{19}$.
\end{proof}

The constant is far from the truth. It comes from bounding $H^{-1}$ by
the slow rate $\frac1{500}$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:sfprop}, and it is used only
to state the margin condition below in terms of the coarse field.

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:sfglsharp}
Let $q\in\mathcal G(\Lambda)$, $0<\kappa_{\rm f}<\kappa$, $t=\lambda
\kappa_{\rm f}^2\ge\frac12$, and let $\gamma$ be a coarse field whose
background has $|(d\varphi^*_q(\gamma))_p|\le\kappa-\kappa_{\rm f}$ for every
plaquette $p$; for $q=Q_{\Lambda_L}$ and $L\ge32$ this holds when $\kappa_c
(\gamma)\le(\kappa-\kappa_{\rm f})/K_*$. Let $Z^{\rm lin}_\emptyset(\gamma)=
\int_{\mathcal V_\gamma}e^{-\lambda q}\prod_ys_y\,dm_\gamma$, where $s_y$ is
the indicator that every plaquette of $\Pi(y)$ has $|(d\varphi)_p|\le
\kappa$. Then
\[
0\le-\log Z^{\rm lin}_\emptyset(\gamma)-\lambda q'(\gamma)+\log Z_q\le
-\log\pi_\emptyset\le\frac{96|\Lambda'|e^{-t}}{1-e^{-t}} .
\]
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Since $\prod_ys_y\le1$, Theorem~\ref{thm:sfglstep}(i) gives the upper
bound $Z^{\rm lin}_\emptyset(\gamma)\le Z_qe^{-\lambda q'(\gamma)}$. If every block is
calm relative to the background, then $|(d\varphi)_p|\le|(d\varphi^*_q
(\gamma))_p|+|(d\psi)_p|\le\kappa$ for every $p$, so $\prod_ys_y\ge\mathbf 1
\{R^{\rm f}=\emptyset\}$ and $Z^{\rm lin}_\emptyset(\gamma)\ge Z_\emptyset
(\gamma)=Z_q\pi_\emptyset e^{-\lambda q'(\gamma)}$. Finally Theorem~\ref
{thm:sfglstep}(ii) and $-\log(1-x)\le x/(1-x)$.
\end{proof}

So on the coarse fields whose background is calm with the margin
$\kappa_{\rm f}$, the sharp calm weight of the linear model is the Gaussian
form up to a factor between $\pi_\emptyset$ and one, and this factor costs at
most $96e^{-t}/(1-e^{-t})$ per block. This is a bound on the total, not a
local representation of $\gamma\mapsto-\log Z^{\rm lin}_\emptyset(\gamma)-
\lambda q'(\gamma)$. With the sharp threshold the calm events at
$\gamma\ne0$ are not symmetric, the correlation inequality does not apply to
them, and the comparison of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:sfglstep}(iv)
leaves the factor $(1-e^{-t})^{-96|\Lambda'|}$, which is not uniform in the
volume. This is why the thresholds are placed on the fluctuation.

\begin{remark}[what the $\SU(2)$ step needs beyond the Gaussian
layer]\label{rem:sfglsu2}
Theorem~\ref{thm:sfglstep} and its corollaries concern the linear model
only. A one-step expansion of the calm weight $Z_\emptyset(c)$ of $\SU(2)$ as
a Gaussian factor times a polymer remainder with the same properties is not
proved here, and the following parts of it are missing.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\alph*)},leftmargin=*]
\item \emph{The background.} The minimiser of $Q$ on the fibre $F_c$ of the
cut-off average, its existence and uniqueness near the linear minimiser,
and a bound of its plaquettes by the coarse curvature, the nonlinear
analogue of Proposition~\ref{prop:sfglbackground}. By
Theorem~\ref{thm:sfgaugeobst} the leading term must be invariant under
coarse gauge transformations, so the background is needed for every $c$ in
the class of Corollary~\ref{cor:sfcoarse}, not only for $c$ near $I$.
\item \emph{The non-Gaussian density.} In the chart of
Theorem~\ref{thm:fibrechart}(iii) around the background, the constrained
law has the density $e^{-\lambda Q(\Phi(\eta))-\psi(\eta)}$, a log-concave
perturbation of a Gaussian law for large $\lambda$; the mass outside the
chart is not bounded (Remark~\ref{rem:fibrechartopen}(a)).
\item \emph{The conditioning bound.} Royen's inequality, used in
Theorem~\ref{thm:sfglstep}(ii)--(iv), is a property of Gaussian measures.
A strongly log-concave law conditioned on a convex set is again strongly
log-concave, with the same constant, and concentrates about its conditional
mean; so the missing input for $\SU(2)$ is a bound on the conditional means
of the plaquette fluctuations, uniform in the convex conditioning event.
\item \emph{Locality.} The Gaussian form $q'$ is not of finite range. Its
kernel decays at the first step by Theorem~\ref{thm:sfprop}(iv), and its
decay at the later scales of Corollary~\ref{cor:sfglscales} is not proved.
Whether it couples blocks three apart is the question whether
$(M_W)_{AB}$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:sfgauss} vanishes, and $(M_W)_{AB}\ne0$ is not
proved by hand (Remark~\ref{rem:sfgaussvalue}).
\item \emph{Thresholds at all scales.} With thresholds on the fluctuation at
every scale, a fine plaquette is a sum of the lifts of the fluctuations of
all scales and of the last background. A bound of these lifts, which would
connect Corollary~\ref{cor:sfglscales} with the single-scale thresholds of
Theorem~\ref{thm:lfmarkov}, is not proved.
\end{enumerate}
\end{remark}

\paragraph*{The next step.}
To repeat the step at the coarse scale with constants $(\lambda_1,
\kappa_1)$, the proofs above need three properties of the weight
$e^{-A_1(c)}$ in place of $e^{-\lambda Q}$:
(H1) it is a product of nonnegative factors attached to the coarse blocks,
each depending on $c$ within distance one, up to a polymer expansion of the
kind just described;
(H2) the factor of a block that owns a coarse plaquette with $\delta(c_P,I)
>\kappa_1$ is at most $e^{-\lambda_1\kappa_1^2}$ times the calm weight,
with $\lambda_1\kappa_1^2-8\log M-c_1(\lambda_1,1)\ge9$;
(H3) the averages of calm coarse fields are calm.
Item (H3) holds at every step for $\kappa_1<\kappa_c$, since
Proposition~\ref{prop:smallframessharp}(iv) is a statement about one field
on any lattice; the threshold then grows by $16.003$ per step, or by
$4\cdot1.023$ along the composed average of Theorem~\ref{thm:defectscales}.
The suppression actually available for (H2) is inherited from the fine
scale, as follows.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:lfinherited}
Let $G=\SU(2)$, $\kappa<\kappa_c$ and $j\ge1$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item If $\delta(c_P,I)>16.003\kappa$, then $N(P)$ meets $\Pi(R(U))$. Each
rough block meets at most $2310$ witness regions, so at most $2310|R(U)|$
coarse plaquettes exceed $16.003\kappa$. On them the kernels carry
$e^{-\lambda Q^{(i)}/C_*}$, that is, the coupling $\lambda/C_*$.
\item Let $\rho\le1.023\cdot10^{-4}$, $\rho_0=\rho/(1.01\cdot1.023\cdot4^j)$,
and call a fine block rough at level $\rho_0$. By
Lemma~\ref{lem:scalewitness} and Theorem~\ref{thm:islandswide}(i), every
bad block of scale $j$ has a rough fine block among the $m_j=(17\cdot2^{j-1}
-2)^4$ blocks that meet its box. A fine block meets the boxes of at most
$H_j$ blocks of scale $j$, with $H_j$ as in that lemma. Hence for a set
$Y$ of blocks of scale $j$ and $a_0>0$,
$\sum_Xe^{-a_0|X|}\le e^{-A_j|Y|}$, where the sum runs over the sets $X$
of fine blocks inside the union of the boxes of $Y$ that meet every box,
and
\[
A_j=\max_{s>0}\Bigl(\frac{a_0-s}{H_j}-m_j\log(1+e^{-s})\Bigr).
\]
\item With $a_0=a(\beta_W/4,\rho_0)$ and $\rho=10^{-4}$, $A_j\ge9$ holds for
$\beta_W\ge\beta^{\rm pw}_j$, where $\beta^{\rm pw}_1=2.733\cdot10^{14}$,
$\beta^{\rm pw}_2=4.393\cdot10^{15}$ and $\beta^{\rm pw}_3=1.095\cdot
10^{17}$, and for $\beta_W\ge2.90\cdot10^{13}\cdot16^j$ whenever $1\le j\le
30$; $A_j<9$ for $\beta_W<1.57\cdot10^{13}\cdot16^j$. For every $\beta_W\in
[10^{22},10^{42}]$, the largest $j\le30$ with $\beta_W\ge2.90\cdot10^{13}
\cdot16^j$ satisfies $k_*-j\in\{1,2\}$, with $k_*$ as in
Corollary~\ref{cor:defectscales}.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
(i) is Lemma~\ref{lem:lfcoarseenergy} and Theorem~\ref{thm:lfmarkov}(ii),
with $N_{\rm ov}=1441$. (ii) The box of
Lemma~\ref{lem:scalewitness} has $17\cdot2^j-4$ points per coordinate, from
an even to an odd coordinate, so it meets $\frac12(17\cdot2^j-4)$ fine
blocks per coordinate. A witness plaquette with corner in the box is owned
by one of these. The number of boxes met by a fine block is the count of
that lemma for the two cubes of the block per coordinate, which is $H_j$. A set $X$ meeting all the boxes of $Y$
has $|X|\ge|Y|/H_j$ and lies in a set of at most $m_j|Y|$ blocks. So the
sum is at most $\sum_{k\ge|Y|/H_j}\binom{m_j|Y|}ke^{-a_0k}\le e^{-(a_0-s)
|Y|/H_j}(1+e^{-s})^{m_j|Y|}$.

(iii) Let $\lambda=\beta_W/4$, $b=16^{-j}\beta_W$ and $c=1.01\cdot1.023$, so
that $\lambda\rho_0^2=b/(4c^2\cdot10^8)$ with $4.27025<4c^2<4.27026$, and,
with $L_p=\log p$ as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:lfkp}(ii), $\log
\lambda=\log b+(4j-2)L_2$. By that proof $a_0\ge\lambda\rho_0^2-67.5\log
\lambda-K_0$ with $K_0<953.06$. Taking $e^s=m_jH_j$ in the maximum, and
using $m_j\log(1+1/(m_jH_j))\le1/H_j$,
\[
A_j\ge\frac{a_0-1-\log(m_jH_j)}{H_j}.
\]
So $A_j\ge9$ holds when $E(b)\ge R_j$, where
\begin{gather*}
E(b)=\frac b{4c^2\cdot10^8}-67.5\log b,\\
R_j=954.06+9H_j+\log(m_jH_j)+67.5(4j-2)L_2 .
\end{gather*}
$E$ increases for $b>3\cdot10^{10}$. Since $m_j<17^4\,2^{4j-4}$ and $\log17
<4L_2+\frac1{16}$, $\log(m_jH_j)<\frac14+(4j+24)L_2$ for $j\le2$ and
$<\frac14+(4j+12)L_2+8L_3$ for $j\ge3$; so $R_1<37931.3$, $R_2<38121.3$, $R_3<
60496.7$, and $R_j\le R_{30}<65624.6$ for $1\le j\le30$. With $\log(1.728
\cdot10^{13})=6L_2+3L_3+10\log10$, $\log(2.7\cdot10^{13})=3L_3+12\log10$
and $\log(3\cdot10^{13})=L_3+13\log10$ as upper bounds for $\log b$, $E(b)$
exceeds $37938$ at $b=2.733\cdot10^{14}/16$, $38127$ at $b=4.393\cdot
10^{15}/16^2$, $60505$ at $b=1.095\cdot10^{17}/16^3$ and $65816$ at
$b=2.90\cdot10^{13}$, which gives the thresholds. Conversely $A_j<a_0/H_j<
\lambda\rho_0^2/H_j$, since $\log M\ge0$ and $c_1(\lambda,1)>0$, so $A_j
\ge9$ needs $b>9H_j\cdot4c^2\cdot10^8\ge36864\cdot4.27025\cdot10^8>1.57\cdot
10^{13}$.

For the last assertion let $j$ be that largest integer, so that $16^j\le
\beta_W/(2.90\cdot10^{13})<16^{j+1}$, and $1\le j\le23$ because $2.90\cdot
10^{13}\cdot16<10^{22}$ and $2.90\cdot10^{13}\cdot16^{24}>10^{42}$. By
Corollary~\ref{cor:defectscales}, $X=10^{-4}/(1.01\rho(\beta_W))$ satisfies
$16^{k_*}\le X^2<16^{k_*+1}$ with $X^2=10^{-8}\beta_W/(1.0201\cdot96(\log
\beta_W+C_1))$, and $57<\log\beta_W+C_1<104$, since $C_1=C_0+\frac16(9L_2
+2L_5)$ with $C_0\in[4.90816,4.90817]$ (proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:islandthreshold}). Hence
\begin{gather*}
16^{k_*-j}\le\frac{X^2}{16^j}<\frac{16\cdot2.90\cdot10^{13}X^2}{\beta_W}
<\frac{4.64\cdot10^6}{97.92\cdot57}<16^3,\\
16^{k_*-j}>\frac{X^2}{16^{j+1}}\ge\frac{2.90\cdot10^{13}X^2}{16\beta_W}>
\frac{2.90\cdot10^5}{1567\cdot104}>1,
\end{gather*}
and $k_*-j\in\{1,2\}$.
\end{proof}

So the next step stands as follows.
Theorem~\ref{thm:islandswide} gives (H3) up to $a_{k_*}/8$ as a statement
about probabilities under the Wilson measure: the labels of the composed
average are rare. It gives neither (H1) nor (H2), which concern the
weight $e^{-A_1}$ for every coarse field. Proposition~\ref{prop:lfinherited}(iii)
reaches $a_{k_*}/4$, but it bounds sums of fine kernels with entropy of
$\ell^\infty$ adjacency rather than of the joining distance of the islands,
and only for activities of the form $e^{-a_0|X|}$ relative to the calm
weight, the hypothesis that is not proved. In both cases the suppression at
scale $j$ is the fine one at the radius $\rho_0\propto4^{-j}$, that is, the
coupling $\lambda/16^{j}$ in units of the scale-$j$ threshold. By
Proposition~\ref{prop:constantcurvature}, fine witnesses carry it no further
than $a_{k_*}$. Iterating the step instead loses the factor $C_*$ of
Theorem~\ref{thm:lfaction}(i), or $H_j\ge4096$ in
Proposition~\ref{prop:lfinherited}(ii), at every scale. What the iteration
needs is (H2) with $\lambda_1\ge(1-\varepsilon_1)\lambda$ and summable
$\varepsilon_k$, a lower bound $A_1\ge(1-\varepsilon)\lambda S_1$ on large
fields, local and relative to the calm weight. That requires a coarse
energy for $\SU(2)$ at every scale, of the kind
Proposition~\ref{prop:torusenergy} gives for torus-valued fields. It is not
proved here, and this subsection gives no bound on the mass gap.

Theorem~\ref{thm:islandwindow} is a union bound over the window, and its
conclusion concerns every island of $W$, so it is void in windows of
more than $10^{28166}$ blocks. The data of Theorem~\ref{thm:manyislands} do not need islands as
their units: the sets $I_u$ are any pairwise separated sets of blocks
off which every block of $\Lambda$ is good. If the islands are grouped into
clusters whose separation grows with their size, the island sums and the
weighted Dobrushin condition hold in every configuration of the labels, on
every torus and in every window. The rarity of the bad blocks then
enters only through the size of the clusters, and it bounds that size
block by block, with no union bound over a window.

\begin{definition}[clusters of bad blocks]\label{def:clusters}
Let $R\ge2s+8$ be an integer and $\kappa>0$, and put $g(m)=(3/\kappa)\log
m$ and $\ell_m=R+2g(m)$ for $m\ge1$. A partition $\mathcal P$ of a finite
set $B$ of blocks of the torus is \emph{separated} if
\begin{equation}\label{eq:clusterrule}
\dist(U,V)>R+g(\lvert U\rvert)+g(\lvert V\rvert)
\end{equation}
for all distinct $U,V\in\mathcal P$.
\end{definition}

\begin{lemma}[clusters]\label{lem:clusters}
Let $B$ be a finite set of blocks of the torus.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item Among the separated partitions of $B$ there is a finest one; its
parts are the \emph{clusters} of $B$. Starting from the partition into
single blocks and merging, in any order, two parts that
violate~\eqref{eq:clusterrule}, one reaches it after finitely many
merges.
\item Two blocks of $B$ at distance at most $R$ lie in one cluster; in
particular every island formed with the joining distance $2s+8$ lies in
one cluster, and distinct clusters are at distance more than $R$.
\item A cluster of $m$ blocks is connected in the graph on $B$ in which
two blocks are adjacent when their distance is at most $\ell_m$; its
blocks lie within distance $(m-1)\ell_m$ of each other.
\item If some cluster has more than $M_1$ blocks, then $B$ contains a set
of between $M_1+1$ and $2M_1$ blocks that is connected in the graph of
distance at most $\ell_{M_1}$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(i) Let $\mathcal Q$ be finer than a separated partition $\mathcal P$, and
let $U,V\in\mathcal Q$ violate~\eqref{eq:clusterrule}. If $U\subset U'$ and
$V\subset V'$ with distinct $U',V'\in\mathcal P$, then, since $g$
increases,
\[
\dist(U',V')\le\dist(U,V)\le R+g(\lvert U'\rvert)+g(\lvert V'\rvert),
\]
which contradicts the separation of $\mathcal P$; so $U\cup V$ lies in one
part of $\mathcal P$, and the partition obtained by merging $U$ and $V$ is
again finer than $\mathcal P$. The partition $\{B\}$ is separated, so the
merging starts below every separated partition and stays below it at each
step. Each merge lowers the number of parts, so the process stops, at a
separated partition finer than every separated partition, which is
therefore the finest one and does not depend on the order of the merges.
(ii) Two single blocks at distance at most $R$
violate~\eqref{eq:clusterrule}, since $g(1)=0$, so by the first step of
(i) they lie in one part of every separated partition. An island is
connected through steps of length at most $2s+8\le R$. The last assertion
is~\eqref{eq:clusterrule} with $g\ge0$.
(iii) By induction over the merges, every part of $m$ blocks of an
intermediate partition is connected at distance $\ell_m$: a single block
is, and if $U$ and $V$ are merged, with $\lvert U\rvert+\lvert V\rvert=m$,
then $\dist(U,V)\le R+g(\lvert U\rvert)+g(\lvert V\rvert)\le\ell_m$, while
$U$ and $V$ are connected at distances $\ell_{\lvert U\rvert},\ell_{\lvert
V\rvert}\le\ell_m$. Two blocks of a connected set of $m$ blocks are joined
by a path of at most $m-1$ steps.
(iv) Consider the first merge of the process of (i) that produces a part
of more than $M_1$ blocks. It merges two parts of at most $M_1$ blocks
each, at distance at most $R+2g(M_1)=\ell_{M_1}$, and each of them is
connected at distance $\ell_{M_1}$ by (iii).
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[the island sums for clusters]\label{thm:clustercomparison}
Let $s\ge1$, $r\le8\cdot10^{-5}$, $0\le\vartheta<1$, $\kappa=2(1-\vartheta)
\alpha_G$, $R\ge2s+8$, and form the clusters of the set of bad blocks of
the torus with these $R$ and $\kappa$. Let the data be those of
Theorem~\ref{thm:manyislands} on a set $\Lambda$ of blocks, under its
hypotheses, with $I_u=U_u\cap\Lambda$ for distinct clusters $U_u$,
$u\in\mathcal I$, every bad block of $\Lambda$ lying in some $I_u$. Put
\begin{gather*}
c_1=\frac{1920}{\beta_W}\bar\Lambda_2^2r^2\cdot45(2s+7)^4
e^{\kappa(2s+9)},\\
\tau=c_1e^{-\kappa R/2}\sigma(\kappa/2),
\end{gather*}
with $\bar\Lambda_2$ as before Theorem~\ref{thm:islandwindow} and
$\sigma(\cdot)$ as in Proposition~\ref{prop:islandmass}, and for
$u\in\mathcal I$ let $\hat T_u=\sum_{v\in\mathcal I\setminus\{u\}}
\varDelta_{uv}e^{2\vartheta\alpha_G\ell(u,v)}$, with $\ell$ the
pseudometric of Corollary~\ref{cor:islandchains}. Then, for every
configuration of the labels:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item $\hat T_u\le\tau$ for every $u\in\mathcal I$; hence $S_a,S_b\le\tau$,
the sums $T_a,T_b$ of Corollary~\ref{cor:islandchains} are at most $\tau$,
and
\[
\varDelta_{ab}\le\min\bigl\{\tau,\ c_1e^{-\kappa R/2}e^{-\kappa\dist(I_a,
I_b)/2}\bigr\};
\]
\item $\varDelta_*\le\varDelta_{ab}+\frac14\tau^2$, and if $\tau<4$ the
weighted Dobrushin condition of Corollary~\ref{cor:islandchains} holds with
$\theta\le\tau/4$ and
\[
\varDelta_*\le\varDelta_{ab}+\frac{e^{-2\vartheta\alpha_G\ell(a,b)}
\tau^2}{4-\tau};
\]
\item for $\beta_W\ge\beta_0>0$ at fixed $R$, $\tau(\beta_W)\le(\beta_W/
\beta_0)\,\tau(\beta_0)$.
\end{enumerate}
At $\rho=2.17\cdot10^{-16}$, $r=43\rho$ and $\beta_W=\beta^*$ of
Theorem~\ref{thm:islandwindow}: for $s=1$, $\log_{10}c_1\le21.74$ and
$\tau\le10^{-1047}$ at $\vartheta=0$, $R=10^7$, and $\tau\le10^{-1045}$ at
$\vartheta=\frac12$, $R=2\cdot10^7$; for $s=5$, $\tau\le10^{-1045}$ and
$\tau\le10^{-1044}$ at the same $\vartheta$ and $R$. By (iii) the same
bounds hold at $\beta_W\ge\beta^*$ with $R$ replaced by $R+\lceil(2/\kappa)
\log(\beta_W/\beta^*)\rceil$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\emph{The data.} The sets $I_u$ are pairwise disjoint and, by
Lemma~\ref{lem:clusters}(ii), at distance more than $R\ge2s+8$, so
$w_{uv}\ge2s+8$, and every block of $\Lambda$ outside $\bigcup_uI_u$ is
good. The proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:lambdatwo} bounds the norm of
$\partial_{x_u}\nabla_z\mathcal U$ by the largest sum, over one $x_u$-link
or one $z$-link, of the norms of the blocks of that matrix, and these are
determined by the plaquettes at one link; as in the paragraph before
Theorem~\ref{thm:islandwindow}, it applies to each $I_u$ and gives
$\Lambda_2\le\bar\Lambda_2$. Every $x_u$-link is based in a block at
distance at most $s+3$ from $I_u$, so $n_u\le45(2s+7)^4\lvert I_u\rvert
\le45(2s+7)^4m_u$, where $m_u=\lvert U_u\rvert$.

\emph{One pair.} Let $u\ne v$ and $d=\dist(I_u,I_v)$, so that $w_{uv}-2s-8
=d-2s-9\ge0$ and $\ell(u,v)\le d-2s-9$. Since $2\alpha_G-2\vartheta
\alpha_G=\kappa$,
\[
\varDelta_{uv}e^{2\vartheta\alpha_G\ell(u,v)}\le c_1\sqrt{m_um_v}\,
e^{-\kappa d} .
\]
By~\eqref{eq:clusterrule}, $d\ge\dist(U_u,U_v)>R+g(m_u)+g(m_v)$, so
that
\[
e^{-\kappa d}\le e^{-\kappa d/2}e^{-\kappa R/2}(m_um_v)^{-3/2},
\]
since $e^{-\kappa g(m)/2}=m^{-3/2}$. Hence
\[
\varDelta_{uv}e^{2\vartheta\alpha_G\ell(u,v)}\le c_1e^{-\kappa R/2}\,
\frac{e^{-\kappa d/2}}{m_um_v}\le\frac{c_1e^{-\kappa R/2}}{m_u}\,
e^{-\kappa d/2}.
\]
\emph{The sum.} For $v\ne u$ let $y_v$ be a block of $I_v$ nearest to
$I_u$; distinct $v$ give distinct $y_v$, and $e^{-\kappa\dist(I_u,I_v)/2}
\le\sum_{x\in I_u}e^{-\kappa\dist(x,y_v)/2}$. Summing over $v$ and using
the preimages of the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:islandmass}(ii),
\[
\sum_{v\ne u}e^{-\kappa\dist(I_u,I_v)/2}\le\lvert I_u\rvert\,
\sigma(\kappa/2)\le m_u\,\sigma(\kappa/2),
\]
so $\hat T_u\le\tau$. The sums $S_a$, $T_a$ and the row sums of the
corollary are sums of terms of $\hat T_a$ or $\hat T_q$, with factors at
most one in the case of $S_a$, and $\varDelta_{ab}$ is one term of
$\hat T_a$; the second bound on $\varDelta_{ab}$ is the bound of one pair
with $m_am_b\ge1$ and $e^{-2\vartheta\alpha_G\ell(a,b)}\le1$. This
proves (i).

(ii) The first form of $\varDelta_*$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:manyislands} and
(i) give the first bound. By $\tanh t\le t$, the sum of
Corollary~\ref{cor:islandchains} at $q$ is at most $\frac14\hat T_q\le
\tau/4$, so $\theta\le\tau/4<1$, and the corollary with $T_a,T_b\le\tau$
gives the second.

(iii) $\bar\Lambda_2(\beta)/\beta$ decreases, so $\bar\Lambda_2(\beta_W)
\le(\beta_W/\beta_0)\bar\Lambda_2(\beta_0)$ and $\bar\Lambda_2^2/\beta_W$
grows at most linearly.

\emph{The numbers.} Let $L_p=\log p$ with the bounds of the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:lfkp}(ii); the same series at $x=\frac1{21}$ and
$\frac1{73}$ gives $\log\frac{11}{10}$ and $\log\frac{37}{36}$ to within
$10^{-10}$, so $2.39789527<L_{11}<2.39789528$ and $3.61091791<L_{37}<
3.61091792$. The function $g(\beta)=\beta\rho^2/16-6(\log\beta+C_0)-\lvert
\log q^*\rvert$ increases for $\beta>96/\rho^2$ and $\beta^*$ is its
largest zero, with $C_0<4.90817$ (proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:islandthreshold}) and $\rho^2=4.7089\cdot10^{-32}$. Since
$N_s<(4s+17)^4$,
\[
\lvert\log q^*\rvert<H\bigl(L_2+8\log(4s+17)\bigr)+1+4L_{11}+4L_2+4L_3,
\]
which is below $32481.69$ for $s=1$, with $\log21=L_3+L_7$, and below
$38354.08$ for $s=5$. At $\beta_1=1.1221\cdot10^{37}$, $\beta_1\rho^2/16>
33024.10$ and, with $\log1.1221<\log\frac98$, $6(\log\beta_1+C_0)<541.33$,
so $g(\beta_1)>1$; at $\beta_5=1.3217\cdot10^{37}$, $\beta_5\rho^2/16>
38898.45$ and, with $\log1.3217<\log\frac43$, $6(\log\beta_5+C_0)<542.35$,
so $g(\beta_5)>2$. Hence $\beta^*<\beta_s$ for $s=1,5$. As $\bar\Lambda_2^2
/\beta_W=(99.0001+4.65\cdot10^6/\beta_W)^2\beta_W$ increases with
$\beta_W$, and $e^x\le1+x+x^2$ for $0\le x\le1$, at $\beta_W=\beta^*$
\[
c_1\le1920\cdot99.0002^2\cdot43^2\cdot45(2s+7)^4\bigl(1+x+x^2\bigr)
\beta_s\rho^2,
\]
where $x=\kappa(2s+9)$.
For $s=1$ this is below $5.4581\cdot10^{21}$ at $\vartheta=0$ and
$5.4431\cdot10^{21}$ at $\vartheta=\frac12$, and for $s=5$ below $8.2171
\cdot10^{22}$ and $8.1779\cdot10^{22}$. In particular $\log_{10}c_1<21.74$
for $s=1$, $\vartheta=0$, as $5.4581<3^7/400$ and $7L_3-4L_2-2L_5<0.74\log
10$. By the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:islandmass}, $\sigma(\kappa/2)
\le1+384(\kappa/2-\kappa^2/8)^{-4}+16(\kappa/2-\kappa^2/8)^{-2}$, which is
below $9.8354\cdot10^{16}$ at $\vartheta=0$, $\kappa/2=2.5\cdot10^{-4}$, and
below $1.5733\cdot10^{18}$ at $\vartheta=\frac12$. In all four cases
$\kappa R/2=2500$, and $e^{-2500}<10^{-1085.736}$ since $1085.736\log10<
2500$. The product $c_1\sigma(\kappa/2)$ is below $5.37\cdot10^{38}<
10^{38.736}$ for $s=1$, $\vartheta=0$, as $\log5.4=3L_3-L_5<0.736\log10$;
below $10^{40}$ for $s=1$, $\vartheta=\frac12$ and for $s=5$, $\vartheta=
0$; and below $1.3\cdot10^{41}<10^{41.736}$ for $s=5$, $\vartheta=
\frac12$. This gives the four bounds on $\tau$.
\end{proof}

The theorem has no exceptional event: the conditions that
Theorem~\ref{thm:islandwindow} obtains outside probability
$10^{-28166}\lvert W\rvert$ hold for the clusters in every window of every
size. What the rarity has to give is that the clusters are small, and this
is a statement about one block at a time. Write $U(y)$ for the cluster of
a bad block $y$ and $I(y)$ for its island.

\begin{theorem}[the size of the clusters]\label{thm:clustersizes}
Let $G=\SU(2)$, $s\ge1$, $\rho$, $r$, $\eta$, $\beta^*$, $q^*$, $M=11^4$
and $H=6^4$ be as in Theorem~\ref{thm:islandwindow}, $\beta_W\ge\beta^*$,
$p=q_\rho(\beta_W)\le q^*$, $A=eMHp$, and form the clusters of the bad
blocks of a torus of $L^4$ blocks with $R\ge2s+8$ and $\kappa>0$. Put
$N_5=11^4-1$, $N_\ell=(2\ell+1)^4-1$ for $\ell\ge5$, and
\[
\nu_\ell=4\bigl(N_5+N_\ell A^{1/2}\bigr)A^{1/(2H)} .
\]
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item For every block $y$ and $m\ge1$,
$\mu_L\{y\in B,\ \lvert U(y)\rvert=m\}\le A^{(H+1)/(2H)}\nu_{\ell_m}^{m-1}$.
\item If $\nu_{\ell_{M_1}}<1$, then
\[
\begin{split}
\mu_L\{&\text{a cluster has more than }M_1\text{ blocks}\}\\
&\le\frac{L^4A^{(H+1)/(2H)}\nu_{\ell_{M_1}}^{M_1}}{1-\nu_{\ell_{M_1}}}.
\end{split}
\]
\item If $1\le m_0\le M_1$ and $\nu_{\ell_{M_1}}<1$, then
$\mu_L\{y\in B,\ U(y)\ne I(y)\}$ is at most
\[
\begin{split}
&(2(m_0-1)\ell_{m_0}+1)^4(2\ell_{m_0}+1)^4(Mp)^2\\
&+\frac{A^{(H+1)/(2H)}\nu_{\ell_{M_1}}^{m_0}}{1-\nu_{\ell_{M_1}}}
+\epsilon_{M_1},
\end{split}
\]
with $\epsilon_{M_1}$ the bound of (ii).
\end{enumerate}
At $\rho=2.17\cdot10^{-16}$, $\beta_W=\beta^*$, $s=1$, $\vartheta=0$,
$\kappa=2\alpha_G$, $R=10^7$ and $M_1=10^{10^{1700}}$: $\ell_{M_1}\le
10^{1705}$, $\nu_\ell\le0.2130$ for every $\ell\le\ell_{M_1}$, the bound of
(ii) is at most $L^4\,10^{-0.67M_1}$, and (iii) with $m_0=10^5$ gives
\[
\mu_L\{y\in B,\ U(y)\ne I(y)\}\le10^{-28126}+L^4\,10^{-0.67M_1}.
\]
At $\vartheta=\frac12$, $R=2\cdot10^7$ the first term is at most
$10^{-28124}$. For $s=5$, $\nu_\ell\le0.0222$, the bound of (ii) is at most
$L^4\,10^{-1.65M_1}$, and the first term of (iii) is at most
$10^{-33227}$ at $\vartheta=0$, $R=10^7$ and $10^{-33224}$ at $\vartheta=
\frac12$, $R=2\cdot10^7$. The
same numbers hold at $\beta_W\ge\beta^*$ with $R$ replaced by
$R+\lceil(2/\kappa)\log(\beta_W/\beta^*)\rceil$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(i) By Lemma~\ref{lem:clusters}(iii), on the event $U(y)$ is a set $S\ni
y$ of $m$ bad blocks, connected at distance $\ell=\ell_m$. Let $S_1,\dots,
S_k$ be the components of $S$ in the graph of distance at most $5$; they
are pairwise at distance at least $6$, so Step~1 of the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:islandwindow} gives
\[
\mu_L(S\subset B)\le\prod_iA^{\lceil\lvert S_i\rvert/H\rceil}\le
A^{k/2+m/(2H)},
\]
since $\lceil n/H\rceil\ge\frac12(1+n/H)$ and $A<1$. Choose a spanning
tree of $S$ formed by spanning trees of the $S_i$ at distance $5$ and
$k-1$ further edges of length at most $\ell$, which exist because $S$ is
connected at distance $\ell$. A walk of $2(m-1)$ steps around the tree
from $y$ recovers $S$: it is fixed by the positions of the $m-1$ forward
steps, at most $4^{m-1}$ choices, by which $k-1$ of them are long, at most
$\binom{m-1}{k-1}$, and by their offsets, $N_5$ for a short step and
$N_\ell$ for a long one. Summing over $k$,
\[
\begin{split}
\mu_L\{&y\in B,\ \lvert U(y)\rvert=m\}\\
&\le A^{\frac12+\frac m{2H}}\sum_{k=1}^m4^{m-1}\binom{m-1}{k-1}
N_5^{m-k}N_\ell^{k-1}A^{\frac{k-1}2}\\
&=A^{\frac12+\frac m{2H}}\bigl(4(N_5+N_\ell A^{1/2})\bigr)^{m-1},
\end{split}
\]
which is (i).
(ii) By Lemma~\ref{lem:clusters}(iv) some block lies in a set of $m\in
(M_1,2M_1]$ bad blocks connected at distance $\ell_{M_1}$; the count of
(i) with $\ell=\ell_{M_1}$, summed over $m>M_1$ and over the $L^4$ blocks,
gives (ii).
(iii) If $\lvert U(y)\rvert>m_0$, either $\lvert U(y)\rvert\le M_1$,
which by (i) and $\nu_{\ell_m}\le\nu_{\ell_{M_1}}$ for $m\le M_1$ has
probability at most the second term, or some cluster has more than $M_1$
blocks. If $\lvert U(y)\rvert\le m_0$ and $U(y)$ contains a second island,
then $U(y)$, connected at distance $\ell_{m_0}$, has an edge between
blocks $z,z'$ of different islands: $z$ lies within distance
$(m_0-1)\ell_{m_0}$ of $y$, and $2s+9\le\dist(z,z')\le\ell_{m_0}$. Step~1
of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:islandwindow} with $S_1=\{z\}$,
$S_2=\{z'\}$ gives $(Mp)^2$, and a union bound over $z$ and $z'$ gives
the first term.

For $\beta_W=t\beta^*$, $t\ge1$, Step~6 of the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:islandwindow} gives $\log(p/q^*)\le f(\beta_W)-f(\beta^*)
\le6\log t-32481(t-1)$, since $\beta^*\rho^2/16>\lvert\log q^*\rvert>
32481$ for $s=1$ and $s=5$, by the bounds below. With $R$ raised by
$\lceil(2/\kappa)\log t\rceil\le1+(2/\kappa)\log t$, the length
$\ell_{m_0}\ge R$ is multiplied by at most $1+10^{-7}+4\cdot10^{-4}\log t$,
and the first term of (iii) by at most $(1+10^{-7}+4\cdot10^{-4}\log t)^8
t^{12}e^{-64962(t-1)}<1+10^{-6}$, since $\log t\le t-1$; the margins below
absorb this factor. The factor $N_\ell$ in $\nu_\ell$ grows by a power of
$1+\log t$ that $A^{1/2}$ absorbs, and the other factors decrease.

\emph{The numbers.} Let $L_p=\log p$ with the bounds of the proofs of
Theorems~\ref{thm:lfkp}(ii) and~\ref{thm:clustercomparison}. By the
definition of $q^*$, with $N_s=(4s+17)^4-1$ as in
Theorem~\ref{thm:islandwindow}, $A\le eMHq^*=(2N_s^2)^{-H}$ and $Mp\le Mq^*=(2N_s^2)^{-H}
/(eH)$. From $4\log(4s+17)-1/N_s\le\log N_s<4\log(4s+17)$, $\log(2N_s^2)$
exceeds $25.049316$ at $s=1$ and $29.580489$ at $s=5$, while $\log(eH)=1+4L_2+4L_3>
8.167037$. Let $s=1$ and $\vartheta=0$, so $\kappa=5\cdot10^{-4}$, $6/\kappa
=12000$ and $\ell_{M_1}=10^7+12000\cdot10^{1700}\log10<10^{1705}$; at
$\vartheta=\frac12$, $\ell_{M_1}<2\cdot10^7+24000\cdot10^{1700}\log10<
10^{1705}$ as well. Since $2N_1^2=75644940800>275000^2$, $A^{1/(2H)}<
1/275000$, and $A^{1/2}<10^{-6998}$ as $2N_1^2>10^{11}/1.5>10^{10.8}$, by $1.5^5<10$; with $N_\ell<
10^{6822}$ for $\ell\le10^{1705}$,
\[
\nu_\ell<\frac{4\cdot14640}{275000}+10^{-176}<0.2130<\frac{16}{75}<
10^{-0.67},
\]
the last since $\log\frac{16}{75}=4L_2-L_3-2L_5<-0.67\log10$. As
$A^{(H+1)/(2H)}<10^{-6998}$ and $1/(1-\nu_\ell)<2$, the bound of (ii) is at
most $L^4\,10^{-0.67M_1}$. In (iii), $\ell_{m_0}=10^7+60000\log10<
10138156$ and $(2(m_0-1)\ell_{m_0}+1)(2\ell_{m_0}+1)<4.125\cdot10^{19}=
\frac{33}8\cdot10^{19}$, so the logarithm of the first term is below
\begin{multline*}
4\bigl(L_3+L_{11}-3L_2+19\log10\bigr)\\
-2592\cdot25.049316-2\cdot8.167037<-64763.49,
\end{multline*}
while $28126\log10<64762.51$; the second term is below $10^{-6998}\cdot
0.213^{10^5}$, so the sum of the first two terms is below $10^{-28126}$.
At $\vartheta=\frac12$, $R=2\cdot10^7$, $\ell_{m_0}<20276311$, the product
is below $1.65\cdot10^{20}=3\cdot5\cdot11\cdot10^{18}$, and the logarithm of
the first term is below $4(L_3+L_5+L_{11}+18\log10)-2592\cdot25.049316-2
\cdot8.167037<-64757.95<-28124\log10$. For $s=5$, $2N_s^2>2650000^2$ gives
$\nu_\ell<4\cdot14640/2650000+10^{-176}<0.0222<\frac1{45}<10^{-1.65}$, since
$\log\frac1{45}=-2L_3-L_5<-1.65\log10$, hence the bound of (ii); and the
logarithm of the first term of (iii) is below $4(L_3+L_{11}-3L_2+19\log10)-
2592\cdot29.580489-2\cdot8.167037<-76508.29<-33227\log10$ at
$\vartheta=0$, and, with the bracket $4(L_3+L_5+L_{11}+18\log10)$ of
$\vartheta=\frac12$, below $-76502.75<-33224\log10$ at $\vartheta=
\frac12$.
\end{proof}

On a torus of at most $10^{M_1/2}$ blocks, $M_1=10^{10^{1700}}$, the
theorem gives, outside probability $10^{-M_1/10}$, that no cluster has
more than $M_1$ blocks, and the expected number of blocks of a window $W$
that lie in a cluster other than a single island is at most
$\lvert W\rvert(10^{-28126}+10^{-M_1/10})$ for $s=1$: a density, not a
union bound. Theorems~\ref{thm:clustercomparison}
and~\ref{thm:clustersizes} thus remove the window size from the island
comparison of item~(ii) of Sec.~\ref{ssec:remains}, given the labels and
with clusters as the units. The size of the torus remains only in the term $\epsilon_{M_1}$
of Theorem~\ref{thm:clustersizes}, at sizes far beyond any other in this
paper. The next proposition shows that a separation growing
with the size of the units is needed, and where the count of (i) stops.

\begin{proposition}[the reach of the clusters]\label{prop:clusterreach}
\leavevmode
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item Let $R'\ge2s+8$ and $m\ge1$, and on a torus of side at least
$2(m+2)(R'+1)$ let the bad blocks be $u_i=iR'e_1$ and $v_i=u_i+(-1)^i
(R'+1)e_2$, $1\le i\le m$. In the finest partition of these blocks into
parts at mutual distance more than $R'$, the $u_i$ form one part $U$ and
each $v_i$ is a part $V_i$, and with $c_0=\frac{1920}{\beta_W}
\bar\Lambda_2^2r^2\cdot45(2s+7)^4e^{-2\alpha_G(R'-2s-8)}$,
\[
\sum_i\bar\varDelta_{UV_i}=c_0m^{3/2},\qquad
\sum_{i,j}\bar\varDelta_{u_jv_i}\ge c_0m .
\]
So no partition whose parts are separated by a distance independent of
their size bounds the sums $\hat T_u$, through $\bar\varDelta$ either for
the parts or for their islands, uniformly in the configuration.
\item With $A=eMHq^*$, $s=1$: $\nu_\ell<1$ for $\log_{10}\ell\le1763.2$
and $\nu_\ell>1$ for $\log_{10}\ell\ge1763.3$, and $N_\ell A\ge1$ for
$\log_{10}\ell\ge3524.5$. For $\ell_{M_1}$ beyond the first value the
count of Theorem~\ref{thm:clustersizes}(i) is void, and beyond the second
the bound $N_\ell A$ on the expected number of bad blocks within distance
$\ell$ of a block exceeds one.
\end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
(i) Consecutive $u_i$ are at distance $R'$ and so lie in one part; the
distance of $v_i$ to $u_j$ is $\max\{\lvert i-j\rvert R',R'+1\}$, and to
$v_j$, $j\ne i$, at least $\min\{2R',2R'+2\}>R'$, so the finest partition
is the one stated, with $\dist(U,V_i)=R'+1$ and $w_{UV_i}=R'$. The
neighbourhoods of radius $s+3$ of the $u_i$ are disjoint, since
$R'>2s+6$, so $\bar n_U=45\,m(2s+7)^4$ and $\bar n_{V_i}=45(2s+7)^4$,
which gives the first identity. The pair $(u_i,v_i)$ alone contributes
$c_0$ to the second sum. Both sums grow without bound in $m$ at fixed
$R'$.
(ii) $\nu_\ell<1$ is $N_\ell<A^{-1/2}(A^{-1/(2H)}/4-N_5)$. By the
definition of $q^*$, $A=(2N_1^2)^{-H}$, so $A^{-1/(2H)}=\sqrt2N_1\in(275036,
275037)$, as $275036^2<2N_1^2=75644940800<275037^2$, and $A^{-1/(2H)}/4-N_5$
lies between $54000=2^43^35^3$ and $54675=3^75^2$. With the
bounds of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:clustersizes},
$25.049316<\log(2N_1^2)<25.049327$, so the logarithm of the right side lies
between $16242.85$ and $16242.88$. For $\log_{10}\ell\le1763.2$, $\log
N_\ell<4\log(2\cdot10^{1763.2}+1)<4(L_2+1763.2\log10)+10^{-1000}<16242.45$,
and for
$\log_{10}\ell\ge1763.3$, $\log N_\ell\ge4(L_2+1763.3\log10)>16243.36$. For
$\log_{10}\ell\ge3524.5$, $\log N_\ell>32464.6>H\log(2N_1^2)=-\log A$. The
expected
number of bad blocks among the $N_\ell$ blocks within distance $\ell$ of a
block is at most $N_\ell A$.
\end{proof}

The count of Theorem~\ref{thm:clustersizes} stops at $M_1$, and the factor
$L^4$ in its term $\epsilon_{M_1}$ cannot be removed: on every large
enough torus the clusters of the bad blocks percolate. Two facts give
this. Every block is bad with a conditional probability bounded below,
by the finite energy of the Wilson measure, and the separation of the
clusters grows with their size, which Proposition~\ref{prop:clusterreach}(i)
and Proposition~\ref{prop:separationneed} below show to be necessary.
What replaces the clusters of the torus are the clusters of the bad
blocks of a window. Lemma~\ref{lem:clusters}(i)--(iii) and their proofs
use of $g$ only that it is nondecreasing and nonnegative, and so does the
next lemma; for such $g$ the clusters are formed by~\eqref{eq:clusterrule}
and $\ell_m=R+2g(m)$.

\begin{lemma}[subsets and absorption]\label{lem:clustermono}
Let $g\ge0$ be nondecreasing.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item If $B'\subset B$ are finite sets of blocks, every cluster of $B'$
lies in a cluster of $B$.
\item If $C$ is a cluster of $B$ and $z\in B$ has $\dist(z,C)\le
R+g(\lvert C\rvert)$, then $z\in C$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(i) Let $\mathcal P$ be the partition of $B$ into its clusters and
$\mathcal P'$ the partition of $B'$ into the nonempty sets $U\cap B'$,
$U\in\mathcal P$. For distinct $U,V\in\mathcal P$ meeting $B'$,
\[
\begin{split}
\dist(U\cap B',V\cap B')&\ge\dist(U,V)>R+g(\lvert U\rvert)+g(\lvert
V\rvert)\\
&\ge R+g(\lvert U\cap B'\rvert)+g(\lvert V\cap B'\rvert),
\end{split}
\]
since $g$ is nondecreasing, so $\mathcal P'$ is a separated partition of
$B'$. The partition of $B'$ into its clusters is finer than $\mathcal P'$
by Lemma~\ref{lem:clusters}(i), so each cluster of $B'$ lies in some
$U\cap B'\subset U$.
(ii) If $z$ lay in a cluster $V\ne C$, then $\dist(C,V)\le\dist(z,C)\le
R+g(\lvert C\rvert)+g(\lvert V\rvert)$, against~\eqref{eq:clusterrule}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[clusters of a window]\label{lem:windowclusters}
Let $\Lambda$ be a set of blocks of the torus, and form the clusters of
$B\cap\Lambda$, with $g$ and the parameters of
Theorems~\ref{thm:clustercomparison} and~\ref{thm:clustersizes}. Each of
them lies in a cluster of $B$, and:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item Theorem~\ref{thm:clustercomparison} holds with $I_u=U_u$ for the
distinct clusters $U_u$ of $B\cap\Lambda$;
\item Theorem~\ref{thm:clustersizes} holds with $U(y)$ the cluster of $y$
in $B\cap\Lambda$, $I(y)$ the component of $y$ in $B\cap\Lambda$ at the
joining distance $2s+8$, and $L^4$ replaced by $\lvert\Lambda\rvert$, with
the same numbers.
\end{enumerate}
In a window $\Lambda$ of at most $10^{M_1/2}$ blocks, on a torus of any
size, no cluster of $B\cap\Lambda$ has more than $M_1$ blocks outside
probability $10^{-M_1/10}$, and for $s=1$ the expected number of blocks $y$
of $\Lambda$ with $U(y)\ne I(y)$ is at most $\lvert\Lambda\rvert
(10^{-28126}+10^{-M_1/10})$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The first assertion is Lemma~\ref{lem:clustermono}(i). (i) The proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:clustercomparison} uses of the clusters only that the
sets $U_u$ are distinct parts of a separated partition of a set of blocks
that contains every bad block of $\Lambda$, with $I_u=U_u\cap\Lambda$:
through Lemma~\ref{lem:clusters}(ii), through $\lvert I_u\rvert\le
\lvert U_u\rvert$, and through~\eqref{eq:clusterrule}. The clusters of
$B\cap\Lambda$ are such parts, with $I_u=U_u$. (ii) The proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:clustersizes}(i) uses that $U(y)$ is connected at
distance $\ell_m$, which Lemma~\ref{lem:clusters}(iii) gives for the
clusters of $B\cap\Lambda$, and bounds $\mu_L(S\subset B)$ for each set
$S$ it counts. In (ii), Lemma~\ref{lem:clusters}(iv) applied to
$B\cap\Lambda$ gives a set of bad blocks containing a block of $\Lambda$,
and the union bound runs over the $\lvert\Lambda\rvert$ blocks of
$\Lambda$. In (iii) an edge of $U(y)$ between blocks of different
components of $B\cap\Lambda$ has length between $2s+9$ and $\ell_{m_0}$,
as before. For the last assertion, (ii) gives at most $\lvert\Lambda
\rvert10^{-0.67M_1}\le10^{-0.17M_1}$, and (iii) with $m_0=10^5$ gives the
bound for each block of $\Lambda$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[one link makes a block bad]\label{lem:onelinkbad}
Let $G=\SU(2)$, let the labels have radius $r\le\frac1{10}$, let $B$ be
the set of bad blocks of a torus under $\mu_L$, with the coarse field
$c=V^\sharp(U)$ of the configuration, and put $p_0=\frac12e^{-12\beta_W}$.
Let $\xi$ be a random set of blocks that contains each block
independently with probability $p_0$. Then $\mu_L(B\in\mathcal E)\ge
\mathbb P(\xi\in\mathcal E)$ for every increasing event $\mathcal E$, that
is, every set of sets of blocks that contains each superset of each of
its members.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
In the tree gauge $\mu_L$ has density proportional to $\exp(\beta_W
\sum_p\frac12\ReTr U_p)$ with respect to the product of the Haar measures
on the active links (Sec.~\ref{ssec:pathblocks}). For a block $y$ let $k=
(y,1)$, with path link $\ell_k=U_{2y+e_1,1}$, let $f_y$ be the link
$(2y+e_1+e_2,1)$, a non-path private link of $k$, and put
\[
G_y=\bigl\{d(U_{f_y},\ell_k)>r+\tfrac\pi3\bigr\}.
\]
\emph{$G_y$ makes $y$ bad.} The link $(2y,1)$ is a tree link, so
$P_{2y}=\ell_k$, and by~\eqref{eq:cutoff} $c_k=\ell_ke^Y$ with $Y=\frac{
\chi_k}{16}\sum_x\log(\ell_k^{-1}P_x)$. If $\chi_k=0$, $c_k=\ell_k$. If
$\chi_k>0$, then $\delta(\ell_k^{-1}P_x,I)=\delta(P_x,\ell_k)<\rho_G=1$ for
every $x$, so $\lVert\log(\ell_k^{-1}P_x)\rVert<\pi/3$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:logbound}, and $\lVert Y\rVert<\pi/3$; the eigenvalues of
$Y$ are $\pm i\theta$ with $\theta<\pi$, so $\log e^Y=Y$ and $d(c_k,
\ell_k)<\pi/3$. The reconstruction value of $f_y$ is $c_k$, and on $G_y$
\[
d(U_{f_y},c_k)\ge d(U_{f_y},\ell_k)-d(\ell_k,c_k)>r ,
\]
so $y$ is bad.

\emph{One link.} The link $f_y$ lies in six plaquettes, each contributing
$\beta_W\frac12\ReTr U_p\in[-\beta_W,\beta_W]$ to the exponent, so given
all the other active links the law of $U_{f_y}$ has a density with respect
to the Haar measure whose values lie within a factor $e^{12\beta_W}$ of
each other, hence a density at least $e^{-12\beta_W}$, and $G_y$ is the
complement of the ball of radius $r+\pi/3$ about $\ell_k$. For $\SU(2)$, by
Lemma~\ref{lem:haarsu2} and bi-invariance a ball of radius $\sqrt2\,t$
has Haar measure at most $\frac{2t^3}{3\pi}$. With $r+\pi/3\le1.15$, $t\le0.82$ and the measure is at most
$2\cdot0.552/(3\pi)<\frac12$. So the conditional probability of $G_y$
given all the other active links is at least $p_0$.

\emph{The coupling.} Enumerate the blocks as $y_1,\dots,y_n$ and put
$X_j=\mathbf 1_{G_{y_j}}$. The event $G_y$ depends only on the two private
links $\ell_k$ and $U_{f_y}$ of the pair $(y,1)$, which belong to no other
pair, so $X_1,\dots,X_{j-1}$ are functions of the active links other than
$U_{f_{y_j}}$, and $\mathbb P(X_j=1\mid X_1,\dots,X_{j-1})\ge p_0$. Let
$V_1,\dots,V_n$ be independent and uniform on $[0,1]$, and put
recursively $X'_j=\mathbf 1[V_j\le\mathbb P(X_j=1\mid X_{<j}=X'_{<j})]$
and $Y_j=\mathbf 1[V_j\le p_0]$. By induction on $j$ the vector $X'$ has
the law of $X$, while $Y_j\le X'_j$ and the $Y_j$ are independent with
mean $p_0$. With $G=\{y:X_y=1\}\subset B$, for increasing $\mathcal E$,
$\mu_L(B\in\mathcal E)\ge\mu_L(G\in\mathcal E)=\mathbb P(X'\in\mathcal E)
\ge\mathbb P(Y\in\mathcal E)$.
\end{proof}

The next theorem is about independent bad blocks of any density and any
separation that grows at least logarithmically. Two blocks of a cube of
side $a$, a translate of $\{0,\dots,a-1\}^4$, and of a neighbouring cube
of the same grid, one whose grid index differs by at most one in each
coordinate, are at distance at most $2a-1$.

\begin{theorem}[the clusters percolate]\label{thm:clusterpercolation}
Let $g\ge0$ be nondecreasing, $R\ge1$, $\gamma>0$, $c_0\ge0$, and suppose
$R+g(m)\ge\gamma\log m-c_0$ for every $m\ge1$.\footnote{The proof is a multiscale construction: the occupied boxes of
one scale are the sites of the next, and joining distances that grow like
the logarithm of the size connect them, as in hierarchical and long-range
percolation.} Let $0<p<1$ and let $\xi$
be a random set of blocks of a torus of side $L$ that contains each block
independently with probability $p$. Let $a_0\ge2$ be an integer with
$\gamma pa_0^3\ge24$ and $pa_0^4\ge23+4c_0/\gamma$, put $M_0=\lceil
e^{(2a_0+c_0)/\gamma}\rceil$ and, for $j\ge1$,
\begin{gather*}
K_j=\bigl\lfloor e^{pa_{j-1}^4/8}\bigr\rfloor,\qquad a_j=\bigl\lfloor
\gamma pa_{j-1}^4/8\bigr\rfloor,\\
\ell_j=\max\{M_0,K_ja_{j-1}\}.
\end{gather*}
Then $a_j\ge2a_{j-1}$, and $K_j$ and $\ell_j$ increase to infinity. For
$J\ge1$, $L\ge\ell_J$, a block $y$, $Q=y+\{0,\dots,\ell_J-1\}^4$ and a set
$\Lambda\supset Q$ of blocks, there is an event that depends only on
$\xi\cap Q$, of probability at least $\frac12p^{M_0}$, on which the
cluster of $y$ in $\xi\cap\Lambda$ contains the $M_0$ blocks $y+ie_1$,
$0\le i<M_0$, and has at least $K_J^4$ blocks.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
\emph{The scales.} Write $a=a_{j-1}$. Since $\lfloor t\rfloor\ge t-1$ and
$\gamma pa^3\ge24$, $a_j\ge\gamma pa^4/8-1\ge3a-1\ge2a$, so $pa_j^4\ge
16pa^4$ and $\gamma pa_j^3\ge\gamma pa^3$; by induction $pa_j^4\ge
23\cdot16^j$, both conditions on $a_0$ hold for every $a_j$, and $K_j$ and
$\ell_j$ increase to infinity. As $e^{pa^4/8}\ge1$ and $\lfloor t\rfloor
\ge t/2$ for $t\ge1$, $\log K_j\ge pa^4/8-\log2$, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:percreach}
\gamma\log K_j^4-c_0\ge\frac{\gamma pa^4}2-4\gamma\log2-c_0\ge
\frac{\gamma pa^4}4\ge2a_j-1 ,
\end{equation}
the middle step by $pa^4\ge16\log2+4c_0/\gamma$, as $16\log2<12$. The
boxes $y+\{0,\dots,K_ja_{j-1}-1\}^4$ and the segment $S_0=\{y+ie_1:0\le
i<M_0\}$ lie in $Q$, which $L\ge\ell_J$ embeds in the torus, and the distance of
the torus is at most that of $\Z^4$.

\emph{The events.} Let $E_0=\{S_0\subset\xi\}$. For $1\le j\le J$ divide
$y+\{0,\dots,K_ja_{j-1}-1\}^4$ into $K_j^4$ cubes of side $a_{j-1}$, the
first of which contains $y$, and let $E_j$ be the event that each of them
contains a block of $\xi\setminus S_0$. These events depend on $\xi\cap
Q$, $E_0$ on $\xi\cap S_0$ and the others on $\xi\cap(Q\setminus S_0)$. A
cube of side $a$ meets $S_0$ in at most $a$ blocks, so
\[
\mathbb P(E_j^c)\le K_j^4(1-p)^{a^4-a}\le e^{pa^4/2-pa^4+pa}\le
e^{-pa^4/4},
\]
as $a^3\ge4$. Summing, $\sum_{j\ge1}\mathbb P(E_j^c)\le\sum_{i\ge0}
e^{-23\cdot16^i/4}<e^{-5.75}(1+e^{-80})<0.004$, since $e^{5.75}>
e^5\cdot2>296$. By independence, $\mathbb P(E_0\cap\dots\cap E_J)\ge
p^{M_0}(1-0.004)\ge\frac12p^{M_0}$.

\emph{The cluster.} On this event let $C$ be the cluster of $y$ in
$\xi\cap\Lambda$. Consecutive blocks of $S_0$ are at distance $1\le R$,
so $S_0\subset C$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:clusters}(ii), and $R+g(\lvert C\rvert)
\ge\gamma\log M_0-c_0\ge2a_0$. Suppose $R+g(\lvert C\rvert)\ge2a_{j-1}-1$
for some $1\le j\le J$. Order the cubes of $E_j$ so that each is a
neighbour of an earlier one, the first containing $y$, and in each cube
other than the first choose a block of $\xi\setminus S_0$. If the earlier
cubes contain blocks of $C$, the chosen block of the next cube lies within
distance $2a_{j-1}-1\le R+g(\lvert C\rvert)$ of $C$, so it lies in $C$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:clustermono}(ii). Hence every cube contains a block of
$C$, $\lvert C\rvert\ge K_j^4$, and $R+g(\lvert C\rvert)\ge\gamma\log
K_j^4-c_0\ge2a_j-1$ by~\eqref{eq:percreach}. Induction on $j$ gives
$\lvert C\rvert\ge K_J^4$.
\end{proof}

Fig.~\ref{fig:percolation} draws the construction and the clusters of a window.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.95\textwidth]{figures/fig_percolation.png}
\caption{Clusters of bad blocks, schematic, in three of the four dimensions.
(a)~The hierarchical construction of Theorem~\ref{thm:clusterpercolation}:
bad blocks grouped into clusters of the first level in boxes of side
$a_1$, and these joined into one cluster of the second level in a box of
side $a_2$; the joining distance grows like the logarithm of the size.
(b)~A window $\Lambda$ of the torus: a cluster of the torus that crosses
its boundary is cut into clusters of the window, the units of
Lemma~\ref{lem:windowclusters}.}
\label{fig:percolation}
\end{figure*}

\begin{corollary}[the bad blocks percolate]\label{cor:clusterpercolation}
Let $G=\SU(2)$, $r\le\frac1{10}$, $\beta_W>0$, and let $B$ be the set of
bad blocks of a torus of side $L$ under $\mu_L$. Let $g$, $R$, $\gamma$
and $c_0$ be as in Theorem~\ref{thm:clusterpercolation}, which for the
clusters of Definition~\ref{def:clusters} holds with $\gamma=3/\kappa$
and $c_0=0$, and let $p=p_0=\frac12e^{-12\beta_W}$, with $a_0$, $M_0$,
$K_j$, $\ell_j$ as there. Then for every $J\ge1$ and $L\ge\ell_J$:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item for every block $y$ and every $\Lambda\supset y+\{0,\dots,\ell_J-1\}
^4$, in particular the torus, the cluster of $y$ in $B\cap\Lambda$ has at
least $\max\{M_0,K_J^4\}$ blocks with probability at least
$\frac12p_0^{M_0}$;
\item if $n\ge1$ is an integer with $n\ell_J\le L$, some cluster of $B$
has at least $K_J^4$ blocks with probability at least $1-(1-\frac12p_0^{
M_0})^{n^4}$.
\end{enumerate}
Hence, for every $K$, $\mu_L\{y\in B,\ \lvert U(y)\rvert>K\}\ge\frac12
p_0^{M_0}$ on every large enough torus, and the probability that some
cluster has more than $K$ blocks tends to one as $L\to\infty$. With
$\gamma=3/\kappa$, $c_0=0$ and $a_0=\lceil\max\{(24/(\gamma p_0))^{1/3},
(23/p_0)^{1/4},2\}\rceil$, if $\kappa\ge2.5\cdot10^{-4}$ and $\beta_W\ge
10^{37}$, then $\log M_0>e^{10^{37}}$, so $M_0>M_1=10^{10^{1700}}$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
For a set $\Lambda$ and a block $y$ the event that $y\in B$ and the
cluster of $y$ in $B\cap\Lambda$ has at least $K$ blocks is increasing,
by Lemma~\ref{lem:clustermono}(i), and so is the event that some cluster
of $B$ has at least $K$ blocks. (i) is Lemma~\ref{lem:onelinkbad} and
Theorem~\ref{thm:clusterpercolation}. (ii) Choose $n^4$ disjoint
translates $Q_i=y_i+\{0,\dots,\ell_J-1\}^4$. The events of
Theorem~\ref{thm:clusterpercolation} for $(y_i,Q_i,\Lambda=Q_i)$ depend on
disjoint parts of $\xi$, so they are independent; on each, the cluster of
$y_i$ in $\xi\cap Q_i$ has at least $K_J^4$ blocks, and it lies in a
cluster of $\xi$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:clustermono}(i). Then apply
Lemma~\ref{lem:onelinkbad}. The consequence follows since $K_J\to\infty$.
For the numbers, $a_0\ge(24/(\gamma p_0))^{1/3}=(48/\gamma)^{1/3}e^{4
\beta_W}$ and $\log M_0\ge2a_0/\gamma$. With $\gamma\le12000$, $2/\gamma
\ge1/6000$ and $(48/\gamma)^{1/3}\ge250^{-1/3}>\frac17$, so $\log M_0>e^{4
\beta_W}/42000>e^{4\beta_W-11}\ge e^{10^{37}}$, while $\log M_1=10^{1700}
\log10<10^{1701}<e^{10^{37}}$.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:clustersizes} is not affected: its bound (i) concerns
clusters of at most $M_1$ blocks, while the clusters of
Corollary~\ref{cor:clusterpercolation} have more than $M_0>M_1$ blocks, and
its bound (ii) grows with $L^4$. The corollary shows that this growth is
not an artefact of the union bound. The next proposition shows that no
choice of the separation avoids it while keeping the island sums
bounded.

\begin{proposition}[the separation the sums need]\label{prop:separationneed}
Let $g\ge0$ be nondecreasing, $R\ge2s+8$ with $R>2g(1)$, and form the
clusters with~\eqref{eq:clusterrule}. For $m\ge1$ put $h=R+\lfloor g(m)+
g(1)\rfloor+1$, and on a torus of side at least $2(m+2)(h+1)$ let the bad
blocks be $u_i=iRe_1$ and $v_i=u_i+(-1)^ihe_2$, $1\le i\le m$. Then the
clusters are $U=\{u_1,\dots,u_m\}$ and $V_i=\{v_i\}$, and with
$\bar\varDelta$ for clusters as in Proposition~\ref{prop:clusterreach} and
$c_2=b_*\cdot45(2s+7)^4e^{-2\alpha_G(R+g(1)-2s-8)}$,
\[
\sum_i\bar\varDelta_{UV_i}\ge c_2\,m^{3/2}e^{-2\alpha_Gg(m)} .
\]
If these sums are at most $\tau_g$ for every $m$, then $R+g(m)\ge\gamma
\log m-c_0$ for every $m$, with $\gamma=3/(4\alpha_G)$ and $c_0=\max\{0,
(2\alpha_G)^{-1}\log(\tau_g/c_2)\}$, and the conclusions of
Corollary~\ref{cor:clusterpercolation} hold for these clusters.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The distances are $\dist(u_i,u_j)=\lvert i-j\rvert R$, $\dist(v_i,u_j)=
\max\{\lvert i-j\rvert R,h\}$, and $\dist(v_i,v_j)\ge\min\{2R,2h\}=2R$ for
$i\ne j$, since $v_i$ and $v_j$ differ by $2h$ in the direction $e_2$ when
$i-j$ is odd; the side of the torus exceeds $2mR$ and $4h$, so these are
the distances on the torus. The partition into $U$ and the $V_i$ is
separated: $\dist(U,V_i)=h>R+g(m)+g(1)$ and $\dist(V_i,V_j)\ge2R>R+2g(1)$.
Consecutive $u_i$ are at distance $R$, so they lie in one cluster by
Lemma~\ref{lem:clusters}(ii); hence $U$ is a cluster, and the finest
separated partition is this one. The neighbourhoods of radius $s+3$ of the
$u_i$ are disjoint, since $R>2s+6$, so $\bar n_U=45m(2s+7)^4$ and $\bar
n_{V_i}=45(2s+7)^4$, and $w_{UV_i}=h-1\le R+g(m)+g(1)$. So $\bar\varDelta
_{UV_i}\ge c_2\sqrt m\,e^{-2\alpha_Gg(m)}$ for each of the $m$ values of
$i$. If the sums are at most $\tau_g$, then $2\alpha_Gg(m)\ge\frac32\log m-
\log(\tau_g/c_2)$, which with $R\ge0$ gives the condition of
Theorem~\ref{thm:clusterpercolation}.
\end{proof}

For the clusters of Definition~\ref{def:clusters}, $g(m)=(3/\kappa)\log m$
with $\kappa\le2\alpha_G$ exceeds $(3/(4\alpha_G))\log m$, as
Theorem~\ref{thm:clustercomparison} needs. So every separation rule of the
form~\eqref{eq:clusterrule} that bounds the island sums uniformly in the
configuration produces clusters that percolate, by
Corollary~\ref{cor:clusterpercolation}, and no bound on the size of the
clusters of the torus is uniform in the torus. The clusters of a window
replace them: by Lemma~\ref{lem:windowclusters} the comparison of
Theorem~\ref{thm:clustercomparison} holds with the clusters of
$B\cap\Lambda$ as units, and in a window of at most $10^{M_1/2}$ blocks
their size is bounded uniformly in the torus. The size of the window
enters only through the term $\lvert\Lambda\rvert10^{-0.67M_1}$, and it
cannot be removed: by the proof of
Corollary~\ref{cor:clusterpercolation}(ii), in a window that contains $n^4$
disjoint boxes of side $\ell_1$ some cluster of $B\cap\Lambda$ has at
least $M_0>M_1$ blocks with probability at least $1-(1-\frac12p_0^{M_0})
^{n^4}$. The covariance of the conditional
probabilities of the labels, the term of Proposition~\ref{prop:hiddenbit},
is not touched by the clusters.

\subsection{The comparison across one step and the conditional iteration}\label{ssec:iterate}

This subsection settles the constants of the comparison between the coarse
action $A_1$ of Sec.~\ref{ssec:lfstep} and $\lambda$ times the coarse
curvature $Q_1$, and states the iteration over scales as a conditional
theorem. The factor $C_*$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:lfaction}(i) is replaced by
$2956$ for every coarse field and by $1/\theta(\kappa_0)=1+O(\kappa_0)$
for the coarse plaquettes below $\kappa_1$, which is about $0.19\,\kappa_0$ for small $\kappa_0$. No two-sided comparison of
$A_1$ with $\lambda Q_1$ has a ratio of constants below $4t_L^2$, which
tends to $4$: the factor four between the block-spin form and the coarse
curvature is attained by a staggered coarse field and is intrinsic. The
conditional theorem names one-step hypotheses $(\mathrm H_k)$, proves that
they compose when their relative errors are summable, and locates the
couplings at which the large-field estimates of Sec.~\ref{ssec:lfstep}
stop. Throughout, $G=\SU(2)$, $L=2^m\ge32$, and the notation is that of
Sec.~\ref{ssec:lfstep}.

\emph{Norms.} For $g\in\SU(2)$ with angle $2x$, $\delta(g,I)=2\sqrt2\sin x$
and $\lVert\log g\rVert=2\sqrt2\,x$ (Sec.~\ref{ssec:witnessradius}), so
$\delta(g,I)\le\lVert\log g\rVert$, and the ratio $x/\sin x$ increases with
$x$. If $\delta(g,I)\le\kappa_0\le10^{-3}$, then $x\le1.001\sin x$, $x^2\le
1.002\,\kappa_0^2/8$ and $(x/\sin x)^2\le(1-x^2/6)^{-2}\le1+x^2/2.98$, so
\begin{equation}\label{eq:iteratenorm}
\lVert\log g\rVert^2\le\Bigl(1+\frac{\kappa_0^2}{20}\Bigr)\delta(g,I)^2,
\qquad
\lVert\log g\rVert\le\Bigl(1+\frac{\kappa_0^2}{40}\Bigr)\kappa_0 .
\end{equation}
For $0<\kappa_0\le9.99\cdot10^{-4}$ put
\begin{gather*}
\theta(\kappa_0)=\Bigl[\Bigl(1+\frac{\kappa_0^2}{20}\Bigr)\bigl(1+6031\,
\kappa_0\bigr)^2\Bigr]^{-1},\\
\kappa_1=\frac{\kappa_0}{\sqrt{28\,\theta(\kappa_0)}} .
\end{gather*}
Then $\theta(\kappa_0)\ge1-12063\,\kappa_0$, since $(1+u)^{-2}\ge1-2u$, and
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\hline
$\kappa_0$ & $\theta(\kappa_0)$ & $\kappa_1/\kappa_0$\\
\hline
$10^{-4}$ & $0.38911\ldots$ & $0.30296\ldots$\\
$10^{-6}$ & $0.98804\ldots$ & $0.19012\ldots$\\
$10^{-8}$ & $0.99987\ldots$ & $0.18899\ldots$\\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\begin{theorem}[comparison constants of one step]\label{thm:stepconstants}
For every coarse field $c$ on the torus:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item $S_1(c)\ge Q_1(c)/2956$, and $A_1(c)\ge\lambda Q_1(c)/2956-4|T|
\log M$;
\item for $0<\kappa_0\le9.99\cdot10^{-4}$,
\[
S_1(c)\ge\theta(\kappa_0)\sum_P\min\bigl\{\delta(c_P,I)^2,\kappa_1^2
\bigr\},
\]
and $A_1(c)$ is at least $\lambda$ times the right side minus $4|T|\log
M$; in particular, if $\delta(c_P,I)\le\kappa_1$ for every coarse
plaquette, $A_1(c)\ge\theta(\kappa_0)\lambda Q_1(c)-4|T|\log M$;
\item for $\lambda\ge100$ and $\eta>0$, $A_1(c)\le4(1+\eta)\lambda Q_1(c)
+c_1(\lambda,\eta)|T|$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(i) Every $U\in F_c$ is in the tree gauge and has $V^\sharp(U)=c$, so
Theorem~\ref{thm:cutoff}(ii) gives $Q_1(c)\le(8+2688\pi^2/9)Q(U)$, and
$8+2688\pi^2/9<2956$. Take the infimum over $F_c$ and use the first
inequality of Theorem~\ref{thm:lfaction}(i).

(ii) Let $U\in F_c$ and let $\mathcal B$ be the set of fine plaquettes
with $\delta(U_p,I)>\kappa_0$. For a coarse plaquette $P$ with sides $\ell
\subset P$ let $D(P)$ be the union of the squares $\square_{2y+o}$ and of
the sets $\mathcal U_\ell$ of the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:smallstep}. That
proof uses its hypothesis on $P$ only through the plaquettes of $D(P)$: the
cut-off of a side $\ell$ depends on the paths of $\ell$, whose surfaces
lie in $\mathcal U_\ell$, and $K_{P,o}$ is the holonomy of $\square_{2y+o}$.
Let $\mathcal P_1$ be the coarse plaquettes with $D(P)\cap\mathcal B=
\emptyset$ and $\mathcal P_2$ the others. Let $E_{\rm g}$ and $Q_{\rm g}$
be the sums of $\lVert\Theta_p\rVert^2$ and of $\delta(U_p,I)^2$ over the
fine plaquettes off $\mathcal B$. By~\eqref{eq:iteratenorm} these have
$\lVert\Theta_p\rVert\le\eta:=(1+\kappa_0^2/40)\kappa_0<10^{-3}$, and
$E_{\rm g}\le(1+\kappa_0^2/20)Q_{\rm g}$.

For $P\in\mathcal P_1$ the first part of the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:smallstep} applies with this $\eta$ and gives the two
inequalities of~\eqref{eq:smallstep} and $r_P\le28.26\,\eta$. Its
summation, restricted to $\mathcal P_1$, involves only plaquettes off
$\mathcal B$, and its multiplicities (a plaquette in four squares
$\square_x$, in at most four sets $\mathcal U_\ell$, a coarse link in six
coarse plaquettes) do not grow under the restriction. The triangle
inequality for the Euclidean norm over $\mathcal P_1$ therefore gives
\[
\Bigl(\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_1}\lVert\log c_P\rVert^2\Bigr)^{1/2}\le(1+6030
\,\eta)\,E_{\rm g}^{1/2}.
\]
Since $6030\,\eta\le6031\,\kappa_0$ and $\delta(c_P,I)\le\lVert\log c_P
\rVert$,
\[
\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_1}\delta(c_P,I)^2\le\theta(\kappa_0)^{-1}Q_{\rm g}.
\]
A fine plaquette lies in $\square_{2y+o}$ for at most four pairs $(P,o)$,
since the pairs are in bijection with the squares $\square_x$, and in
$\mathcal U_\ell$ for at most four coarse links, each a side of six coarse
plaquettes. So it lies in $D(P)$ for at most $28$ coarse plaquettes, and
$|\mathcal P_2|\le28|\mathcal B|$. Hence
\begin{align*}
Q(U)&=Q_{\rm g}+\sum_{p\in\mathcal B}\delta(U_p,I)^2\\
&\ge\theta(\kappa_0)\sum_{P\in\mathcal P_1}\delta(c_P,I)^2+\frac{
\kappa_0^2}{28}\,|\mathcal P_2| .
\end{align*}
Each term of $\theta\sum_P\min\{\delta(c_P,I)^2,\kappa_1^2\}$ is at most
the corresponding term on the right, as $\theta\kappa_1^2=\kappa_0^2/28$.
Take the infimum over $F_c$ and apply Theorem~\ref{thm:lfaction}(i).

(iii) Theorem~\ref{thm:lfaction}(ii) with $U=R(c)$, which is regular, and
$Q(R(c))=4Q_1(c)$.
\end{proof}

The constant $2956$ of (i) is less than $C_*/555$. Part (ii) is the
small-field form: the coarse plaquettes below $\kappa_1\approx0.19\,
\kappa_0$ are compared with the factor $\theta(\kappa_0)$, which tends to
one with $\kappa_0$, and every larger coarse plaquette costs at least
$\theta\kappa_1^2=\kappa_0^2/28$. The upper constant $4$ of (iii) and the
lower constant $\theta(\kappa_0)$ of (ii) cannot be brought together, by
the next theorem.

For a real field $\gamma$ on the coarse links of the torus let
\[
q_1(\gamma)=\min\Bigl\{\sum_p(d\varphi)_p^2:\varphi\ \text{real on the
links of}\ \Lambda_L,\ V(\varphi)=\gamma\Bigr\},
\]
the linear block-spin form, with $V$ the block average of
Definition~\ref{def:blockgauge} and the curvature $(d\varphi)_p=\varphi_
\mu(x)+\varphi_\nu(x+e_\mu)-\varphi_\mu(x+e_\nu)-\varphi_\nu(x)$. By
Proposition~\ref{prop:effective}(i), whose proof applies on every lattice,
$q_1\ge Q_1$. Let $s(y)=(-1)^{y_0+y_1}$ and define $\gamma_B$ by
$\gamma_{B,(y,0)}=s(y)$, $\gamma_{B,(y,1)}=-s(y)$ and zero in the
directions $2,3$; let $n=L/2$ and $\gamma_A$ equal $\cos(2\pi y_0/n)$ on
the coarse links $(y,1)$ and zero on the others. Put $t_L=\frac34+\frac14
\cos(4\pi/L)$ and $f(u)=4(1-\cos(u/\sqrt2))$, so that $\delta(e^{u\tau},I)^2=
f(u)$ for $\lVert\tau\rVert=1$ and $u^2(1-u^2/24)\le f(u)\le u^2$.

\begin{theorem}[the factor four is intrinsic]\label{thm:stepsharp}
Let $\tau\in\g$ with $\lVert\tau\rVert=1$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)},leftmargin=*]
\item $q_1(\gamma_B)=64|T|=4\,Q_1(\gamma_B)$, attained at the field
$\varphi^*(\gamma_B)$ of Proposition~\ref{prop:effective}(ii), and $q_1(
\gamma_A)\le t_L^{-2}Q_1(\gamma_A)$.
\item There is $C$, depending on $L$, such that $c^\varepsilon=e^{
\varepsilon\tau\gamma_B}$ has $Q_1(c^\varepsilon)=|T|f(4\varepsilon)\le16
\varepsilon^2|T|$ and $S_1(c^\varepsilon)\ge(64-C\varepsilon)\varepsilon^2
|T|$ for $0<\varepsilon\le C^{-1}$.
\item For $0<\varepsilon\le C^{-1}$ the field $c_\varepsilon=e^{\varepsilon
\tau\gamma_A}$ has a regular $U_\varepsilon\in F_{c_\varepsilon}$ with
$Q(U_\varepsilon)\le t_L^{-2}(1+C\varepsilon^2)\,Q_1(c_\varepsilon)$.
\item If $a,b>0$ and $e(\lambda)$ with $e(\lambda)/\lambda\to0$ satisfy
\[
a\lambda Q_1(c)-e(\lambda)\le A_1(c)\le b\lambda Q_1(c)+e(\lambda)
\]
for every $c$ and every $\lambda\ge100$, then $b\ge4$ and $a\le t_L^{-2}$.
So $b/a\ge4t_L^2$, which is above $3.849$ for $L\ge32$ and tends to $4$.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
(i) Write $\varphi^*=\varphi^*(\gamma_B)$, equal to $\gamma_{B,(y,\mu)}$
on the links $(x,\mu)$, $x\in B(y)$, $o_\mu=1$, and to zero elsewhere. By
Proposition~\ref{prop:effective}(ii), $V(\varphi^*)=\gamma_B$ and $\sum_p(
d\varphi^*)_p^2=4Q_1(\gamma_B)$, and its curvature is $(d\gamma_B)_P$ on the
four plaquettes at $x\in B(y)$ with $o_\mu=o_\nu=1$ and zero elsewhere.
Here $(d\gamma_B)_P=4s(y)$ in the plane $\{0,1\}$, since $s$ changes sign
under $e_0$ and $e_1$, and zero in the other planes, so $Q_1(\gamma_B)=
16|T|$. We claim
\begin{equation}\label{eq:kktidentity}
d^{\mathsf T}d\varphi^*=4\varphi^*=V^{\mathsf T}(32\,\gamma_B).
\end{equation}
Only plaquettes in the plane $\{0,1\}$ are curved. For the link $(x,0)$
the plaquettes at $x$ and at $x-e_1$ in that plane enter with signs $+$
and $-$; the first is $4s(y)$ when $o_0=o_1=1$, and the second is
